en: The Expanded Version of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of India, together with Dharmagupta, during the Sui Dynasty. 1.
The Introduction: The First Chapter, the Introduction to the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma Sutra.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, who had attained their own benefit, who had ended the fetters of existence, and whose minds had attained mastery. Their names were as follows:

Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Aniruddha, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja, Bakula, Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Sundarananda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Ānanda, Rāhula—such were the great arhats, renowned to all.
Furthermore, there were two thousand monks, both those still in training and those beyond training.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was present with her retinue of six thousand,
as was the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, together with her own retinue.

There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they had all attained dhāraṇīs and possessed the eloquence of joyful exposition, turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Having made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, he planted the roots of all virtues in the presence of those Buddhas and was constantly praised by them.
Cultivating his body with loving-kindness, he skillfully entered the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Having attained mastery of great wisdom and reached the other shore,
their fame was heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and they were able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
Their names were as follows:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Nityodyukta Bodhisattva, Anikṣiptadhura Bodhisattva, Ratnapāṇi Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Sūradatta Bodhisattva, Ratnacandra Bodhisattva, Candraprabha Bodhisattva, Pūrṇacandra Bodhisattva, Mahābala Bodhisattva, Anantabala Bodhisattva, Trailokyavikrama Bodhisattva, Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Ratnākara Bodhisattva, and Vinayaka Bodhisattva—these and other such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, numbering eighty thousand, were all present together.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra was present together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras.

Also present were the devaputra Candraruci, the devaputra Samantagandha, the devaputra Ratnaprabha, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each accompanied by their own retinues of ten thousand devaputras;
as well as the devaputra Īśvara and the devaputra Maheśvara, each accompanied by their own retinues of thirty thousand devaputras.
The Brahmā King Śikhin, Lord of the Sahā World, together with Mahābrahmā Prabhāsa and others, accompanied by his retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.

There were eight dragon kings—Nanda Dragon King, Upananda Dragon King, Sāgara Dragon King, Vāsuki Dragon King, Takṣaka Dragon King, Anavatapta Dragon King, Mānasa Dragon King, and Utpala Dragon King—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
There were four kinnara kings—Dharmakinnara-rāja, Sudharmakinnara-rāja, Mahādharmakinnara-rāja, and Dharmadhārakinnara-rāja—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
There were four gandharva kings—Gandharvarāja Rati, Gandharvarāja Ratigvara, Gandharvarāja Surati, and Gandharvarāja Surativara—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
There were four asura kings—Asura King Bāli, Asura King Kharaskandha, Asura King Vemacitrin, and Asura King Rāhu—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

There were four garuḍa kings—the Garuḍa King of Great Majestic Virtue, the Garuḍa King of Great Body, the Garuḍa King of Great Fulfillment, and the Garuḍa King of Sovereign Power—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of attendants, each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, revered, honored, and praised him. For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings, the Dharma for Bodhisattvas, Protected and Mindful of by the Buddhas*.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings, his body and mind unmoving.

At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly; the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways.

At that time, within the assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; as well as minor kings and universal monarchs—all these great multitudes attained what they had never experienced before. With joy, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction without exception; reaching downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it allowed all beings within these worlds to see clearly the six realms of existence in those lands.
Furthermore, they saw the Buddhas currently residing in those lands and heard the sūtras and teachings expounded by those Buddhas;
they also saw the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās there who were practicing the path and had attained realization.
Furthermore, he saw various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the bodhisattva path through various causes and conditions, various faiths and understandings, and various manifestations;
he also saw various Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa;
and he further saw, after those Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, the construction of stupas made of the seven treasures using their relics.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought:
"Now the World-Honored One has manifested these signs of supernatural transformation; by what causes and conditions does this auspicious omen exist?
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered into samādhi; this is an inconceivable manifestation of a rare event. Whom should I ask about it?"
"Who is able to answer?
He further thought to himself:

"This is Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, who has already drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past; he must surely have seen this rare and marvelous sign. I shall now question him."
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, all had this thought:
"This is the mark of the Buddha’s radiance and supernormal power; whom should we now ask about it?"

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts and also observing the minds of the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as the multitude of devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, asked Mañjuśrī:

"By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared, emitting a great radiance that illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, such that the adornments of those Buddha-fields are all clearly seen?"
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
“Mañjuśrī! For what reason does the Teacher’s white tuft between his eyebrows emit a great light that shines everywhere?”
Mandāravas and Mañjūṣakas rain down; sandalwood-scented breezes gladden the hearts of all.
By these causes and conditions, the earth is everywhere adorned and purified; and this world shakes in six ways.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was filled with joy; their bodies and minds were refreshed, having attained what they had never experienced before.
From between his eyebrows, a radiance shone forth, illuminating eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, all of which became the color of gold.
Reaching upward as far as the Peak of Existence, throughout all worlds, one sees therein all that beings in the six realms of existence undergo in their cycles of birth and death;
the causal conditions of their good and evil karma, and the beauty or ugliness of the retributions they receive—
all this is clearly perceived.
Furthermore, I behold the Buddhas, the holy sovereigns and lions,
who expound the sutras, supreme and subtle;
their voices are pure, emitting sounds that are gentle and soft.
He instructs countless billions of bodhisattvas;
his Brahma-voice is profound and wondrous, causing all to delight in hearing it,
as he expounds the True Dharma in each of their worlds.
Through various causes and conditions, and by means of immeasurable parables,
he illuminates the Buddha-dharma and awakens sentient beings.
If there are those who encounter suffering and grow weary of old age, sickness, and death;
For them, he preaches nirvāṇa, the end of all suffering.
If there are those with merit who have previously made offerings to the Buddha and aspire to seek the supreme Dharma, for them he preaches the path of the pratyekabuddha.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices and seek unsurpassed wisdom, for them I shall expound the pure path. Mañjuśrī!
I dwell here; having seen and heard such things, as well as thousands of billions of other matters—so numerous in kind—I shall now briefly describe them:
I see in that land bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.
Some practice giving, joyfully bestowing gold, silver, coral, pearls, mani-jewels,
musaragalva, agate, diamond, and all manner of rare treasures; slaves, vehicles,
and precious decorated litters and carriages, dedicating these merits toward the Buddha-way.
May they obtain this vehicle, the foremost in the three realms, praised by all Buddhas.
There may be bodhisattvas who give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, adorned with railings, flowered canopies,
and elegant ornaments.
Again I see Bodhisattvas who, seeking the unsurpassed path, give away their own flesh, hands, feet, wives, and children;
I also see Bodhisattvas who, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, joyfully and gladly give away their heads, eyes, bodies, and limbs.
Mañjuśrī! I have seen various kings go to the presence of the Buddha to inquire about the unsurpassed path;
they then abandon their pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and consorts, shave off their hair and beards, and don the dharma robes.
In some instances, one sees a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in quietude and delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.
One also sees a bodhisattva who, with courageous diligence, enters deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, I see those who have detached from desire, dwelling perpetually in seclusion, deeply cultivating meditative concentration, and attaining the five supernormal powers.
I also see bodhisattvas, settled in dhyāna with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with tens of millions of verses.
Furthermore, I see bodhisattvas whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm; they are able to question the Buddhas and, having heard [the teachings], receive and uphold them all.
Using immeasurable parables, they expound the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes, delighting in the preaching of the Dharma.
They transform all bodhisattvas, shatter the hosts of Māra, and beat the Dharma drum.
Furthermore, they see bodhisattvas sitting in silent tranquility; though devas and nāgas pay them reverence, they feel no joy.
Furthermore, I see Bodhisattvas dwelling in forests, emitting light to rescue those in the hells from suffering and lead them into the Buddha-way.
I also see these sons of the Buddha who never indulge in sleep, walking in meditation within the groves, diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, seeing those endowed with precepts, their majestic deportment flawless and pure as a precious gem,
seeking the path to Buddhahood;
even when arrogant people revile them with foul language or strike them with blows, they are able to endure it all.
Seeking the Buddha-way,

together with their foolish retinues, they draw near to the wise; with single-mindedness they eliminate distraction and withdraw their thoughts in mountain forests for billions of koṭis of years, seeking the Buddha-way.
Some see Bodhisattvas bestowing various delicacies, foods, and drinks, as well as hundreds of kinds of medicinal decoctions,
upon the Buddha and the Sangha;
or bestowing famous garments and superior robes worth ten million, or even priceless robes, upon the Buddha and the Sangha.
Millions upon billions of kinds of sandalwood jewel-palaces and various exquisite bedding were offered to the Buddha and the Sangha;
pure groves with flourishing flowers and fruits, and flowing springs and bathing pools,
were offered to the Buddha and the Sangha.
With such various and subtle offerings, they joyfully give without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path.
Some Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma of quiescence, providing manifold instructions to countless sentient beings;
others are seen contemplating the nature of all phenomena, finding not a single characteristic therein.
They are like empty space;
furthermore, one sees these sons of the Buddha, their minds free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics.
They also see sons of the Buddha constructing various stūpas and temples, as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers.
The boundaries of the land were magnificently adorned;
the jeweled stupas were sublime and lofty, five thousand yojanas in height, and two thousand yojanas in both length and breadth, being perfectly symmetrical.
At each stupa and temple, there were a thousand banners and streamers, with canopies of interlaced pearls and precious bells chiming in harmony.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, humans and non-humans alike,
constantly made offerings of incense,
flowers, and music. Mañjuśrī!
All you sons of the Buddha, in order to make offerings to the śarīra, have adorned the stūpas and temples;
the realm of the kingdom is naturally exquisite and wondrously beautiful,
like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.
The Buddha emits a single ray of light, and I, along with the assembled multitude, behold this realm in all its various wonders and excellences.
The spiritual power of the Buddhas and their wisdom are truly rare and marvelous!
He emits a pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands.
We have seen this and attained what we have never experienced before.
O Mañjuśrī, Son of the Buddha!
We pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly; the fourfold congregation looks up to you with joy and admiration, as do we who gaze upon your benevolence.
World-Honored One, for what reason have you emitted this radiance?
The Son of the Buddha replied at that time, resolving doubts and bringing joy:
"What benefit does he provide, manifesting this radiance?
It is the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment."
Is it because you wish to speak of this, or are you about to bestow a prophecy?
To reveal these buddha-fields, adorned and purified with various jewels,
and to allow us to behold the Buddhas— this is no small cause.
Mañjuśrī, you should know!
The fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits gaze upon you, the Benevolent One; what do you intend to teach them?
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and the other great beings:
"Sons of good family!

As I contemplate it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now desires to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the Great Dharma-rain, to blow the Great Dharma-conch, to beat the Great Dharma-drum, and to expound the Great Dharma-meaning."
"Good sons! In the past, I have witnessed this very omen among the Buddhas of former times: once they had emitted such light, they immediately preached the Great Dharma.

Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so; desiring to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe, he has manifested this omen."
“O sons of good family!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He expounded the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is skillful, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy Brahma-conduct.”

For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Four Noble Truths, so that they may transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, and ultimately attain nirvāṇa;
for those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and for all bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the six pāramitās, enabling them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and realize the knowledge of all modes.
Next there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa;
next there was yet another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
In this manner, twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name, Candrasūryapradīpa, and also shared the same clan name, Bharadvāja.

“Maitreya, you should know that the first Buddha and the subsequent Buddhas all share the same name, Sūryacandrapradīpa, fully endowed with the ten epithets; the Dharma they teach is excellent in the beginning, the middle, and the end.”
Before that last Buddha had left the household life, there were eight princes:

the first was named Meaningful (Yìyì), the second Good Meaning (Shànyì), the third Immeasurable Meaning (Wúliàngyì), the fourth Jewel Meaning (Bǎoyì), the fifth Increasing Meaning (Zēngyì), the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Meaning (Chúyíyì), the seventh Echo Meaning (Xiǎngyì), and the eighth Dharma Meaning (Fǎyì). These eight princes possessed sovereign majesty and virtue, each governing four continents.

When these princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all renounced their royal positions and followed him into the homeless life. They resolved upon the Mahāyāna path, constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and all became Dharma-preachers; they had already planted the roots of goodness under tens of millions of Buddhas.
"At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings, the Dharma for Bodhisattvas, Protected by the Buddhas*.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the *Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings*, remaining with body and mind unmoving.

At that moment, it rained *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, which fell upon the Buddha and the great assembly; the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways."

At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others in the assembly—including minor kings and universal monarchs—this great multitude attained what they had never experienced before; with joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

"At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, just as these various Buddha-lands are seen now."
“Maitreya, you should know!

At that time, within the assembly, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who desired to hear the Dharma. These bodhisattvas, seeing this radiance universally illuminating the Buddha-land, attained what they had never experienced before and wished to know the causes and conditions for which this light appeared.”

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light who had eight hundred disciples. Then, the Buddha Sun Moon Lamp Brightness arose from his samādhi and, for the sake of the bodhisattva Wonderful Light, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas; he did not rise from his seat for sixty minor kalpas.

Those in the assembly who were listening also remained seated in one place for sixty minor kalpas with body and mind unmoving, yet they perceived the time of the Buddha’s preaching as being like the duration of a single meal.
At that time, not a single person among the assembly, whether in body or mind, felt any weariness or fatigue.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, he addressed these words to the assembly of Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras:
"Today, at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa then bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment and addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a buddha, titled Viśuddhakāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
After the Buddha had bestowed this prediction, he entered *nirvāṇa* without remainder during the middle watch of the night.
Following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Mārajit as their teacher; through Mārajit’s instruction and transformation, they were made firm in their resolve for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
After these princes had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, they all attained the Way of the Buddha.

The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara. Among his eight hundred disciples, there was one known as Yaśaskāma, who was greedy for gain and offerings; although he recited many sutras, he did not master them and forgot much of what he had learned, which is why he was called Yaśaskāma. Because this person had also planted various roots of goodness, he encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, whom he served, honored, revered, and praised.
“Maitreya, you should know this!
At that time, was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light anyone else?
It was I myself.”
"Seeking Fame Bodhisattva, you are this very person.

Now, seeing that this auspicious sign is no different from what it was before, I have reflected that today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas."
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to restate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall past ages, Immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago;
There was a Buddha, the Honored One among men, Named Candrasūryapradīpa."
The World-Honored One expounds the Dharma, delivering immeasurable sentient beings;
he causes countless billions of bodhisattvas to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Before the Buddha left the household life, eight princes were born to him.
Seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, they also followed him to practice the holy life.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Mahāyāna, a sūtra titled "The Immeasurable Meanings";
amidst the great assembly, he analyzed it in detail.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
he sat cross-legged upon the Dharma-seat in samādhi, called the "Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly *māndārava* flowers rained down, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
All the buddha-fields immediately shook with great trembling;
the Buddha emitted light from between his brows, manifesting various rare and wondrous events.
This light shines upon the east, reaching eighteen thousand Buddha-lands;
it reveals to all sentient beings the places where they undergo the retribution of their karma in birth and death.
Furthermore, one sees those various Buddha-lands adorned with myriad jewels.
The colors of lapis lazuli and crystal arise from the light of the Buddha’s radiance.
Therein one also beholds the various devas and humans, as well as the hosts of nāgas,
spirits, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras, each making offerings to that Buddha.
Furthermore, I see all the Tathāgatas, Spontaneously attaining the Way of the Buddha;
Their bodies are like mountains of gold, Exquisite and most subtle in their majesty.
Like a true golden image appearing within Pure lapis lazuli, they shine forth.
The World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, expounds the profound meaning of the Dharma.
In each and every Buddha-land, there are countless śrāvakas;
through the illumination of the Buddha’s light, they all behold that great assembly.
There were some bhikṣus dwelling amidst the mountain forests,
who practiced with diligence and maintained the pure precepts as if guarding a bright pearl.
Furthermore, they saw various bodhisattvas practicing generosity, patience, and the like.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges, all due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
Again, one sees various bodhisattvas deeply entering various dhyāna-samādhis;
their bodies and minds are tranquil and unmoving as they seek the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, I see various bodhisattvas, who know the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena;
each in their own land, they preach the Dharma seeking the path to Buddhahood.
At that time, the fourfold assembly beheld the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
Manifesting great supernormal powers, their hearts were all filled with joy.
Each asked one another: "What is the cause and condition for this?
The Honored One, revered by gods and men, has just arisen from samādhi.
He praised the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light:
"You are the eye of the world, the one in whom all take refuge and place their trust; you are able to receive and uphold the treasury of the Dharma.
Regarding the Dharma as I have taught it, only you are able to realize and know it."
After the World-Honored One had thus offered praise, he caused Miaoguang to rejoice.
As he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he remained seated upon this very throne for a full sixty minor kalpas.
The sublime and wondrous Dharma that was preached, the Dharma Master Miaoguang was able to receive and uphold it all.
After the Buddha had finished preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and brought joy to the assembly,
on that very day he addressed the multitude of devas and humans:
"The meaning of the true reality of all phenomena has already been explained for you;
tonight at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
You must practice with single-minded diligence and remain free from negligence."
The Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter; Only once in billions of eons do they appear.
The Sons of the World-Honored One, Hearing that the Buddha has entered nirvana, Each harbors grief and distress: "How swift was the Buddha's passing!"
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, comforted the immeasurable multitudes:
"When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not grieve or fear;
this Bodhisattva Guṇagañja [Treasury of Virtue] shall, regarding the outflow-free true reality,"
His mind has already attained penetration; next he shall become a Buddha named Pure Body (Śuddhakāya), who will likewise deliver immeasurable multitudes.
This night the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
The śarīras were distributed everywhere, and immeasurable stūpas were erected.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
redoubled their diligent efforts in their quest for the unsurpassed path.
This Dharma Master Wonderful Light, upholding the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings,
widely proclaimed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* throughout eighty intermediate kalpas.
These eight princes, transformed by the Light of Subtlety, have become firm in the unsurpassed Way; they shall behold countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all these Buddhas, they will practice the Great Way in accordance with it.
They attained Buddhahood one after another, receiving their predictions in succession.
The last among them was the God among Gods, known as the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
he was the guide of all sages, who delivered and liberated immeasurable multitudes.
This Dharma Master Wondrous Light had at that time a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence; he was greedily attached to fame and profit,
never satiated in his pursuit of them, and frequented the households of the noble families.
Abandoning what they have practiced and recited, they fall into forgetfulness and lack proficiency;
for these reasons, they are called "those who seek fame.
Yet they also perform various wholesome deeds and manage to see countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all Buddhas, practicing the Great Way in accordance with it,
and being endowed with the six pāramitās, he now beholds the Lion of the Śākyas;
hereafter he shall become a Buddha, named Maitreya.
He extensively delivered all sentient beings, their number being immeasurable.
After that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, you were that indolent one;
the Dharma Master Wondrous Light was none other than my own self.
I have seen the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, whose original radiance was such as this;
by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The present signs are as they were originally auspicious; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas.
Now the Buddha emits radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark.
All you people should now know this: join your palms and wait with a single mind.
The Buddha shall rain down the rain of Dharma, Satisfying all seekers of the Way.
For those seeking the Three Vehicles who harbor doubts or regrets,
The Buddha shall eliminate and sever them, Until they are exhausted, leaving none remaining.
Chapter Two: The Expedient Means At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from his samādhi and addressed Śāriputra:

“The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is this? The Buddha has personally attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; he has fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma of all Buddhas, and through his courageous diligence, his fame is heard everywhere. He has accomplished profound and unprecedented dharmas, and the underlying intent of what he teaches according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand.

Śāriputra! Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables, employing countless skillful means to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the pāramitās of expedient means, knowledge, and vision. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, immeasurable and unimpeded; his powers, fearlessnesses, dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis penetrate the boundless depths, having accomplished all unprecedented dharmas.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and expound all dharmas in various ways, using words that are gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude. Śāriputra!
To speak briefly, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
Cease, Śāriputra! There is no need to say more.

Why is this? Because the Buddha has realized a most rare and difficult-to-understand Dharma; only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). That is to say, regarding all phenomena: such is their characteristic, such is their nature, such is their essence, such is their power, such is their function, such is their cause, such is their condition, such is their fruit, such is their retribution, and such is their equality from beginning to end.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; Neither the devas nor the people of the world, Nor any class of sentient beings, Is able to know the Buddha."
The Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses, his liberations and various samādhis,
as well as all other qualities of a Buddha— none can measure them.
Having followed countless Buddhas in the past, he has fully practiced all paths.
The most profound and subtle Dharma is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of kalpas, I have attained the fruit at the site of enlightenment; all this I have fully known and seen.
Such great fruits of retribution, with their various natures, characteristics, and meanings—only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know these matters.
This Dharma cannot be shown; its words and signs are quiescent.
None among the other classes of sentient beings are able to understand it,
except for the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm,
and the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples who have made offerings to the Buddhas in the past.
All outflows are exhausted, dwelling in this final body;
such persons as these cannot be overcome by any power.
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, [they would still not be able to surpass him].
Exhausting all thought to measure it together, one cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even if those who fill the ten directions were all like Śāriputra,
and the other disciples likewise filled the lands of the ten directions, [they still could not fathom it].
Even if they were to exhaust their thoughts and deliberate together, they still could not know [it].
Pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom, free from outflows, in their final bodies,
filling the worlds of the ten directions, their number being like that of bamboo groves—
If these beings were to unite their minds for immeasurable billions of eons,
desiring to contemplate the Buddha’s true wisdom, they would not be able to know even a small fraction of it.
Even Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment, though they have made offerings to countless Buddhas, [cannot fathom it].
Thoroughly comprehending all meanings and purposes, and being further able to skillfully expound the Dharma—
like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, filling the lands of the ten directions—
with a single mind and wondrous wisdom, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All together they reflect upon it, yet cannot know the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
though they seek it with a single mind, likewise cannot know it.
Again, he addressed Śāriputra:
"The profound and subtle Dharma, which I have now fully attained—
only I know its characteristics, and so it is with the Buddhas of the ten directions."
Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, you should give rise to the power of great faith.
After a long time, O World-Honored One, you must speak the truth.
To the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, you have said:
"I have caused them to be released from the bonds of suffering and have enabled them to attain nirvāṇa."
"By the power of skillful means, the Buddha reveals the teachings of the three vehicles;
for sentient beings are attached everywhere, he leads them so that they may attain liberation.

At that time, within the great assembly, there were various śrāvakas who had exhausted their outflows and attained arhatship, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and his one thousand two hundred followers, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had resolved upon the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, each of whom thought to themselves:
“Now, World-Honored One, for what reason do you so earnestly praise skillful means, saying:

‘The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand; its expressed teachings have an underlying intent that is difficult to discern, and it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas’?”
“The Buddha has taught the meaning of a single liberation; we too have attained this Dharma and reached nirvana, yet now we do not know where the meaning of this teaching leads.
At that time, Śāriputra, perceiving the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly and being himself also uncertain, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
For what cause and for what reason do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
From the past until now, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha.
Now the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts; we only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter.
World-Honored One!
For what reason do you so earnestly praise this profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, Has long since preached this Dharma.
He himself has declared that he has attained Such powers, fearlessnesses, and samādhis."
The dharmas such as dhyāna and liberation, these inconceivable dharmas attained at the site of enlightenment— there is no one able to pose questions about them.
My intention is difficult to fathom, and there is likewise no one able to question it.
Without being asked, he speaks of his own accord, extolling the path he has practiced:
"The wisdom is most subtle and profound; it is that which all Buddhas have attained.
[It is for] the outflow-free Arhats and those who seek Nirvana."
Now all have fallen into a web of doubt: Why did the Buddha speak this?
Those who seek pratyekabuddhahood—monks and nuns, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—[all share this uncertainty].
Gazing at one another with lingering hesitation, we look up to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings:
what is the meaning of this matter?
We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
Among the assembly of śrāvakas, the Buddha declared me to be the foremost;
yet now, regarding my own wisdom, I am beset by doubt and cannot discern whether this is the ultimate Dharma.
Is this the path to be practiced?
The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth join their palms and gaze upward in expectation;
we pray that you will utter a subtle and wondrous sound and, at this time, speak according to reality.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges;
the bodhisattvas seeking buddhahood, numbering eighty thousand in the great total;
furthermore, from ten trillion lands, the wheel-turning sage-kings arrived.
"With palms joined in a reverent heart, I wish to hear the complete path.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "Stop, stop!
"There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were explained, all the devas and humans in the entire world would be struck with alarm and doubt.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will speak of it; we pray that you will speak of it! Why is this? Because—”

This assembly consists of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings who have previously seen various Buddhas; their faculties are sharp and keen, and their wisdom is clear and lucid, so that upon hearing what the Buddha teaches, they are able to respond with reverence and faith.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“O Dharma King, Supreme Honored One, Please speak; have no concern.
In this assembly there are immeasurable multitudes Who are capable of reverent faith.”
The Buddha again restrained Śāriputra, saying:
"If you were to speak of this matter, all the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—would be struck with alarm and doubt; moreover, monks of overweening pride would fall into a great abyss."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Stop! Stop!"
"There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.
Those who possess overweening pride will certainly not show respect or faith upon hearing it.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will speak of it; we pray that you will speak of it!

Those in this assembly who are like us, having already been transformed by the Buddha throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lifetimes, are certain to be able to revere and believe it, attaining peace and security for a long night and receiving manifold benefits.”
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Unsurpassed One, Honored among Two-legged Beings, I pray you will expound the foremost Dharma;
As I am the eldest son of the Buddha, I beseech you to grant me a detailed explanation."
In this assembly are immeasurable multitudes who are able to revere and believe in this Dharma;
the Buddha has already, throughout countless lifetimes, taught and transformed such as these.
All now join their palms with single-minded devotion, desiring to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
We, twelve hundred in number, along with others who seek Buddhahood,
pray that for the sake of this assembly you will deign to explain it in detail;
having heard this Dharma, they shall give rise to great joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Since you have earnestly requested this three times, how could I not speak?
Listen attentively now and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you."

When these words were spoken, five thousand members of the assembly—consisting of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—immediately rose from their seats, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.

Why is this? Because these people have deeply rooted and heavy karmic offenses and are possessed of overweening pride; they claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized. Having such faults, they do not abide [in the Dharma].
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not stop him.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves; it consists purely of the solid and essential."
Śāriputra! It would be well indeed for such people of overweening pride to fall back!
Listen now attentively; I shall speak for you.
Śāriputra said: "So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals; it appears but once in a long while, like the udumbara flower."
Śāriputra! You all should have faith; that which the Buddha has spoken is not false. Śāriputra!
The Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and their underlying intentions are difficult to comprehend. Why is this?

By means of countless skillful expedients, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, I have expounded all dharmas; yet these dharmas cannot be understood through mere calculation or discrimination, but can only be known by the Buddhas themselves.
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is solely for the sake of one great cause and condition that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world. Śāriputra!
What is meant by saying that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to bring it to purity;
they appear in the world because they desire to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings.
He appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
he appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
“Śāriputra! It is for the sake of this one great causal matter that all Buddhas appear in the world.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas; whatever they do is always for a single purpose: solely to reveal and awaken sentient beings to the Buddha's knowledge and vision."
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the single Buddha-vehicle; there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third. Śāriputra!
The Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise.

Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expounded the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; yet these dharmas were all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Consequently, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, ultimately attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Śāriputra! In the future, all Buddhas shall appear in the world and, likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful methods, through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, they shall expound the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings. These dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle; thus, when these sentient beings hear the Dharma from the Buddhas, they will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Śāriputra! At present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bring great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings. These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; yet these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. When these sentient beings hear the Dharma from the Buddhas, they will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Śāriputra! These Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas because they wish to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, because they wish to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Śāriputra! I am now likewise thus: knowing that all sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments, I preach the Dharma for them through the power of skillful means, employing various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression in accordance with their fundamental natures.
Śāriputra! All this is for the sake of attaining the single Buddha-vehicle and the knowledge of all modes. Śāriputra!
"In the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.

Śāriputra! The Buddhas appear in the five turbidities of the evil world—namely, the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of views, and the turbidity of life. It is thus, Śāriputra!"

In times of turmoil during the defilement of the kalpa, sentient beings are heavily burdened by impurities; because they are stingy, greedy, and jealous, they bring to fruition various unwholesome roots. Therefore, through the power of skillful means, the Buddhas distinguish and teach the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.

Śāriputra! If any of my disciples claim to be Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, yet do not hear of or know that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only Bodhisattvas, these are not disciples of the Buddha, nor Arhats, nor Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves that they have already attained arhatship— that this is their final body and their ultimate nirvāṇa— and thus no longer aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you should know that such people are all those possessed of overweening pride (adhimāna).

Why is this? If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible, except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before them.

Why is this? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and understand the meaning of such sutras as these will be difficult to find; yet if they should encounter other Buddhas, they will attain definitive realization within this Dharma.
Śāriputra! You all should with one mind believe and understand, and receive and uphold the words of the Buddha.
The words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without falsehood; there is no other vehicle, but only the single Buddha-vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride,
Upāsakas with arrogance, and upāsikās lacking faith— ”
Thus, among these four assemblies, there were five thousand who did not see their own faults;
they had deficiencies and omissions in their precepts and cherished their own blemishes—
these were those of small wisdom who had already departed.
The chaff and dregs among the assembly have departed due to the Buddha’s majestic power;
these people lacked merit and were unable to receive this Dharma.
This assembly is now free of branches and leaves, consisting only of the pure and solid core.
Śāriputra, listen well: the Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through the power of immeasurable skillful means.
According to what is contemplated in the minds of sentient beings and the various paths they practice, [the Buddhas teach accordingly].
Regarding the various dispositions toward desires and the wholesome or unwholesome karma of previous lives,
the Buddha, having fully known them all, uses the power of skillful means— through words, analogies, and parables— to cause everyone to rejoice.
Some speak of the Sūtras, Gāthās, Itivṛttakas, Jātakas, Adbhutadharmas, and also speak of the Nidānas,
Avadānas, and Geyas, as well as the Upadeśa-sūtras.
For those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings, who are greedily attached to birth and death,
and who do not practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas,
but are instead distressed and distracted by manifold sufferings— for their sake, I preach *nirvāṇa*.
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha-wisdom;
I have never said to you that you shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason I have not said so is that the time for such a teaching has not yet arrived.
Now is precisely the time to definitively expound the Mahāyāna.
These ninefold teachings of mine were spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
since they take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation, I have therefore preached this sūtra.
There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, Supple and also of sharp faculties;
In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, They have practiced the profound and wondrous Way.
For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra.

I bestow this prediction upon such people: that in a future life they shall attain the Buddha-way, because they have recited the Buddha’s name with a profound mind and have practiced and maintained the pure precepts.
Upon hearing that they shall attain Buddhahood, great joy fills their entire bodies.
The Buddha, knowing their mental activities, therefore expounds the Mahāyāna for them.
Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I preach—
even if only a single verse— they shall all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma;
there is neither a second nor a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means of speaking.
He employs only provisional names to guide sentient beings.
It is for the sake of expounding the Buddha’s wisdom that the Buddhas appear in the world;
this alone is the one true reality, while all else is not real.
They never, by means of the Lesser Vehicle, seek to deliver sentient beings.
The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle, according to the Dharma he has realized.
Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, he uses this to deliver sentient beings;
he has personally realized the unsurpassed path, the equal Dharma of the Great Vehicle.
If I were to convert even a single person by means of the Lesser Vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is not permissible.
If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive them.
Furthermore, being free from covetousness and envy, and having severed all evils within the dharmas,
the Buddha alone among the ten directions is without fear.
Adorned with the marks upon my body, my radiance illuminates the world.
Honored by immeasurable multitudes, he expounds for them the seal of the true mark.
Śāriputra, you should know:
I originally established a vow, desiring to cause all multitudes to be no different from myself.
As I have vowed in the past, it is now fulfilled:
I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way.
Whenever I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way.
Those lacking wisdom are confused and deluded, refusing to accept the teaching.
I know these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness;
they are stubbornly attached to the five desires, and because of their ignorant craving, they give rise to affliction.
Due to the causes and conditions of various desires,
one falls into the three evil realms and wanders through the six destinies, enduring all manner of bitter suffering.
Receiving a subtle form within the womb, this condition constantly increases from lifetime to lifetime.
Those of meager virtue and little merit, oppressed by manifold sufferings,
enter the dense forest of false views— such as "existence" or "non-existence.
Relying upon these various views, they are fully possessed of the sixty-two [wrong views].
Deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, they stubbornly cling to them and cannot let go;
conceited and self-aggrandizing due to their pride, their minds are crooked and insincere.
For thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, they shall not hear the name of the Buddha.
Nor do they hear the True Dharma; such people are difficult to deliver.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I employ skillful means to teach the path that exhausts all suffering and reveal to them Nirvāṇa.
Although I speak of nirvāṇa, even this is not true extinction;
all dharmas from the very beginning have always been characterized by quiescence.
When the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in a future age.
I possess the power of skillful means, To reveal and teach the Dharma of the three vehicles.
All the World-Honored Ones Speak only of the path of the One Vehicle;
Now, this entire great assembly Should all eliminate their doubts and delusions.
The words of all Buddhas are without difference; there is only the One Vehicle, not two.
Throughout countless kalpas in the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who attained parinirvāṇa—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of kinds, their number beyond measure.
Thus these World-Honored Ones, through various causes, conditions, and parables,
and by the power of countless skillful means, expound the characteristics of all dharmas.
All these World-Honored Ones alike preach the Single Vehicle Dharma.
He transforms immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, all the Great Holy Lords know the deep-seated desires of all beings in the world—
gods, humans, and the various classes of living creatures.
Furthermore, by means of other skillful expedients, I assist in manifesting the ultimate truth.
If there are classes of sentient beings who encountered the Buddhas of the past,
whether they heard the Dharma and practiced giving, or observed the precepts and practiced patience,
Through diligence, meditation, wisdom, and so forth, practicing various forms of merit and insight—
all such persons as these have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
After the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, if a person possesses a virtuous and gentle mind,
All such sentient beings have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics shall erect billions of kinds of stupas made of gold, silver, and crystal.
With carnelian and agate, Rosa mundi and lapis lazuli beads,
Pure and vast adornments, They decorated the various stupas;
Or some erected stone shrines, Of sandalwood and aloeswood.
Whether using sandalwood or other timbers, bricks, tiles, clay, or earth,
if one builds a temple for the Buddha by piling up soil in the wilderness; or even if,
in the play of children, they gather sand to make a stupa for the Buddha—
All such persons as these have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
If anyone, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images,
carving them to represent the manifold marks, they too have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Some may fashion images of the Buddha using the seven precious gems, brass,
red or white copper, tin, lead, and pewter, or iron, wood, and clay;
or they may use lacquer and cloth to adorn and create such images.
All such persons as these have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Those who paint images of the Buddha, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings—
whether they do so themselves or cause others to do so— all have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Even those who, in the play of children, Have drawn images of the Buddha With grass, wood, or a brush, Or even with their fingernails—
All such people as these Gradually accumulate merit.
Endowed with the mind of great compassion, they have all already attained the Way of the Buddha;
they merely transform the various bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
If a person, at a stupa or temple, [makes offerings to] a jeweled image or a painted image,
With flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, they make offerings with a reverent heart;
or they cause musicians to perform, beating drums and blowing horns and conchs,
flutes, pipes, lutes, and harps, as well as *pipas*, gongs, and cymbals.
All such wondrous sounds, held in their entirety as offerings,
or with a heart of joy, singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues—
even a single minor sound— all have already led to the attainment of the Way of the Buddha.
If a person with a distracted mind offers even a single flower as an offering to a painted image, they will gradually come to see countless Buddhas.
Or there may be someone who prostrates, or perhaps one who merely joins their palms in reverence.
Even raising a single hand, or slightly bowing the head,
by making such offerings to the images, one will gradually behold immeasurable Buddhas;
one shall personally realize the Unsurpassed Way and extensively deliver countless multitudes.
Entering into nirvana without remainder is like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and utters "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Among all the Buddhas of the past, those currently living, or those who have entered parinirvāṇa—
whosoever has heard this Dharma has already attained the path of Buddhahood.
As for the World-Honored Ones of the future, their number is immeasurable.
These Tathāgatas likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means;
all Tathāgatas, by means of infinite expedients,
deliver all sentient beings and cause them to enter the untainted wisdom of the Buddha.
If there are those who hear this Dharma, there shall be none who do not attain Buddhahood.
This is the fundamental vow of all Buddhas: "The Buddha-path that I have practiced, I desire to cause all sentient beings universally to likewise obtain this path."
Though the Buddhas of future ages may preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, their reality is but the One Vehicle. The Buddhas,
the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature.
The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions; therefore, the One Vehicle is taught.
This Dharma abides in the station of phenomena; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher of the Way speaks through skillful means.
The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions,
whose number is like the sands of the Ganges, who are honored by devas and humans,
have appeared in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings; they, too, preach this very Dharma.
Knowing the supreme tranquility, yet by the power of skillful means, he manifests various paths;
though they appear diverse, their reality is the Buddha-vehicle.
He knows the various conducts of sentient beings and what their deep minds intend.
The karma accumulated in the past, the nature of desire and the power of diligence,
as well as the sharpness or dullness of the faculties— through various causes and conditions,
by means of parables and verbal expressions, he teaches with appropriate skillful means.
I am now likewise so; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim and reveal the Buddha-way through various Dharma-gates.
By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings.
I teach all dharmas through skillful means, causing all to attain joy.
Śāriputra, you should know this:
seeing the sentient beings of the six realms, impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom,
Entering the perilous path of birth and death, the succession of suffering continues without end;
deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak cherishing its tail,
they veil themselves with craving and greed, blind and dark, seeing nothing at all.
Seeking neither the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that severs suffering,
they have deeply entered into various false views, seeking to abandon suffering through further suffering.
For the sake of these sentient beings, I give rise to a heart of great compassion.
When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I gazed at the tree and also practiced walking meditation;
During the three periods of seven days, I contemplated these matters:
"The wisdom I have attained Is subtle, wondrous, and supreme."
Sentient beings have dull faculties; Attached to pleasure, they are blinded by ignorance.
How can such as these be delivered? At that time, the Brahma Kings And the various Śakras, Lords of Devas, [spoke thus].
The Four World-Protecting Kings, as well as Maheśvara and the rest of the celestial hosts,
with their hundreds of thousands of millions of attendants,
joined their palms in reverence and paid homage, entreating me to turn the wheel of Dharma.
I then reflected to myself:
"If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma.
Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms."
"I would rather not preach the Dharma, but quickly enter into nirvana.
Then he recalled the skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past:
"The path I have now attained should likewise be taught through the three vehicles."
While I was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared;
with Brahma-like voices they comforted and encouraged me, saying: "Excellent, Śākyamuni!"
The Supreme Guide has attained this unsurpassed Dharma;
following all Buddhas, he employs the power of skillful means,
and we too have all attained the most wondrous and foremost Dharma.
For the sake of all classes of sentient beings, I have distinguished and taught the three vehicles.
Those with little wisdom who delight in inferior teachings do not believe they can become Buddhas themselves;
therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I have distinguished and taught various fruits.
Although the three vehicles are taught, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra, you should know:
having heard the deep, pure, subtle, and wondrous voice of the Holy Lion, I cry out, "Namo to all Buddhas!"
Again, he formed this thought:
"I have emerged from this world of turbid evil; as all the Buddhas have taught, I too shall practice in accordance with their words.
Having reflected upon these matters, he immediately set out for Vārāṇasī.
The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words;
yet, by the power of skillful means, it was taught for the sake of the five bhikṣus.
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and with it came the sound of nirvāṇa.
As well as the Arhats, and the distinct names for the Dharma and the Saṅgha;
from time immemorial, I have constantly taught and demonstrated the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, wherein the suffering of birth and death is forever extinguished. Thus have I always spoken.
Śāriputra, you should know!
Those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way, numbering immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis,
have all come to the presence of the Buddha with hearts of reverence.
I have heard from the various Buddhas the teachings they expounded through skillful means.
I then had this thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to proclaim the Buddha-wisdom."
"Now is precisely that time.
Śāriputra, you should know:
those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and full of pride, cannot believe in this Dharma."
Now I rejoice and am fearless; among all the bodhisattvas, I have set aside expedient means with straightforwardness and taught only the unsurpassed path.
When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts has been entirely removed.
The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become buddhas.
Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have established the ritual for preaching the Dharma,
so do I now likewise preach the Dharma free from conceptual discrimination.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is rare and difficult to encounter;
even when they appear in the world, it is further difficult for them to preach this Dharma.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, it is likewise difficult to hear this Dharma.
Those who are able to hear this Dharma are likewise rare.
Like the udumbara flower, which all love and cherish,
it is seldom seen by gods and men, appearing only once in a great while.
To hear the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering but a single word,
is to have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is most rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower.
Do not harbor any doubt; I am the King of all Dharmas.
I proclaim to the great assembly: I teach and transform all bodhisattvas solely through the path of the One Vehicle; there are no śrāvaka disciples.
"You, Śāriputra, and all you śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
should know that this wondrous Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
Because in this world of the five turbidities, people take pleasure only in being attached to various desires,"
Sentient beings such as these will never seek the Buddha-way.
In future ages, evil persons, hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will be deluded and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into the evil paths.
To those who possess a sense of shame and remorse, who are pure, and who aspire to seek the Buddha-way—
one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such as these.
Śāriputra, you should know this!
By means of billions of skillful expedients, he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
those who have not practiced and studied cannot understand this.
Since you all already know that the Buddhas are the Teachers of the World, [you should now act accordingly].
Regarding these matters of skillful means as appropriate, they no longer harbor any doubts;
their hearts give rise to great joy, knowing for themselves that they shall become Buddhas.
— *The Added Chapters of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle One.
The Added Chapters to the Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India, together with Dharmagupta, during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Three: The Parable. Chapter Three: The Parable (Upamā-varga)
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and, rising immediately with palms joined, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy in a manner never before experienced.”

Why is this? In the past, I heard such a teaching from the Buddha, seeing various bodhisattvas receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, while we ourselves were not included in this matter; we felt deeply grieved, realizing we had lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
“World-Honored One!
When I was once dwelling alone in the mountains and forests beneath the trees, whether sitting or walking, I would constantly think:
‘We have all entered the same Dharma-nature; why does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna teachings?’”
"This is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One. Why is this?
Had we waited for the explanation of the causes through which one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have attained liberation by means of the Mahāyāna."

However, we did not understand that these were teachings spoken by the Buddha through skillful means according to what was appropriate for each case; upon first hearing the Buddha’s Dharma, we accepted it immediately and contemplated it until we attained realization.

World-Honored One! From the past until now, day and night, I have constantly reproached myself. But today, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, all my doubts and regrets have been severed; my body and mind are at ease, and I have swiftly attained peace and security. Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha—born from the Buddha’s own mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma, and having obtained a share of the Buddha-Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before;
My heart harbors great joy, And the net of doubt has been entirely removed.”
Since ancient times I have been graced by the Buddha’s teaching, never losing sight of the Mahāyāna;
the Buddha’s voice is most rare and marvelous, able to remove the afflictions of sentient beings.
I have already attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); hearing [the Dharma] likewise removes my grief and distress.
Dwelling in mountain valleys, or beneath the trees of the forest,
whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter:
Alas, how deeply I reproach myself— how have I deceived myself?
"We too are sons of the Buddha, having entered together into the outflow-free Dharma;
yet we are unable, in the future, to expound the unsurpassed Way.
[We lack] the golden hue and the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations."
Within this same single Dharma, I have not attained these things:
the eighty minor marks of excellence, the eighteen unique qualities,
and all such merits as these— I have lost them all.
While I was walking in meditation alone, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly;
his fame filled the ten directions as he extensively benefited all sentient beings.
Reflecting that I had lost this benefit, I realized I had been deceiving myself.
Day and night, I constantly contemplate this matter.
I wish to ask the World-Honored One: is it lost, or is it not lost?
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise all the bodhisattvas.
Thus, throughout the day and night, I have deliberated upon this matter.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate—
this untainted and inconceivable teaching that leads all beings to the site of enlightenment.
Originally I held false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins;
the World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and spoke of nirvāṇa.
I have completely eliminated all false views and attained realization in the Dharma of emptiness.
At that time, I thought to myself, "I have attained nirvana";
yet now I realize for myself that this was not true nirvana.
When I attain Buddhahood, I shall be endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Revered by the multitudes of devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits, it was only at that time that it could be said: "I have forever extinguished [defilements] without remainder";
for amidst the great assembly, the Buddha declared, "I shall become a Buddha."
Hearing such a sound of the Dharma, all doubt and regret have been entirely removed.
When first hearing what the Buddha has spoken, my heart was greatly startled with suspicion:
"Could it not be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?"
The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, skillfully explained with parables;
my mind became as calm as the ocean, and upon hearing this, the net of my doubts was severed.
The Buddha spoke of the Buddhas of the past, the immeasurable ones who have attained parinirvāṇa.
Abiding within skillful means, they likewise all preach this Dharma;
the Buddhas of the present and the future, whose number is immeasurable,
also employ various skillful means to expound such a Dharma.
Now, as for the World-Honored One— from his birth and renunciation,
to his attainment of the Way and turning of the wheel of Dharma— he has likewise taught through skillful means;
the World-Honored One speaks the true Path, whereas Pāpīyān possesses none of this.
By this I know for certain that this is not Māra acting as a Buddha;
it was because I had fallen into the net of doubt that I thought this was the work of Māra.
Now I hear the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle.
As you eloquently expound the pure Dharma, my heart is filled with great joy.
Doubts and regrets have forever ceased; dwelling securely within true wisdom, I am certain that I shall become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans alike.
"Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, he teaches and transforms all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"I now declare before this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brahmins: In the past, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I constantly taught and transformed you in the presence of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas. You, too, followed me through the long night to receive instruction. It was by my skillful means that I guided you, so that you were born within my Dharma."
"Śāriputra! In the past, I instructed you to set your will upon the path to Buddhahood, yet you have now completely forgotten this and instead claim that you have already attained parinirvāṇa.

Because I now wish to cause you to remember your original vow and the path you were to practice, I am preaching this Mahāyāna sūtra for the sake of all śrāvakas, titled *The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas."

Śāriputra! In a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed, you shall make offerings to many thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, uphold the True Dharma, and fulfill the path practiced by Bodhisattvas. You shall then attain Buddhahood, with the name Flower Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Your land shall be named Free from Defilement; its terrain will be level and even, pure and magnificently adorned, peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with a vast multitude of gods and humans. Its ground will be made of lapis lazuli, featuring eight intersecting roads bordered by golden cords. Alongside these roads will stand rows of trees made of the seven treasures, always bearing flowers and fruit.
The Tathāgata Padmaprabha likewise teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the three vehicles.

Śāriputra! Although that Buddha appeared at a time when it was not an evil age, he preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles by virtue of his original vows; that kalpa was named Mahāratnavyūha (Great Jewel Adornment).
Why is it named "Great Jewel Adornment"?
It is because in that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as great jewels.
Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy, and none can know them except through the power of a Buddha’s wisdom.

When they wish to walk, precious lotuses support their feet. These bodhisattvas have not merely set their minds on enlightenment for the first time; they have long planted the roots of virtue and have purely cultivated the Brahma-faring under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas. They are constantly praised by all buddhas, always cultivate the wisdom of the buddhas, and possess great supernormal powers. They are well-versed in the gateways of all dharmas, upright and sincere without guile, and firm in their resolve and mindfulness. Bodhisattvas such as these fill that land.

Śāriputra! The lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma will be twelve small kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained Buddhahood; the lifespan of the people in that land will be eight small kalpas.
After twelve intermediate kalpas had passed, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha bestowed upon the bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati shall next become a Buddha, named Padmavṛṣabhavikrāmin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"The Buddha-land of that world shall be likewise.
