Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha Puṣpārāma, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall also remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In a future age, Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom;
his name shall be Flower Light (Puṣyarāja), and he shall deliver immeasurable multitudes."
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas and perfected the bodhisattva practices,
he realized the unsurpassed path through merits such as the ten powers.
After immeasurable kalpas had passed, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha.
The world is named Vimalā, pure and free from all blemish.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, with golden cords demarcating its paths;
there are trees of various colors made of the seven jewels, always bearing flowers, fruits, and seeds.
The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve;
they have fully perfected the supernatural powers and the pāramitās.
Having studied the bodhisattva path well under countless buddhas, they are now established therein.
Such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower-Light.
When that Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory;
in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of the Buddha.
The Buddha Flower-Light will dwell in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas;
the people of his land shall have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world.
For thirty-two minor kalpas, he extensively delivers all sentient beings.
After the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma lasts for thirty-two [kalpas];
his relics are widely disseminated, and gods and humans everywhere make offerings to them.
Whatever was performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha, all such matters were exactly like this;
that Most Victorious One, the Peerless Honored One among bipeds,
is none other than your own self— you should truly rejoice.

At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as the great multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with immense joy and leaped for boundless delight. Each of them removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it as an act of worship to the Buddha.

Śakra Devānām-indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and countless sons of gods likewise made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and so forth. The celestial garments they scattered remained suspended in mid-air, revolving of their own accord;
hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music played simultaneously in the sky, and as a rain of various celestial flowers fell, they spoke these words:
"In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he once again turns the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, You turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths;
You analyzed and explained all phenomena, The arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
Now you further turn the most wondrous, supreme, and great wheel of Dharma;
this teaching is exceedingly profound and subtle, and few are those capable of believing it.
Since time immemorial, we have repeatedly heard the World-Honored One’s discourse.
Never before have we heard such a profound and sublime supreme Dharma;
as the World-Honored One preaches this Dharma, we all rejoice.
The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has now received the Honored One’s prediction of enlightenment.
We, too, shall be just like this; we will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Among all worlds, there is none more honored or supreme. The Buddha-way is inconceivable;
it is taught through skillful means according to what is appropriate.
"Whatever meritorious deeds I have performed, whether in this life or in past lives,
together with the merit of seeing the Buddha— all these I dedicate entirely to the path of the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I am now free from all doubt and regret, having personally received before the Buddha the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. As for these twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds, they formerly dwelt in the stage of training, and the Buddha constantly taught and transformed them, saying:
‘My Dharma can bring one away from birth, old age, sickness, and death, leading ultimately to Nirvana.’”
"These learners and those beyond learning also each considered themselves to have attained nirvana by being free from the view of self, as well as the views of existence and non-existence;
yet now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, hearing what they have never heard before, they all fall into doubt."
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“Did I not previously say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, using various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of speech, skillfully teach the Dharma for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
All that has been said is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas. However, Śāriputra,
I shall now further clarify this meaning through a parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding by means of parables.
Śāriputra! Suppose there is a great elder in a kingdom, city, or village who is advanced in years, possesses immeasurable wealth, and owns many fields, houses, and servants;
his household is vast, yet it has but a single gate, and within it dwell many people—perhaps one hundred, two hundred, or even five hundred—who reside therein.

The halls and pavilions were dilapidated and ancient; the walls and partitions had collapsed; the bases of the pillars were rotten; the beams and rafters were leaning precariously; and all around, a fire suddenly broke out at once, burning down the house.
The elder’s sons—whether ten, twenty, or even thirty in number—are within this house.
Seeing this great fire breaking out from all four sides, the elder is seized with great alarm and fear, and he thinks to himself:

"Although I am able to escape safely through this gate that is ablaze, my sons are attached to their play within the burning house; they do not perceive it, they do not know it, and they feel neither alarm nor fear."
"The fire comes and presses upon my body with such piercing pain that my mind feels no weariness or distress, nor do I have the intention to seek escape.
Śāriputra! This elder then reflects thus:
"I possess strength in my hands and body; I shall carry them out from the house using my lap or a small table. He further reflected:

"This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small. My children are young and lack understanding; they are attached to their playthings and might fall down and be consumed by the fire. I must speak to them of this perilous matter: 'This house is already burning; you should quickly come forth at once, lest you be harmed and destroyed by the fire.'"
Having had this thought, he informed his sons in detail of what he had contemplated:
"All of you, come out quickly!

Although the father, out of compassion, used kind words to entice and exhort them, the sons were so attached to their play that they refused to believe or accept him; they were neither startled nor afraid, and had no intention at all of coming out.
Furthermore, they do not know: what is the fire?
What is the house? And how is it lost?
They merely ran about here and there, playing and looking at their father.
At that time, the elder had this thought:
"This house has already been consumed by a great fire; if I and my children do not exit immediately, we will surely be burned to death."
"I must now employ skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity.

The father, knowing that each of his sons had their own particular preferences and that their hearts were surely attached to various rare, precious, and extraordinary playthings, addressed them, saying:

"The toys you delight in are rare and difficult to obtain; if you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later. Such various carts—goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts—are currently outside the gate for your amusement. You should come out quickly from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you."

At that time, having heard of the rare and precious playthings described by their father, the sons’ hearts were each filled with vigor and resolve; they pushed and shoved one another, racing together in competition to be the first to flee from the burning house.

At that time, the elder saw that his sons had all emerged safely; they were sitting on the open ground at the crossroads, free from all obstacles, their minds serene as they leaped for joy with great exultation.
Then the sons each said to their father:
"Father, please grant us now those playthings you previously promised—the goat carts, the deer carts, and the ox carts."

“Śāriputra! At that time, the elder bestowed upon each of his sons an identical great carriage. These carriages were high and wide, adorned with various jewels; they were surrounded by railings with bells suspended on all four sides. Furthermore, canopies were spread over them, likewise embellished with rare and miscellaneous gems;
jeweled cords crisscrossed as adornments, while flower tassels hung down, and thick carpets were layered within, upon which red pillows were placed.”
He was drawn by white oxen whose coats were pure and clean, their forms beautiful and well-proportioned; they possessed great strength and moved with steady, level gait, as swift as the wind;
moreover, he was attended by many servants who guarded him.
Why is this? This great elder possesses immeasurable wealth, and his various treasuries are all overflowing; he thinks to himself:

"My riches are infinite, and it would not be right to give my children inferior, small carts. Now these young children are all my own sons, and my love for them is without partiality. I possess such great chariots made of the seven treasures, numbering in the countless; I ought to give them to each with an equal mind, and it is not fitting to treat them differently."
"Why is this? Because even if I were to distribute these goods throughout the entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted; how much less so for my sons.
At that time, each of the sons mounted a great carriage, experiencing what they had never before encountered—far beyond what they had originally hoped for.
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Would it be considered false for this elder to give his sons these precious great chariots?”
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!
This elder merely enabled his children to escape the calamity of fire and preserve their lives; it was not a falsehood.”

Why is this? If one were merely to preserve their own life and body, that would already constitute having obtained objects of pleasure; how much more so, then, when one employs skillful means to rescue others from that burning house!
World-Honored One!
Even if that elder had not given so much as the smallest single chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood. Why is this?
This elder first formed this intention: "I shall use skillful means to enable my sons to escape. For this reason, there is no falsehood in it.
How much more so for the elder, who knows his own wealth is immeasurable and wishes to benefit his sons by giving them great chariots.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is likewise thus: he is the father of all the world. Having forever extinguished, without remainder, all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the darkness of ignorance, he has fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge, vision, powers, and fearlessnesses. Possessing great power of spiritual transformation and the power of wisdom, he is endowed with the perfection of skillful means and wisdom. With great kindness and great compassion, he is ever without weariness; constantly seeking what is good to benefit all, he enters this decayed and ancient fire-housed of the triple world to deliver sentient beings from the fires of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress, and from the darkness of ignorance and the three poisons, teaching and transforming them so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

I see all sentient beings being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; they also undergo various sufferings for the sake of the five desires and material gain.

Furthermore, because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they experience manifold sufferings in the present life, and in the future, they will undergo the sufferings of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.

Whether born in the heavens or among humans, they endure the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from loved ones, and the suffering of encountering those one hates. Immersed in such various sufferings as these, sentient beings frolic and play with joy, neither perceiving nor knowing them, neither being startled nor terrified, nor giving rise to weariness or seeking liberation. Within this burning house of the three realms, they run back and forth, and though they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.
“Śāriputra! Having seen this, the Buddha thought: ‘I am the father of sentient beings;
I should uproot them from their suffering and hardship, bestow upon them the immeasurable and boundless joy of the Buddha’s wisdom, and cause them to sport therein.’”
“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata further reflects:

‘If I were to rely solely on the power of my spiritual transformations and the power of my wisdom, setting aside skillful means, to praise for all sentient beings the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision and his fearlessnesses, sentient beings would not be able to attain liberation through this.’”

Why is this? Because these sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress; they are being scorched by the burning house of the triple world—how, then, could they understand the Buddha’s wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Just as that elder, although possessing strength in his body and arms, did not employ it, but instead used diligent skillful means to rescue his children from the perils of the burning house, and subsequently gave each of them a great precious carriage;

so too is the Tathāgata. Although he possesses power and fearlessness, he does not employ them, but uses only the skillful means of wisdom to deliver sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world. For their sake, he proclaims the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha—and speaks these words:”

"You should not take pleasure in dwelling within this burning house of the triple world; do not crave coarse and inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. If you become attached and give rise to craving, you will be consumed by it. You must quickly escape the triple world, for you shall obtain the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle. I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. You need only diligently cultivate yourselves with vigor."
The Tathāgata uses these skillful means to guide and encourage sentient beings. He further says:

"You should know that these vehicles of the Threefold Dharma are all praised by the Noble Ones; they are sovereign, unbound, and free from any basis for seeking. By mounting these three vehicles, you shall delight yourselves through the untainted faculties, powers, factors of awakening, path, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, thereby attaining immeasurable peace and happiness."

“Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who possess an internal nature of wisdom, who hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and accept it with faith; who apply themselves with earnest diligence and desire to quickly escape the triple world to seek their own nirvāṇa—this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle, like those sons who left the burning house seeking the goat carts.”

If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and accept it, who diligently and vigorously seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), who delight in solitary tranquility, and who deeply understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena—this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, like those sons who left the burning house in search of deer carts.

If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and practice it with diligent effort, seeking all-encompassing wisdom, the Buddha-wisdom, self-existent wisdom, and teacherless wisdom—the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, his powers, and his fearlessnesses; and who, out of compassion for immeasurable sentient beings, seek their peace and happiness, benefiting devas and humans and delivering all, these are called Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.
Because they seek this vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas, just as those sons sought ox-carts and emerged from the burning house.

Śāriputra! Just as that elder, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness, reflects upon his own immeasurable wealth and bestows great chariots equally upon all his sons;

so too is the Tathāgata, who is the father of all sentient beings. If he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings emerging from the perilous path of the three realms—the suffering and terrors—through the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching and attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata then forms this thought:

"I possess an immeasurable and boundless treasury of the Buddha-dharmas, including wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses. All these sentient beings are my children; I bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, so that no one shall attain extinction alone. I cause all to attain extinction through the Tathāgata’s own extinction. To those sentient beings who have escaped the triple world, I grant the various implements for enjoyment—such as the meditative concentrations and liberations of the Buddhas—all of which are of a single characteristic and a single kind, praised by the sages, and capable of producing the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss."

"Śāriputra! Just as that elder first used the three vehicles to entice his children and later gave them only great chariots—adorned with treasures, secure, and foremost in excellence—that elder was not guilty of falsehood."
The Tathāgata is likewise thus: being free from falsehood, he first teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and subsequently delivers them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses an inexhaustible treasury of all dharmas—immeasurable wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses—and is able to bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma upon all sentient beings; yet they are simply unable to receive it all.

“Śāriputra! By these causes and conditions, you should know that it is through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas that they distinguish and preach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Desiring to restate this meaning, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"It is like an elder who has a large house; that house is ancient and has long been dilapidated.
The halls and chambers are high and perilous; the bases of the pillars are decayed and rotten;
the beams and rafters are slanting; the foundations and steps have collapsed; and the walls are crumbling and split."
The plaster and coating have fallen away; it is covered with suffering and lies in utter ruin.
The rafters and eaves are sagging and detached, the surrounding walls are crooked and bent, and various impurities fill the place.
Dwelling within it are owls, crows, vultures, eagles, ravens, magpies, doves, and pigeons.
Vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; centipedes and millipedes;
lizards, many-legged insects, monkeys, wildcats, and mice—these various species of evil vermin scurry about, crossing paths in every direction.
In places reeking with excrement and urine, filth flows out in abundance.
Dung beetles and various other insects swarm upon it;
foxes, wolves, and jackals gnaw, trample, and bite at the corpse, leaving its bones and flesh strewn in disarray.
They vied with one another to pounce and seize him; famished and emaciated, they were terrified and panicked.
Seeking food everywhere, they fought and clawed at one another, snarling and barking; his house was filled with such terrors and strange transformations.
Everywhere there are *chimei* and *wangliang*, yakṣas and malevolent spirits who devour human flesh;
various species of venomous insects and all manner of wicked birds and beasts breed, give birth, and each protects its own young.
Yakṣas vied with one another to come and scramble for the food;
having eaten their fill, their evil intent grew even more fierce, and the sound of their quarreling was truly terrifying.
Kumbhāṇḍa spirits crouched upon earthen mounds, or at times leaped up from the ground.
One or two feet high;
they roam back and forth, indulging in wanton play.
They seize the dogs by their two hind legs, throw them down until they cry out, and press their feet against their necks.
They take pleasure in frightening dogs.
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose bodies are tall and large, naked, black, and emaciated, who constantly dwell therein;
they emit great, evil sounds, wailing and crying out for food.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles;
there are also various ghosts whose heads are like ox-heads;
some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
With disheveled hair and a cruel, predatory appearance;
driven by hunger and thirst, they shriek and run about.
Yakṣas, pretas, and various evil birds and beasts;
Driven by hunger and urgency, he peers out through the windows and doors; faced with such perils, his fears are immeasurable.
This situation falls upon a single person, who has recently gone out;
not long after, a fire suddenly breaks out within that house.
The flames blazed together intensely; the ridgepoles, beams, rafters, and pillars burst with a thunderous crack, breaking and falling, while the walls collapsed.
All the ghosts and spirits raised their voices in loud cries.
Vultures, eagles, and various birds, along with kumbhāṇḍas and the like, were filled with panic and terror, unable to escape;
predatory beasts and venomous insects hid themselves in holes and crevices;
piśāca demons likewise took up residence therein.
Due to their meager merit, they are oppressed by fire; they harm one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh.
Those belonging to the species of jackals have all already perished before them.
Various great and wicked beasts vied with one another to come and devour [them].
Foul smoke billowed and filled the four directions;
centipedes, millipedes, and species of venomous snakes, scorched by the fire, scrambled to flee from their burrows.
The kumbhāṇḍa ghosts seize whatever they find and eat it.
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose heads are ablaze;
tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they run about in frantic agitation.
The house was like this, most terrifying;
with poisonous harms and fires, its many perils were not just one.
At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate.
I heard someone say:
"All you sons, having previously entered this house while playing,
were young and ignorant, delighting in and attached to its pleasures."
Upon hearing this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house;
he felt it necessary to provide rescue and relief so that no one would suffer from the fire’s harm.
He exhorted his children, describing their many afflictions and perils, including the evil spirits and venomous insects.
The flames of calamity spread and entwine;
manifold sufferings follow one after another in an uninterrupted succession.
There are venomous snakes, vipers, and pythons, as well as various yakṣas and kumbhāṇḍa spirits.
Jackals, foxes, and dogs;
vultures, eagles, crows, and owls; and species such as centipedes—all tormented by hunger and thirst, they are truly terrifying to behold.
In this place of suffering and hardship, how much more so with the great fire!
Though the sons have heard their father’s instruction, they remain ignorant;
they still take pleasure and attachment in it, playing and sporting without ceasing.
At that time, the elder had this thought:
"My sons being thus, they only increase my grief and distress.
Now this house has not a single thing that is pleasant, yet these sons of mine—"
"Addicted to play and sport, you do not accept my instruction; you will surely be harmed by fire.
He then reflected and devised various skillful means, saying to his sons:
"I have all kinds of precious playthings and wonderful, excellent jeweled chariots."
The sheep-drawn carts, the deer-drawn carts, and the great ox-drawn carts;
come forth, all of you! I have fashioned these carts for you, so that you may play and sport according to your own pleasure.
Upon hearing this description of the various chariots, the sons immediately vied with one another, rushing out;
they reached an open space and were freed from all suffering and distress.
The elder saw his sons had emerged from the burning house and were standing at the crossroads, seated upon lion thrones.
He spoke to himself in celebration:
"I am now happy! These children of mine were so difficult to raise; they were foolish and ignorant, yet they entered this perilous dwelling."
There are many venomous insects and terrifying malevolent spirits;
fierce flames of a great fire arise on all four sides;
yet these children, out of greed and pleasure, continue their play.
"I have already rescued them and enabled them to escape this peril;
therefore, O people, I am now joyful.
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where he was and addressed him, saying:
"We pray that you grant us three kinds of precious chariots,
just as was previously promised:
'When my children come forth, I shall give them three chariots according to each of their desires.'"
"Now is precisely the right time; please deign to grant it.
With gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, and various other precious materials, construct great chariots."
Bells hang from all four sides, crisscrossed by golden cords; nets of pearls are spread and suspended above them.
Golden flower tassels dangle everywhere, and various colorful ornaments encircle it on every side.
With soft silk and cotton down, they made quilts and mattresses;
with exquisite, fine karpāsa cloth, worth hundreds of billions in value, pure white and immaculate, they covered them above.
There was a great white ox, fat, sturdy, and full of strength, with a beautiful form, yoked to a precious chariot;
it was attended by a large retinue who guarded it,
and this wondrous vehicle was bestowed equally upon all his sons.
"Riding upon this precious chariot, one travels through the four quarters, sporting and rejoicing with sovereign ease and without hindrance.
Thus he addressed Śāriputra:
"I am likewise so: the most honored among all sages, the father of the world;
all sentient beings are my children, yet they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the heart of wisdom.
There is no peace in the three realms, which are like a house on fire, filled with manifold sufferings."
It is truly terrifying;
there is constant birth and aging, sickness, death, grief, and affliction—such fires as these blaze fiercely without ceasing.
The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world; he dwells in tranquil seclusion, peacefully settled in the forests and wilds.
This triple world is now all mine, and the sentient beings within it are all my children.
Now, in this place, there are many afflictions and hardships; I alone am able to provide protection and refuge.
Although I instruct and exhort them, they do not believe or accept [my words], because their greed and attachment to the defilements of desire are profound.
Therefore, through skillful means, I preach the Three Vehicles to cause all sentient beings—
Knowing the suffering of the three realms,
he reveals and expounds the supramundane path.
If these sons are firm in their resolve, [they shall attain it].
Possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, there are those who have attained pratyekabuddhahood and non-retrogressive bodhisattvas; you, Śāriputra!
For the sake of sentient beings, I have used this parable to preach the Single Buddha Vehicle;
if you are able to believe and accept these words, all of you shall surely attain the path of Buddhahood.
This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, the foremost in purity; among all worlds, it is unsurpassed.
It is what the Buddhas delight in, and that which all sentient beings should praise, make offerings to, and prostrate before.
Through meditative concentration and wisdom, as well as the other dharmas of the Buddha,
they obtain such a vehicle that they may cause all these sons to constantly sport and play day and night throughout kalpas;
together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, they ride upon this precious vehicle.
Until reaching the site of enlightenment;
for this reason, if one seeks with utmost sincerity throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle to be found, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
He addressed Śāriputra: "All of you people are my children, and I am your father.
For many kalpas, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings; I have rescued and delivered you all."
To cause them to emerge from the triple world;
although I previously said that you have attained parinirvāṇa, this was merely the exhaustion of birth and death, for in reality there is no extinction.
What you must now accomplish is solely the wisdom of a Buddha.
If there are bodhisattvas among this assembly who are able to listen with a single mind to the true Dharma of all Buddhas—
though the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means to transform sentient beings, they are all, in fact, bodhisattvas.
For those of small wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire,
the Truth of Suffering is taught; thereupon the hearts of sentient beings rejoice,
having attained what they have never experienced before.
The Buddha has taught the Truth of Suffering, which is real and without deviation.

If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering, who are deeply attached to its causes, and cannot relinquish them even for a moment—for their sake, he employs skillful means to speak of the Way: that which is the cause of all sufferings.
Craving is the root.
If craving is extinguished, there is nothing upon which to rely; all suffering is utterly ceased—this is called the Third Truth.
For the sake of the Truth of Cessation, one practices the Path; being freed from all bonds of suffering, this is called attaining liberation. From what is such a person liberated?
"Merely being free from delusion is called liberation;
yet in reality, they have not attained any liberation at all.
The Buddha says that such people have not truly entered parinirvāṇa."
Because this person has not yet attained the Unsurpassed Way, it is not my intention that they should enter parinirvāṇa.
I am the Dharma King; I possess sovereign mastery over the Dharma.
I appear in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. Śāriputra!
This Dharma-seal of mine is taught for the purpose of benefiting the world.
Wherever you travel, do not propagate this recklessly.
If there are those who hear it, rejoice in it and receive it upon their heads; you should know that such persons are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
If there are those who believe in and accept this sutra-dharma, these people have already seen past Buddhas;
they have paid them respectful offerings and have also heard this Dharma.
If there are those capable of believing what you have said,
they shall see me, as well as you, the community of bhikṣus, and all the bodhisattvas.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is taught for those of profound wisdom; those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be confused and fail to comprehend it.
All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power within this sūtra.
"O Śāriputra! Even you have gained entry into this sutra through faith; how much more so the other śrāvakas?
Those other śrāvakas, because they trust the Buddha’s words, follow this sutra, though it is not within the scope of their own wisdom."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant and indolent, or to those who harbor views of a self.
Nor should you preach it to ordinary people of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires; they will hear it and yet be unable to comprehend it.
If a person does not believe and slanders this sutra, they sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world;
or if they frown and harbor doubts, you should hear me describe the retribution for such a person’s sins.
Whether the Buddha is in the world, or after his parinirvāṇa, those who slander such a sūtra as this;
those who treat with contempt and disdain those who copy or uphold the sūtra, harboring resentment and hatred—
the karmic retribution for these people, listen now once more.
Entering the Avīci Hell, they remain there for a full kalpa; when the kalpa ends, they are reborn again, continuing in this manner through countless kalpas.
They shall fall among the animals, such as dogs or jackals, their forms emaciated and gaunt.
Dark-skinned and afflicted with scabies and leprosy, they are harassed and provoked by others; furthermore, they are detested and despised by men.
Constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst, their flesh and bones are withered away.
While alive they suffer agonizing torment, and at death they are struck by tiles and stones, because they have severed the lineage of the Buddha.
Receiving this retribution for their sins,
they constantly carry heavy burdens and are subjected to beatings with canes and clubs; they think only of water and grass,
knowing nothing else.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these:
they become jackals that enter villages with bodies covered in scabs and sores,
and lacking one eye, they are beaten and pelted by children.
Experiencing various agonies, sometimes even meeting death;
they further receive the body of a python, its form vast and long, five hundred yojanas in length,
deaf, dull-witted, and footless, crawling along on its belly.
Devoured by various small insects, they suffer day and night without respite;
because they slandered this sutra, they incur such retribution as this.
Their faculties are dull and obtuse; they are short, deformed, or crippled; blind, deaf, or hunchbacked.
Whatever they say, people do not believe or accept.
Their breath is constantly foul, and they are possessed by malevolent spirits. Poor and lowly, they are made to serve others.
Afflicted by many illnesses and emaciated, they have no one to rely upon; though they seek the company of others, people pay them no heed.
If they acquire anything, they soon lose it again; yet if they practice the way of medicine, they treat diseases according to the prescriptions.
They further increase the illnesses of others, or even cause death;
if they themselves fall ill, no one will provide medical treatment, and even if they take excellent medicine, their condition will only worsen;
or if others commit acts of rebellion, plunder, or theft, they will suffer the calamities resulting from such crimes.
Such a sinner shall never behold the Buddha, the King of all Sages,
preaching the Dharma to transform and edify beings.
Such a sinner shall always be born in places of hardship.
Mad, deaf, and with a distracted mind, they shall never hear the Dharma for as many incalculable kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
from birth to birth they will be deaf and mute, their faculties incomplete.
Constantly dwelling in hell as if wandering through a pleasure garden;
being in other evil realms as if in one’s own home;
camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs—these are the places where they roam.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these:
being deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired; being destitute and beset by various misfortunes;
being afflicted with dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and abscesses—such diseases as these.
They take these as their clothing;
their bodies are constantly foul-smelling, defiled and impure;
they are deeply attached to the view of self, which increases their anger and resentment.
"With lust so rampant that they do not distinguish between humans and beasts;
because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"If one were to describe the offenses of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For this reason, I tell you: do not preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom."
If there are those of sharp faculties whose wisdom is clear and lucid;
who have heard much and possess strong memory; and who seek the Buddha-way—for such persons as these, you may indeed preach it.
If there are those who have previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, who have planted various roots of goodness,
and whose profound resolve is firm— only for such people as these may you preach this Dharma.
If a person is diligent and constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness;
if they do not begrudge their own body or life—then you may speak for them.
If a person is respectful and possesses no divided mind;
"Those who have distanced themselves from all ordinary fools and dwell alone in mountains and marshes—to such persons as these, you may preach this.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
If you see someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends—
such a person is one for whom you may preach this.
If you see a son of the Buddha, pure in the observance of precepts like a bright,
clear pearl, seeking the Mahāyāna sūtras— only to such a person as this may you preach.
If a person is free from anger, upright and gentle, always compassionate toward all beings,
and reverent toward the Buddhas—
only for such a person may you preach this.
Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, with a pure mind,
use various causes and conditions, parables, and eloquent expressions to preach the Dharma without impediment;
to such persons as these, you may indeed speak.
Seeking the Dharma in all four directions for the sake of omniscience, they join their palms and receive it upon their heads;
they delight only in upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras, even to the point of not accepting a single verse from any other scripture.
To such a person as this, one may preach it.
Like a person who with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so does he seek this sutra;
having obtained it, he receives it upon the crown of his head, and that person no longer sets his mind on seeking other sutras.
"Nor have they ever thought of the scriptures of the non-Buddhists;
to such persons as these, one may preach.
He then addressed Śāriputra:
“I have described these characteristics of those who seek the Buddha-way, which could not be fully exhausted even in the course of an eon; such persons as these are able to believe and understand.
You should preach for them the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.”

Chapter Four: The Chapter on Resolute Faith (Adhimukti-parivarta) At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma and seeing the World-Honored One bestow upon Śāriputra the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, were struck with a sense of rare wonder. They leaped for joy, rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in single-minded devotion, bowed respectfully. Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, they addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We occupy the foremost positions among the Saṃgha; our years are advanced and we are decrepit. We considered ourselves to have already attained Nirvāṇa and were incapable of further effort, no longer seeking Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

In the past, when the World-Honored One had been preaching the Dharma for a long time, I was seated in the assembly with my body weary and exhausted; I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and my mind took no delight in the Bodhisattva dharmas—such as sporting in supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is so that you may cause us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana.

Furthermore, we are now advanced in years; regarding the Buddha’s teaching of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to bodhisattvas, we have not produced even a single thought of delight or aspiration. Yet, hearing before the Buddha today that the śrāvakas are to receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, our hearts are filled with a joy never known before.

We did not expect to suddenly hear such a rare Dharma today; we deeply congratulate ourselves for having obtained this great and wholesome benefit—immeasurable treasures acquired without seeking them.
“World-Honored One!
We now wish to employ a parable to clarify this meaning.

Suppose there is a man who, while still young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another land for a long time—perhaps ten, twenty, or even fifty years. Having grown up and becoming further impoverished, he wandered in all directions in search of food and clothing, and in the course of his travels, he eventually arrived back at his native country.”

His father had previously come seeking his son but could not find him, so he stayed in a certain city. His family was immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, and pearls—and all his storehouses were overflowing. He had many servants, retainers, officials, and subjects; his elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, and sheep were beyond counting. The interest from his investments and loans spread throughout other countries, and his merchants and traders were also exceedingly numerous.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through many kingdoms and cities until he eventually reached the city where his father resided.

For more than fifty years since their separation, the father had constantly thought of his son, yet he had never mentioned this matter to anyone; he merely reflected within himself with a heart full of regret. He thought to himself: "I am now old and infirm, yet my wealth is vast. My gold, silver, rare jewels, and granaries are overflowing. Yet I have no son; were I to pass away one day, my property would be lost and scattered, as there would be no one to whom it could be entrusted. For this reason, he remembered his son with persistent longing. Furthermore, he thought:
"If I were to obtain a son to whom I could entrust my wealth, I would be at ease and happy, free from further anxiety. "World-Honored One!

At that time, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened to come upon his father’s house. Standing by the side of the gate, he saw his father from afar, seated upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting his feet. He was surrounded by all the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders, who paid him respectful homage. His body was adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold. Officials, citizens, and servants stood in attendance on his left and right, holding white whisks. A jeweled canopy covered him above, with various flowered banners hanging down. Fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground and various famous flowers were scattered about. Precious objects were arrayed as he gave orders for their removal or delivery. Such were the various adornments, and his majestic virtue was exceptionally sublime."
When the impoverished son saw that his father possessed such great power and influence, he was immediately seized by fear and regretted having come here. He thought to himself in secret:
"This man must be either a king or someone like a king; this is no place for me to earn goods through hired labor.

It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood where there is room to exert my strength and where food and clothing are easily obtained. If I remain here long, I may be coerced and forced to work against my will."
Having thought this, he hurried away.
At that time, the wealthy elder, sitting upon his lion throne, recognized his son as soon as he saw him and his heart was filled with great joy.

He immediately thought to himself: "Now there is someone to whom my wealth and storehouses may be entrusted. I have constantly longed for this son, yet had no means to see him; that he has come here of his own accord fulfills my wishes most perfectly. Though I am advanced in years, I still cherish [this wealth] so dearly."
He immediately dispatched an attendant to pursue and bring him back.
At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him; the impoverished son was startled and terrified, crying out in grievance:
"I have done you no wrong, why do you seize me?"
The messengers held him even more tightly and forcibly dragged him back.
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "I am innocent yet I have been imprisoned; this must mean certain death. He became increasingly terrified, fainted, and collapsed to the ground.
The father saw him from afar and said to his attendants:
"There is no need for this man; do not force him to come here. Sprinkle cold water on his face to bring him back to his senses, and do not speak with him again."

Why is this? Because the father knew that his son’s aspirations were inferior, and he himself was aware that his own noble and wealthy status would be difficult for his son to accept. Although he recognized him clearly as his son, he employed skillful means and did not tell others, "This is my son."
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you please.
The impoverished son was filled with joy at having experienced something never before known; he rose from the ground and went to the poor quarter to seek food and clothing.
"At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised a skillful means and secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
'You should go to where that impoverished son is and speak to him gently:
"There is work to be done here; we will pay you double wages. "
If the impoverished son agrees to come and work for him,
and if he asks, "What shall I do?
one should then say to him:
“We will hire you to remove the refuse, and we two shall also work together with you.
At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son; having found him, they fully explained the aforementioned matter.
At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately began clearing away the filth; his father saw his son and felt both pity and wonder.
On another day, looking from afar through a window, he saw his son’s body—emaciated, haggard, and defiled by the impurities of dust and dirt.

He then cast off his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments, and instead donned coarse, tattered, and greasy clothes, with dust covering his body. Holding a refuse-clearing tool in his right hand, he appeared as though filled with apprehension as he spoke to the laborers:
"Work diligently and do not be indolent.
By means of this skillful expedient, he was able to draw near to his son.
He spoke to him again, saying:

"Come now, man! You shall always work here and not go elsewhere; I shall increase your wages. Whatever you may require—pots, vessels, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and the like—do not hesitate or feel any doubt. I also have old and worn-out servants who will provide whatever you need. Set your mind at ease; I am like a father to you, so do not worry."
Why is this? I am old and you are young;

yet when you work, you never show deceit, indolence, anger, or resentment. I have not seen in you any of these evils found in other laborers. From this day forward, you shall be as a son born of my own body.
Immediately, the elder gave him another name and called him his son.
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer;

for this reason, for twenty years he was constantly made to clear away dung. After this period had passed, their hearts came to trust one another, and he could enter and leave without hindrance; nevertheless, the place where he resided remained as it was before.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the elder was ill and, knowing for himself that he would soon die, spoke to the impoverished son, saying:

‘I now possess much gold, silver, and rare treasures, and my storehouses are overflowing. You should know all that is to be taken from or given to within them; such is my mind, and you should grasp this intent.’”
"Why is this? Now you and I are no different; you should apply yourself with diligence so as not to let anything be lost.

At that time, the impoverished son accepted the instructions and took charge of the various goods—the gold, silver, precious gems, and all the storehouses—yet he had no intention of seeking even a single meal from them. Moreover, he continued to reside in his former place, and his lowly mind was still unable to be relinquished.

After a short while had passed, the father perceived that his son’s mind had gradually become open and serene; he had achieved great resolve and came to despise his former inclinations. As death approached, he summoned his son and gathered together his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders, until they were all assembled.
He then made this public declaration: "Gentlemen, you should know! This is my son, begotten by me.

Having abandoned me and fled from such-and-such a city, he has wandered in hardship for over fifty years. His original name was so-and-so, and my own name is so-and-so. Formerly, while in that city, I sought him out with great anxiety; now, unexpectedly meeting him here, I have found him. He is truly my son and I am truly his father. All the wealth and property I currently possess belong entirely to my son; all that has been previously disbursed or received is known to him."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, when the impoverished son heard these words from his father, he was filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence and thought to himself:
‘Originally I had no intention of seeking anything, yet now this treasure store has come to me of its own accord.’”
“World-Honored One!
The great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata; we are all like sons of the Buddha, for the Tathāgata has always spoken of us as his children.
World-Honored One!”
"Because of the three kinds of suffering, we have endured various torments within birth and death; deluded and ignorant, we took pleasure in and were attached to inferior teachings.

Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate and eliminate the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena. We have applied ourselves with diligent effort therein and obtained the price of a single day’s worth of nirvana. Having obtained this, our hearts were filled with great joy and we considered ourselves satisfied; we then said to ourselves that because of our diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma, what we had attained was vast and abundant."

However, the World-Honored One previously knew that our minds were attached to base desires and delighted in inferior teachings; thus, he overlooked us and did not provide individual instruction, saying: "You all shall have a share in the treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision."

“The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, has preached the wisdom of the Tathāgata. We have obtained from the Buddha the price of a single day’s worth of nirvāṇa and considered this a great gain; thus, we have had no aspiration for this Great Vehicle. Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, we have revealed and expounded it for the sake of the bodhisattvas, yet we ourselves have had no aspiration for it.”

Why is this? The Buddha knew that our minds delighted in the lesser Dharma and, through the power of skillful means, taught us accordingly; yet we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha. Now we finally understand that the World-Honored One is not stingy with his Buddha-wisdom.

Why is this? We have been true sons of the Buddha from of old, yet we took pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma. Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma], the Buddha would have taught us the Mahāyāna. In this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle; as for his former disparagement of śrāvakas who delight in the Lesser Dharma before the bodhisattvas, the Buddha was in fact teaching and transforming them through the Mahāyāna. Therefore, we say that originally we had no heart that sought anything; now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously, and all that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been attained.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching; With joy and exultation, we have attained what we never had before.”
The Buddha says that śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood;
this supreme mass of jewels is obtained spontaneously without seeking.
It is like a child, young and ignorant, who leaves his father and flees, wandering far away to another land.
He wandered through various countries for more than fifty years;
having searched in all directions until he was exhausted, he settled in one city,
built a residence, and amused himself with the five desires.
Abounding in gold and silver, *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*, pearls and *vaidūrya*;
elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; palanquins, carriages, and vehicles; fields and estates, servants and attendants;
and a vast multitude of people.
The profits from their transactions spread throughout other lands;
merchants and traders were found everywhere. Surrounded and honored by assemblies of many hundreds of thousands of millions, they were revered by all.
He is always cherished and remembered by kings;
the ministers and noble clans all together revere him;
for these various reasons, those who come and go are numerous.
Though he was thus wealthy and possessed great power, he had grown old in years and his anxiety for his son increased. Day and night he thought:
"The time of my death is approaching; my foolish son has left me for over fifty years.
What shall become of the treasures and goods in my storehouses?"
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from country to country;
sometimes he obtained something, and sometimes he obtained nothing, until he became emaciated by hunger and malnutrition, and sores and scabs broke out upon his body.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city where his father lived; wandering about seeking employment, he eventually reached his father’s house.
At that time, the elder was within his gate, seated upon a lion throne beneath a great jeweled canopy.
Some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects; they recorded the income and expenditure of their property in written vouchers and ledgers.
When the impoverished son saw his father—so noble, wealthy, and majestic—he thought, "This must be a king," or "He is one of the royal class."
Terrified and filled with self-wonder, he thought, "For what reason have I come to this place? He further reflected:
"If I remain here for long, I may be subjected to coercion and forced into labor."
Having reflected thus, he hurried away, inquiring after a poor neighborhood where he wished to go and seek employment.
At that time, the elder was on his lion throne; seeing his son from afar, he recognized him silently.
He immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him.
The impoverished son cried out in alarm and, falling into confusion and distress, collapsed to the ground:
"This man is seizing me; he will surely kill me! What use have I for food and clothing that he should bring me to this state?"
The elder, knowing that his son was foolish and narrow-minded, did not believe his words nor recognize him as his father;
he therefore employed a skillful means and sent others—men who were one-eyed, short, and ugly, and lacking in majesty—saying to them: "You may say this to him:"
"I shall hire you; if you clear away all manner of filth and refuse, I will pay you double wages.
Hearing this, the impoverished son followed him with joy, and set about clearing away the filth and refuse.
He cleansed the various rooms and chambers.
From the window, the elder constantly saw his son; thinking of his son’s folly and inferiority, he noted that the boy delighted in menial tasks.
Thereupon the elder, wearing tattered and soiled garments and carrying a dung-removal vessel, went to where his son was;
employing skillful means to draw near, he spoke to him, ordering him to work diligently, saying:
"I shall increase your wages, provide you with oil for your feet, ensure your food and drink are sufficient, and furnish you with thick and warm bedding."
With such words of exhortation, you should diligently apply yourself;
yet with gentle words, as if toward his own son.
After twenty years have passed, having been entrusted with the management of the household affairs, he shows him the gold and silver.
Pearls and crystal, all things coming and going, he makes them known;
yet he remains outside the gate, dwelling in a thatched hut, thinking to himself of his poverty:
"I have no such things."
Desiring to bestow wealth and property, he immediately gathered his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders; before this great assembly, he declared, "This is my son.
He left me to travel elsewhere for fifty years, and now that I have seen him come as my son..."
It has already been twenty years.
Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; having wandered everywhere in search of him, I have finally arrived here.
"Whatever I possess—my house, my people, and all else—I entrust it all to you; use it as you please.
Remembering your former poverty and your lowly aspirations, you have now obtained from your father great treasures, as well as this house and all its wealth."
They were filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
The Buddha was likewise; knowing that we delighted in the lesser [vehicle], he never said to us, "You shall become Buddhas."
Yet you have said that we have attained all the outflows-free states and achieved the stage of the Lesser Vehicle as śrāvaka disciples.
The Buddha has commanded us to preach the supreme path, saying that those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood.
Receiving the Buddha’s instruction, I act as a great bodhisattva, using various causes and conditions and diverse parables,
as well as manifold expressions, to expound the unsurpassed path.
"O sons of the Buddhas, having heard the Dharma from me, you shall contemplate it day and night and practice it with diligent effort.
At that time, the Buddhas immediately bestowed upon them their predictions of enlightenment.
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
This Dharma of the secret treasury is expounded only for the sake of bodhisattvas to reveal its true reality;
it was not for my sake that this essential truth was taught."
Just as that impoverished son, having come near his father, although he knew of all the goods, did not desire to take them;
so too it is with us: though we speak of the Buddha’s precious treasury, we ourselves lack the aspiration for it.
"We have attained internal extinction and consider ourselves sufficient; we understand only this matter and nothing more.
If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands or teaching and transforming sentient beings, we would feel no joy at all. Why is this?"
All dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; they are without arising and without cessation, without greatness and without smallness, and without outflows and without conditioned activity.
Reflecting thus, they do not give rise to joy or delight.
Throughout the long night, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, we have been without craving or attachment, and have had no further aspiration;
instead, we considered our own [limited] dharma to be the ultimate.
For a long night, we have practiced the dharma of emptiness;
having attained liberation from the afflictions of suffering within the three realms, we abide in our final bodies within the nirvana with remainder.
The teachings of the Buddha bring the attainment of the Way to fruition; thus, one has already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
Although we, as sons of the Buddhas, have expounded the Bodhisattva Dharma to seek the path of the Buddha, we have never had any longing or delight for this Dharma.
The Teacher, seeing that [the disciples] were being neglected, observed their state of mind and did not at first encourage them by speaking of actual benefits;
rather, through the power of skillful means, he subdued their minds, and only then entrusted [the teaching to them].
Regarding all wealth and treasures;
for those who know contentment with little, he uses the power of skillful means to discipline their minds,
and only then teaches them great wisdom.

Today we have attained what we have never had before; it was not what we previously hoped for, yet now we have obtained it ourselves—just like that impoverished son who obtained immeasurable treasure.
World-Honored One, we have now attained the Way and its fruition; regarding the outflow-free Dharma, we have obtained the pure eye.
Throughout the long night, we upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and only today have we begun to receive their fruit and retribution.
Within the Dharma of the Dharma-King, we have long cultivated the holy life, and now we have attained the outflow-free state.
The unsurpassed supreme fruit;
we who are now truly śrāvakas shall, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, cause all to hear.
A true Arhat, among all the worlds— including devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās—
is universally worthy of receiving offerings therein.
The World-Honored One’s great kindness, through this rare occurrence, has compassionately taught and transformed us for our benefit;
throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could ever repay it?
Providing for them with hands and feet, prostrating with head and crown, and offering every form of worship— none of these can repay their kindness;
even if one were to carry them upon the head or bear them on both shoulders with a devoted heart of reverence throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
As well as various bedding and furniture, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood,
and all manner of precious jewels— using these to erect stupas and temples, spreading jeweled robes upon the ground,
and performing such deeds as these for the sake of making offerings;
Even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not repay [their kindness].
The Buddhas possess rare, immeasurable, and boundless, inconceivable, and great supernormal powers;
they are the Kings of all dharmas, untainted and unconditioned, yet they are able to endure such matters for the sake of those who are inferior.
For ordinary people who grasp at signs, [the Buddha] speaks according to what is appropriate.
Having attained supreme mastery, he knows the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings,
as well as their mental capacities and strengths, and teaches according to what each can bear.
Using immeasurable parables, he preaches the Dharma according to the roots of goodness cultivated by sentient beings in their past lives;
furthermore, knowing who has reached maturity and who has not, and having discerned these various distinctions through careful consideration,
he teaches the One Vehicle path as three vehicles according to what is appropriate.
The Added Chapters of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Two;
The Added Chapters of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India together with Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Five: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples:
“Excellent, excellent!
“Kāśyapa! You have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits.

It is indeed as you have said; furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, which you would be unable to exhaustively describe even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.”
Kāśyapa, you should know this:
the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never in vain. Regarding all dharmas, he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means.

All the teachings he proclaims reach the ground of omniscience. The Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all dharmas, and he also knows the deep-seated inclinations and practices of all sentient beings, penetrating them all without obstruction.
Furthermore, he thoroughly investigates and clearly understands all phenomena, demonstrating to all sentient beings every form of wisdom.
Kāśyapa, it is like this:
for example, within a trichiliocosm, there are mountains, rivers, valleys, and the various things produced by the soil.
The various species of herbs, trees, groves, and medicinal plants, each differing in their kind, names, and forms— when dense clouds spread everywhere,
covering the entire trichiliocosm, and rain falls equally at once, its moisture universally saturating them—
the herbs, trees, groves, and medicinal plants with small roots, small stems, and small...
Branches, small leaves, medium roots, medium stems, medium branches, medium leaves, large roots, large stems,
large branches, and large leaves— according to the superior, middling, or inferior size of each tree, they each receive their portion;
rained upon by a single cloud, they grow according to their respective natures, bearing flowers and fruit.
Kāśyapa, you should know that although these plants grow from the same ground and are moistened by the same rain, each species of grass and tree has its own distinctions.
Kāśyapa, you should know!

The Tathāgata is also like this: appearing in the world like the rising of a great cloud, he proclaims with a great voice throughout the world of devas, humans, and asuras. Just as that great cloud covers the trichiliocosm, he utters these words amidst the great assembly:

"I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān. I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall cause those who have not been liberated to be liberated; I shall cause those who have not found peace to find peace; I shall cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa. I know the present and future worlds as they truly are."

"I am the all-knowing one, the all-seeing one; I am the knower of the path, the opener of the path, and the teacher of the path. You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma."

At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to hear the Dharma. The Tathāgata then observed the sharpness or dullness of these beings' faculties, their diligence or indolence, and preached the Dharma to them according to what they were capable of bearing. In various and immeasurable ways, he caused them all to rejoice and to swiftly obtain excellent benefit.

When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will enjoy peace and security in the present life and be reborn in favorable realms in future lives. Through the Path they shall experience happiness and also hear the Dharma; having heard the Dharma, they will be freed from all obstacles and, according to their individual capacities among all dharmas, gradually enter the Path. It is like that great cloud raining down upon all the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs, which, according to their respective natures, fully receive its moisture and each attains growth.

The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation—which ultimately culminates in all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and if they uphold it, read and recite it, or practice according to its teachings, they will not themselves perceive or know the merit they thereby obtain. Why is this?
Only the Tathāgata knows the seeds, characteristics, and essential natures of these sentient beings:
what they contemplate, what they ponder,
and what they cultivate.
What is mindfulness?
What is volition?
What is cultivation?
By means of what dharma does one recollect?
By means of what dharma does one contemplate?
By means of what dharma does one cultivate?
By what dharma is what dharma attained?

Sentient beings abide in various stages; only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clear and unimpeded knowledge, just as grasses, trees, thickets, and medicinal herbs do not themselves know whether their nature is superior, middling, or inferior.

The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation—which is ultimately the state of nirvāṇa, eternally quiescent, and finally returning to emptiness.

The Buddha, having known this, observes the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and protects them; for this reason, he does not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) to them.
"You, Kāśyapa, are truly rare, for you are able to understand that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and you are able to believe and accept it."
"Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Dharma King who destroys existence has appeared in the world; according to the desires of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma in various ways.
The Tathāgata is revered, his wisdom profound and far-reaching; for a long time he has kept this essential teaching in silence, not being in a hurry to speak it."
Those with wisdom, upon hearing it, will be able to believe and understand;
those without wisdom will harbor doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss. Therefore, Kāśyapa!
He teaches according to their capacities, using various causes and conditions to enable them to attain right view.
Kāśyapa, you should know:
it is like a great cloud that arises in the world and covers everything.
Benevolent clouds held moisture, and flashes of lightning gleamed; the sound of thunder reverberated afar, bringing joy to all.
The sunlight was obscured, the earth became cool and refreshing, and the clouds hung low and thick as if they could be grasped.
That rain falls equally upon all, descending simultaneously from the four quarters; it flows in measureless torrents, saturating the entire land.
Whatever grows in the deep recesses—herbs, trees, medicinal plants, small and large shrubs, the various grains and crops, sugarcane, and grapes—all are moistened by the rain.
There is nothing that is not abundantly satisfied.
From those clouds, a water of a single flavor issues forth; the grasses, trees, and forests receive its moisture according to their respective capacities.
Among all the various trees—whether superior, middling, or inferior—each is nourished accordingly.
According to their size, each attains growth;
roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and their luster and color—wherever this single rain reaches, all attain freshness and brilliance;
according to their physical forms and the capacities of their natures, though the moisture they receive is one and the same.
Each flourishes and thrives.
The Buddha is likewise; appearing in the world like a great cloud, he universally covers all.
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings, he analytically expounds the reality of all phenomena.
The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, amidst all the devas and humans, within the entire assembly,
proclaims these words:
"Appearing in the world like a great cloud, he moistens and nourishes all."
May all withered sentient beings be made to leave suffering behind and attain peaceful happiness;
may the world’s joys and the bliss of nirvana be heard with single-minded devotion by all the hosts of devas and humans.
All should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.

I am the World-Honored One, whom none can equal; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I have appeared in this world to preach for the great assembly the pure Dharma of ambrosia.
That Dharma is of a single flavor: liberation and nirvana.
With a single wondrous voice, he expounds this meaning;
it constantly serves as the causal condition for the Mahāyāna.
I observe all things as universally equal, Without the notions of self and other,
or love and hatred.
Free from attachment and without obstruction, I constantly preach the Dharma equally for all.
As for one person, so it is for many; he constantly expounds the Dharma, never having any other concern.
Whether walking, coming, sitting, or standing, he never grows weary; he satisfies the world, just as rain provides moisture.
Whether they are complete in dignified deportment or incomplete, whether they possess right view or wrong view,
and whether their faculties are sharp or dull— to all of them he rains down the rain of Dharma without weariness.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide upon various stages:
some dwell among humans or devas, as universal monarchs, Śakras, or Brahmās; these are the minor medicinal herbs.
Those who are able to attain nirvāṇa, give rise to the six supernormal powers,
and obtain the three insights; who dwell alone in mountain forests, constantly practice meditative concentration, and realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha—
these are the medicinal herbs.

Seeking the state of the World-Honored One, thinking "I shall become a Buddha," and practicing the concentration of diligence— these are the superior medicinal herbs. Single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha-way,
constantly practicing loving-kindness and compassion, knowing for themselves that they will become Buddhas with certainty and without doubt— these are called small trees.
Turning the wheel of non-retrogression, they deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
such Bodhisattvas are called "Great Trees."
Just as a rain of a single flavor, according to the natures of sentient beings, is received differently—
just as those grasses and trees each receive it uniquely—
the Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to reveal and teach the one Dharma through various words and phrases.
Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, it is like a single drop in the ocean.
It fills the world with the Dharma of a single flavor; according to their capacities they practice, just as the various trees and medicinal herbs in a forest, each according to its size.
Gradually increasing in growth and excellence,
may all beings in the world universally attain fulfillment; through gradual cultivation,
may they all realize the fruits of the Path.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwelling in mountain forests in their final bodies, hear the Dharma and attain the fruit;
these are called medicinal herbs, each attaining growth.
Having thoroughly understood the three realms and seeking the Supreme Vehicle, this is called a small tree that attains growth.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna and attain the power of supernatural faculties; hearing that all phenomena are empty, their hearts are filled with great joy.
Emitting countless rays of light, they deliver all sentient beings; this is called a great tree that attains growth.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is like a great cloud; with rain of a single flavor, it moistens the flowers of humanity, each attaining its own fruition.
Kāśyapa, you should know:
by means of various causes and conditions and diverse parables, I have revealed the Buddha-way; this is my skillful means, and so it is with all Buddhas.
Now for your sake, I shall speak of the most ultimate reality:
none of you śrāvakas have yet attained final nirvāṇa.
What you are practicing is the bodhisattva path; by training and studying gradually, you shall all attain buddhahood.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
the Tathāgata is impartial in his discipline toward all sentient beings. Kāśyapa!"

For example, when the light of the sun and moon illuminates the world, whether it be good or evil deeds, whether one dwells in a high place or a low place, and whether it be fragrant or foul—everywhere the light shines equally and without partiality.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

The light of the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who possesses all-knowledge, as it manifests among the beings born within the five destinies, turns the wheel of the sublime Dharma with equality according to their respective inclinations toward the Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddhayāna, or the Śrāvakayāna; yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases, arising as it does from the accumulation of merit and knowledge.
“Kāśyapa! There are no three vehicles; it is only because those sentient beings have diverse practices that the three vehicles are provisionally established.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are no three vehicles, for what reason do you manifest in the world and establish the designations of śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
