"It is like a potter who mixes clay with water to fashion vessels; among them, some may be vessels for holding granulated sugar, some for holding ghee, some for holding milk or curd, and some for holding foul excrement. Yet the clay itself possesses no such various distinctions. Rather, it is according to the substance placed within and the capacity of what it receives that the vessels are designated as being variously distinct."
"In this way, Kāśyapa, there is only this single vehicle, namely the Great Vehicle; there are no two vehicles, nor three vehicles.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those sentient beings have various inclinations and understandings; if they emerge from the triple world, will they attain one nirvāṇa, or should it be two or three?”
The Buddha told the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
“If one realizes that the essence of all phenomena is equal to nirvāṇa, that too is solely one, without a second or a third.”
Kāśyapa! For that reason, I shall provide you with a simile; by means of this simile, a wise person will understand the meaning of what I have said.
Kāśyapa! It is, for example, like a man born blind who says:
"There are no beautiful or ugly forms, nor are there any beautiful or ugly forms to be seen;..."
"There are no sun, moon, or constellations, nor are any such constellations visible.
Then, another man said these words before the one born blind:
"There are beautiful and ugly forms, and there are beautiful and ugly forms that can be seen;..."
"There are the sun, the moon, and the constellations, and the constellations and so forth are indeed visible.
Although the man blind from birth heard this explanation, he did not believe or accept it.
At that time, there was a skilled physician who understood all diseases. Seeing that man born blind, he thought to himself:
"That man previously committed evil karma, and now this disease has arisen. There are four types of such diseases, namely: wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination."
At that time, the skilled physician, wishing to extinguish the illness, again employed skillful means and reflected thus:
"The medicinal substances currently used in the world are unable to cure this disease; only on the King of Snow Mountains, the Himavat, are there four kinds of medicine."
What are these four? They are:

first, that which is called "harmoniously entering the spheres of the flavors of all forms"; second, that which is called "liberation from all illnesses"; third, that which is called "destroying all poisons"; and fourth, that which is called "bestowing peace and happiness wherever it dwells. These are the four kinds.

At that time, the skilled physician, having conceived compassion for those born blind, gave rise to such skillful means and reflections. Employing those means, he went to the King of Snow Mountains (Himavat). Upon reaching it, he ascended to its summit, descended into its depths, or traversed its slopes, examining everywhere. Having completed his examination, he obtained four kinds of medicine;

from among these, he either chewed them with his teeth and gave them to them, or ground them with stones, or else boiled them together with other medicinal substances before giving them, or else prepared them by mixing them with raw medicinal herbs before giving them.

Some pierce their bodies to create orifices; some subject them to cauterization with fire; or they mix various medicinal substances together, even incorporating them into food and drink, and give these to them.

At that time, because of his application of skillful means, the one born blind immediately regained his sight. Having regained his sight, he was able to see all forms—internal and external, distant and near, the sun, the moon, light, and the constellations—and he spoke these words: "Alas!..."

I was extremely foolish; when I heard what was previously taught, I did not believe or accept it. Now, at this time, I have seen everything clearly. My blindness has been removed, and I have also gained sight; there is none superior to me.

“At that time, there was also a seer possessing the five supernormal powers, who had the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds; who recollected his past lives and was well-versed in the supernormal power of wisdom.
He spoke to the man, saying: ‘O man!’”
"You have only obtained eyes, yet you know nothing else; why have you already given rise to arrogance? You likewise do not yet possess wisdom or skill.
He then spoke again as follows: "O Noble One!"
When you sit within the room, you do not see or know any external forms;
you likewise do not know whether sentient beings possess wholesome or unwholesome minds;
and as for all speech, drums, conchs, and other sounds occurring five *yojana*s away, you neither hear nor know them.

If you cannot walk even one krośa without lifting both feet, and once you have grown up, you do not even remember the activities performed while in your mother's womb, how can you possess skillful wisdom?
"How can you speak thus, saying, 'I have seen them all'?
Furthermore, you man, you mistake darkness for light and light for darkness.
Then that man spoke to the seer:
"By what skillful means,
and having performed what kind of pure deeds,
shall one attain this wisdom?"
"Furthermore, by virtue of the power of your pure faith, I too shall attain such merit.
Then that seer said to the man:

"If you wish for this, you should dwell in a secluded mountain cave, sit and contemplate the Dharma while severing the afflictions; thus you shall attain supernatural powers and be fully endowed with merit."

At that time, having received this teaching, the man went forth into homelessness and dwelt in a secluded place. With single-minded devotion, he severed worldly craving and attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Having attained these five supernormal powers, he reflected:
"In the past, I performed various separate karmic deeds; because of those causes, there is not a single merit by which I can be fully known."
"I recall that at that time, wherever I directed my thoughts, I was able to go there immediately;
yet in those former times, I had little knowledge and little wisdom, remaining as if blind.
"Kāśyapa! [the Buddha said.]
This parable is intended to make the meaning known; within this meaning, one should further perceive it as follows:

Kāśyapa, those who are born blind are all sentient beings dwelling within the cycle of the six realms of existence who have not yet attained awakening regarding the True Dharma. Their blindness of afflictions increases, as does the darkness of their ignorance (*avidyā*); because of the darkness of ignorance, karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) accumulate.
With volitional formations as condition, name-and-form arises, and so on, until this entire mass of suffering comes to be.

Thus, sentient beings dwell within the cycle of transmigration, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance; only the Tathāgata has transcended the three realms. Moved by compassion—just as a loving father cherishes his only son—he enters the three realms out of pity. There he beholds those sentient beings wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra, failing to know, as it truly is, the way to escape from that cycle.

The Buddha beheld them with his Buddha-eye; having seen them, he fully understood that these sentient beings had performed wholesome deeds in previous lives, yet some had little anger and great desire, while others had little desire and great anger; some possessed little wisdom, while others possessed skillful intelligence; some were mature and pure, while others held wrong views. For the sake of these sentient beings, the Buddha skillfully taught the Three Vehicles through expedient means:
those who are like seers possessing the five supernormal powers and the pure eye are the Bodhisattvas;

those who give rise to the thought of enlightenment, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and realize unexcelled, perfect, and true awakening are the Tathāgatas, who are like the great physicians.
One should view it in this way:
those who are born blind are like sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance;
one should view them in this way.
One should view those [afflictions] such as wind, jaundice, and rheumatism as being identical to desire, hatred, delusion, and the sixty-two views.
One should view them as being like the four kinds of medicine, which are identical to the gates of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and nirvana.
One should see it in this way:

just as a disease is extinguished according to the medicine one takes, so too, through the correct cultivation of mindfulness of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—ignorance shall be extinguished; because ignorance is extinguished, volitional formations are extinguished, and so on until only the great mass of suffering is extinguished.

Reflecting in this way, one dwells neither in the good nor in the evil; like a blind person regaining their sight, this is the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—one should view it in this manner.

Having severed the fetters of the afflictions that cause cyclic existence, they are liberated from those afflictions and liberated from the six destinies and the three realms. For this reason, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle think to themselves:
"There is no other dharma further to be realized; I have now attained nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for them: "If one has not yet fully reached the realization of all dharmas, how could there be ultimate *nirvāṇa* for them?

To them, the Buddha taught through *bodhi*; they gave rise to the *bodhicitta*, neither dwelling in saṃsāra nor reaching *nirvāṇa*. They realized that the three realms and the ten directions are empty and still, like illusions, dreams, mirages, and echoes. They perceived all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, neither bound nor liberated, neither dark nor bright. Thus seeing the profound Dharma, their very vision was a non-vision, yet they constantly saw the various inclinations and understandings of sentient beings filling the three realms."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as the light of the sun and moon Shines equally upon the three thousandfold world,
Upon the good and the evil alike, Their radiance neither increases nor diminishes."
The light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is impartial like the sun and moon;
in teaching and transforming all sentient beings, it neither increases nor decreases.
It is like a potter making vessels, who treats the clay with equal consistency.
Within them, some vessels may be filled with sugar, milk, ghee, or water;
some may be filled with impurities, while others are filled with curd.
The potter takes only a single lump of clay and fashions it into these various vessels.
If an object falls within it, one knows the name of the vessel because of that;
so too, for sentient beings without exception, the Tathāgata, according to their individual inclinations,
speaks of the distinctions between vehicles, yet they are definitively only the Buddha-vehicle.
Due to ignorance, one wanders in saṃsāra and does not know nirvāṇa;
if a person can know emptiness and remain far removed from the self of phenomena,
they will know the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the truly attained perfect enlightenment.
One who abides in the wisdom of the middle way is called a Pratyekabuddha;
one who, having been taught by the wisdom of emptiness, manifests it, is called a Śrāvaka;
and one who can awaken to all phenomena is called a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Suppose there were one born blind, who does not see the sun, moon, or stars;
he would then say, "No such things as forms exist.
For the sake of such a person born blind, the Great Physician enters into compassion for him.
Having gone to the Snowy Mountains, he traveled above, below, and across;
there he sought out excellent medicines and entered the realms of form and flavor.
Combining these four kinds [of elements], he administered the treatment.
Some use their teeth to bite, some grind with stones,
or pierce the body with needles to treat those born blind.
Once they have regained their sight, they immediately behold the light of the sun and moon.
Again, he reflects thus: "In the past, those lacking wisdom spoke [thus].
These transmigrating sentient beings are born blind and utterly ignorant;
driven by the wheel of dependent origination, they suffer the path of ignorance."
In this world of ignorance and delusion, the Tathāgata—
the Great Physician who possesses all-knowledge— manifests a body of compassionate essence.
Through skillful means, he proclaims the peaceful and correct Dharma.
The unsurpassed Buddha’s awakening wisdom expounds the most excellent vehicle;
he extensively teaches the middle way, the Guide of middling wisdom.
For those who fear cyclic existence, he praises the distinction of enlightenment.
Having emerged from the three realms, the śrāvaka knows for himself that he abides thus:
"I have attained the stainless peace of nirvāṇa;
I shall attain the awakening to all dharmas, the state of the nectar of nirvāṇa."
Because of that, the Great Sage, out of compassion for him, said: "You are foolish; do not think, 'I am wise.
If there is a granary, when you dwell within it,"
If you do not know what exists outside, you are one of small intelligence.
Even when dwelling within that [interior], if you do not know what has been done or left undone outside, even that is not true knowledge; how much less so for you of small intelligence?
If a sound were to arise from a distance of five yojanas, you would not be able to hear it; how much less so if one dwells elsewhere far away?
Whether others harbor thoughts of love or malice toward you—
Since you cannot know that [reality], how can you give rise to universal pride?
If you wish to go to a krośa, you cannot reach it without walking;
you have likewise forgotten all that occurred while in the womb.
If one attains the five supernormal powers, Only then is one called "All-Knowing.
You are deluded and possess not a single wisdom, Yet you claim to be a wise one.
If you desire all-knowledge, It must arise from the supernormal powers.
If one dwells in a secluded place, supernatural powers may emerge;
by contemplating the pure Dharma, one shall attain such powers.
Having received the meaning of the teachings, one goes to a secluded place and enters a quiet chamber for contemplation.
Having attained the five supernormal powers, they will soon be endowed with merit;
yet these śrāvakas conceive the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa.
When the Buddhas speak at that time, they say it is merely a brief rest, not nirvāṇa.
This is the skillful means of all Buddhas, who preach such a path for this purpose.
Apart from omniscience, there is no awakening to nirvāṇa;
the wisdom of the three times is boundless, and the practice of the six perfections is pure.
Emptiness, tranquility, and signlessness; the relinquishing of aspirations as well;
the bodhicitta and distinct dharmas directed toward nirvāṇa;
the four kinds of brahma-conduct, and the four means of attraction are also praised and taught.
To teach and transform sentient beings, the Supreme Sage has spoken this.
If one further knows that all phenomena have a self-nature like an illusion or a dream,
unreal like a plantain tree, and equal to an echo;
And knowing that very nature, there remains nothing further within the three realms;
neither bound nor liberated, one does not perceive even nirvana.
All phenomena are equal and empty, for there exists no distinct entity.
This, too, is without anything seen; one does not observe even a single dharma.
Those who see the Great Wise One perceive the Dharmakāya without remainder;
therein are no three vehicles, for within it there is but the One Vehicle.
"All dharmas are equal; They are eternally equal and uniform.
Having realized such wisdom, One dwells in the peace of the nectar of Nirvāṇa.

Chapter Six: Bestowal of Prophecies The Added Chapter of the Lotus Sutra, Chapter Six: Bestowal of Prophecies At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly, proclaiming these words:

"This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, shall in a future age behold three hundred trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them. He shall widely proclaim the immeasurable Great Dharma of these Buddhas, and in his final body, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Prabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land shall be named Prabhāśrī, and his eon shall be named Mahāvyūha. The lifespan of that Buddha shall be twelve minor kalpas; the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas."

The realm is magnificently adorned, free from all impurities, filth, rubble, thorns, excrement, and uncleanness. Its ground is level and even, without elevations, depressions, pits, ravines, mounds, or hillocks. It has lapis lazuli for its floor and rows of jewel-trees; golden cords demarcate the sides of the roads, and various precious flowers are scattered everywhere, making it utterly pure.

In that land, there are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas, and the assembly of śrāvakas is likewise incalculable. There are no demonic disturbances; though there are māras and their followers, they all protect the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"With my Buddha-eye, I see that this Kāśyapa, in a future age, after the passing of incalculable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood."
And in a future age, they shall offer worship and pay homage to three million billion Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones;
for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom, they shall purely cultivate the Brahma-faring.
Having made offerings to the Most Supreme, the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings,
and having cultivated and accumulated all unsurpassed wisdom, he attained Buddhahood in his final body.
That land is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground; many jewel trees stand in rows along the roadsides, and golden cords mark the boundaries of the paths, bringing joy to all who behold them.
It constantly emits exquisite fragrances and scatters various famous flowers of every kind of wonder.
It serves as an adornment;
its ground is level and even, without mounds or pits;
the assembly of bodhisattvas is beyond measure, their minds being harmonious and supple.
Having attained great supernormal powers, they uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras of all Buddhas.
The assembly of śrāvakas—those in their final bodies who are free from outflows, the sons of the Dharma King—is likewise incalculable; even with the divine eye, one could not count or know them.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas;
the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas;
and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas.
"Such was the matter concerning the World-Honored One Prabhāsa.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and the others were all struck with awe and trepidation; with single-minded devotion they joined their palms, gazing up at the World-Honored One without so much as blinking for a moment, and then together in one voice, they spoke this verse:
"The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, The Dharma King of all the Śākyas."
Out of compassion for us, you have bestowed the Buddha’s melodic voice.
If you know our profound intent and grant us this prediction of enlightenment,
it will be like sprinkling us with nectar, removing our fever and bringing us refreshing coolness.
Like one who has come from a land of famine, Suddenly encountering the meal of a great king,
The heart still harbors doubt and fear, And does not dare to eat it immediately;
Only after receiving the king’s command Does one then dare to eat.
We are also like this; constantly reflecting upon the faults of the Hīnayāna, we did not know how we might attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
Although we heard the Buddha’s voice saying that we shall become Buddhas, [we remained in doubt].
My mind still harbors anxiety and fear, as if I have not yet dared to eat;
if I am granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Buddha, only then shall I find swift peace and joy.
O Great Hero, World-Honored One, you who ever desire to bring peace to the world.
“We pray that you grant us an instruction, just as one who is hungry must be taught what to eat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of his great disciples, addressed the bhikṣus:

“Subhūti, in a future age, you shall behold three hundred trillion nayutas of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising them. Constantly practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and perfecting the path of a Bodhisattva, in your final existence you shall attain Buddhahood, with the title of Vimalanāman Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The kalpa shall be named Ratnasaṃbhava, and the land shall be named Ratnasambhava. That realm will be level and even, with crystal for its ground, adorned with jeweled trees; it will be free from mounds, pits, gravel, thorns, and the impurities of excrement and urine, with precious flowers covering the ground everywhere in pure clarity.”
The people of that land all dwell in jeweled terraces and exquisite, precious pavilions;
his śrāvaka disciples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy;
and the assembly of bodhisattvas consists of countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be twelve small kalpas; the True Dharma will remain in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma will likewise remain for twenty small kalpas.
That Buddha will constantly abide in the void, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly and delivering immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“O assembly of bhikṣus, I now address you all: You should all listen with a single mind to what I say.”
"My great disciple, Subhūti, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Mingxiang (Renowned Aspect).
He shall make offerings to countless billions of Buddhas;
following what the Buddhas perform, he shall gradually fulfill the Great Way and, in his final body, obtain the thirty-two marks."
His appearance is upright and exquisite, like a mountain of jewels;
his buddha-field is foremost in its solemn purity, and among sentient beings who behold it, there are none who do not feel love and joy.
Within that land, the Buddha delivers immeasurable multitudes;
within his Dharma, there are many bodhisattvas, all of whom possess sharp faculties and turn the wheel of non-retrogression;
that land is constantly adorned by such bodhisattvas.
All have attained the three insights and are endowed with the six supernormal powers; abiding in the eight liberations, they possess great majestic virtue.
When that Buddha preaches the Dharma, he manifests immeasurable supernatural transformations that are inconceivable.
Devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all joined their palms together to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas;
the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas.
"The Semblance Dharma shall also remain for twenty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"I now tell you: this Mahākātyāyana, in a future age, shall provide offerings and serve eight thousand koṭis of buddhas with all manner of requisites, honoring and respecting them."
After the parinirvāṇa of each of these Buddhas, stupas and temples shall be erected, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly symmetrical;

they shall be composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—and shall be honored with offerings of various flowers, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers.
After this period has passed, he shall again make offerings to twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, likewise in the same manner.

Having made offerings to these Buddhas and perfected the path of a Bodhisattva, he shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Jambūnada-prabhāsa-golden-light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land shall be level and even, with ground of crystal, adorned with jeweled trees, and demarcated along its borders with golden cords. Wondrous flowers shall cover the ground everywhere, pure and pristine, bringing joy to all who behold it.
There are no four evil realms—the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras; rather, there are many devas and humans, as well as a multitude of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Countless tens of billions adorn that land.
The Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas; the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All you assembly of bhikṣus, listen with one mind;
what I have spoken is true and without deviation."
This Kātyāyana shall, with various kinds of exquisite offerings, make offerings to the Buddhas;
after the Buddhas have passed into extinction, he shall erect stupas of the seven treasures and likewise offer flowers and incense to their relics.
In his final body, he shall attain the wisdom of a Buddha, realize equal and perfect enlightenment,
and possess a pure land;
he shall deliver and liberate immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings.
All are honored by the ten directions; none can surpass them. That Buddha’s name is Jambūnada-prabhāsa;
his bodhisattvas and śrāvakas have severed all existence.
"Immeasurable and innumerable [deities] shall adorn that land.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly:

"I now tell you: this Mahāmaudgalyāyana shall, with various kinds of offerings, make offerings to eight thousand Buddhas, honoring and respecting them. After those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, he shall each erect a stūpa and temple one thousand yojanas high, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearl, and ruby—and using various flowers, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers as offerings."

After this period has passed, he shall again make offerings to two hundred trillion Buddhas, likewise as before. He shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Tāmālapatrānulepanacandanagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The eon shall be named Priyapūrṇa, and the land shall be named Manojña;

its ground will be level and even, made of crystal, adorned with jeweled trees, strewn with pearls and flowers, pure throughout, bringing joy to all who see it, and filled with countless devas, humans, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be twenty-four minor kalpas; the True Dharma will remain in the world for forty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma will likewise remain for forty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“This disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, after casting off this body,
shall behold eight thousand two hundred myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.”
For the sake of the Buddha-way, they made offerings and paid homage;
in the presence of all Buddhas, they constantly practiced the pure life (brahmacarya) and upheld the Buddha-dharma throughout immeasurable kalpas.
When the Buddhas passed into parinirvāṇa, they erected stupas of the seven treasures, with golden finials rising high as banners.
With the fragrance of flowers and the music of instruments, they made offerings to the stupas and temples of all Buddhas.
Having gradually fulfilled the path of a bodhisattva, they attained Buddhahood in the land of Abhirati.
His name was Tamāla, and his fragrance was like that of sandalwood; the lifespan of that Buddha was twenty-four kalpas.

In the south are two buddhas: the first is named Ākāśapratisthita, and the second is named Nityanirvṛta.
In the southwest are two buddhas: the first is named Indradhvaja, and the second is named Brahmaketu.
In the western direction are two Buddhas: the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātudurgatipariśodhana.
In the northwestern direction are two Buddhas: the first is named Tamālapatrakandanagandhābhijña, and the second is named Merukūṭa.
In the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Cloud Sovereignty (*Megheśvara*), and the second is named Cloud Sovereignty King (*Megheśvararāja*).
In the northeast is a Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Terrors (*Sarvalokabhayapraśamana*).
The sixteenth is I, Śākyamuni Buddha, who has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system. O bhikṣus!

"When we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us converted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; having heard the Dharma from us, they set their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Among these sentient beings, there are those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvaka; I constantly teach and transform them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for these individuals should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time are none other than you, monks, and my śrāvaka disciples in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.

After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples who have not heard this sutra; they do not know and are not aware of the conduct of bodhisattvas, yet regarding the merits they have attained themselves, they give rise to the notion of having attained parinirvāṇa and think they shall enter nirvana.

In other lands I shall become a Buddha under different names; although these people may conceive the thought that they have attained extinction and entered *nirvāṇa*, they will seek the Buddha’s wisdom in those lands and hear this sutra;
they shall attain extinction solely by means of the Buddha-vehicle, for there is no other vehicle, except for the skillful means employed by the Tathāgatas in their preaching of the Dharma.

"O Bhikṣus! When the Tathāgata knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and when the assembly is pure, their faith and understanding firm, they have thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness and entered deeply into meditative concentration, he then gathers the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas and preaches this sūtra for them."
"In this world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the Single Buddha Vehicle that one attains extinction.
Bhikṣus, you should know!

Through the skillful means of the Tathāgata, he has deeply entered the nature of sentient beings and knows that their aspirations and inclinations lie in inferior teachings, and that they are deeply attached to the five desires. For their sake, he speaks of nirvāṇa, so that when these people hear it, they immediately believe and accept it."

Suppose there were a perilous and difficult evil road five hundred yojanas long, desolate, uninhabited, and a place of terror; if there were a great multitude wishing to traverse this path to reach a place of precious jewels, and there was a guide who was wise, discerning, and thoroughly understood the characteristics of the obstacles and clear passages of that dangerous road, leading the people across this hardship.
The multitude he led grew weary and despondent along the way, and they said to the guide:
"We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear; we can go no further. The path ahead is still long, and we now wish to turn back."
The guide, possessing many skillful means, thought to himself:
"These people are to be pitied; why do they wish to turn back, abandoning such great treasures?"
Having formed this thought, by the power of skillful means, he created an illusory city within the perilous path, three hundred *yojanas* away.
He addressed the multitude, saying:

"Do not be afraid; do not turn back. You may halt here in this great city and do as you please. If you enter this city, you will find swift peace and security; if you can proceed further to the place of treasures, you may go there as well."
At that time, the exhausted multitude was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying:
"We have now escaped this evil path; we have swiftly attained peace and security."
Thereupon, the multitude entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought of having attained peace and security.
At that time, the guide, knowing that this multitude had found rest and was no longer weary, immediately caused the conjured city to vanish and said to the multitude:
"You all, come! The place of jewels is near. That great city you saw earlier was merely a conjuration of mine for the purpose of providing rest."
“Monks! The Tathāgata is likewise;
he now acts as your great guide, knowing the various paths of birth and death, the afflictions, and the evil realms—those perilous and distant places that must be left behind and crossed over.”
If sentient beings were to hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha nor wish to draw near him, and would instead think:
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring toil and suffering for a long time can it be accomplished."
The Buddha, knowing that their minds were timid, weak, and inferior, employed skillful means to provide them with rest along the way, and thus spoke of two nirvāṇas.
If sentient beings abide in the second stage, the Tathāgata then immediately says to them:

"What you have accomplished is not yet complete; the stage upon which you abide is close to the Buddha-wisdom. You should observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality; it is merely the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means to differentiate and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."
"Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjured a great city, and once he knew they had rested, he told them:
'The place of jewels is near; this city is not real, for I conjured it.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas;
yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood."
The various devas and nāga kings, along with the hosts of asuras and others,
constantly rained down celestial flowers to make offerings to that Buddha.
The devas beat celestial drums and performed all manner of musical arts.
A fragrant breeze blows away the withered flowers and rains down new and beautiful ones;
after ten intermediate kalpas have passed, he shall attain the Way of the Buddha,
and all the devas and people of the world will harbor hearts of exultant joy.
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, each surrounded by their own retinues of thousands of myriads of koṭis, all proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was;
bowing their heads at the Buddha’s feet, they entreated him to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
The Dharma-rain of the Holy Lion fills me and all beings;
the World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter, appearing but once in the course of vast eons.
To awaken all living creatures, he causes all things to tremble.
In the various worlds of the eastern direction, across five hundred myriads of koṭis of lands,
the palaces of the Brahmās shone with a brilliance such as had never been seen before;
seeing these signs, the Brahmās immediately came to where the Buddha was.
Scattering flowers as an offering, and presenting palaces,
he requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma and praised him with verses;
knowing that the time had not yet come, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
In the three directions and the four intermediate points, and likewise above and below, they scattered flowers and offered palaces, entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
"The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter; we pray that with great compassion," [you will grant our request].
He widely opened the gate of ambrosia and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
The World-Honored One of immeasurable wisdom, having accepted the invitation of the multitude, proclaimed for them various teachings:
the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
From ignorance through old age and death, all arise conditioned by birth;
such are the manifold afflictions—you all should know them.
When this Dharma was proclaimed, six hundred trillion nayutas [of beings attained realization].
They attained the end of all suffering and all became Arhats.
During the second discourse on the Dharma, a multitude as vast as the sands of ten million Ganges Rivers,
through non-attachment to all phenomena, likewise attained Arhatship.
From that time onward, those who attained the Way were beyond measure;
even through the calculation of ten trillion kalpas, one could not reach their limit.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras.
We all together entreat that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma.
We, along with our retinues, shall all attain the path of Buddhahood;
may we obtain a wisdom-eye as supremely pure as that of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, knowing the mind of the youth and his practices in past lives,
through immeasurable causes and conditions and various similes,
taught the six pāramitās as well as the matters of the supernormal powers.
Discerning the true Dharma is the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Having spoken this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
that Buddha, having finished preaching the sutra, entered meditative concentration in a quiet chamber.
Sitting with single-minded focus in one place for eighty-four thousand kalpas,
these śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had not yet emerged from his meditation;
for the sake of immeasurable billions of beings, they expounded the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.
Each sat upon the Dharma-seat and preached this Mahāyāna sūtra;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation through the Dharma.
Each and every śrāmaṇera likewise delivered all sentient beings.
There were six trillion beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
After that Buddha had passed into extinction, all those who had heard the Dharma were born together with their Teacher in every Buddha-field wherever they may be.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras, having fully practiced the path of the Buddha,
now currently dwell throughout the ten directions, each having attained perfect enlightenment.
Those who heard the Dharma at that time are each now present before various Buddhas.
Those who abide in the stage of śrāvaka, I gradually instruct in the Buddha-way.
When I was among the sixteen, I also spoke for you;
therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I lead you toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
For these fundamental reasons, I now preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to lead you into the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm.
It is like a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, filled with many venomous beasts;
furthermore, it lacks water and grass, a place feared by all people.
Countless tens of millions of beings desire to cross this treacherous path.
The road was exceedingly vast and remote, spanning five hundred yojanas.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed a powerful memory and wisdom;
with a clear and resolute mind, he rescued the multitude from their perils.
All the people were weary and said to the Guide:
"We are now utterly exhausted; we wish to turn back here.
The Guide thought to himself:
"These people are truly pitiable; how can they wish to turn back and lose such a great treasure?
I shall immediately contemplate a skillful means and employ my supernatural powers to manifest a great city, adorned with various mansions and dwellings."
Surrounded by gardens and groves, with flowing canals and bathing pools, and with double gates and lofty pavilions, men and women were all present in abundance.
Having created these transformations, he comforted the multitude, saying: "Do not fear!"
"Enter this city, each according to your pleasure.
Once all the people have entered the city, their hearts will be filled with great joy;
they will all conceive a sense of security and believe that they have already attained deliverance."
The Guide, knowing they were rested, gathered the assembly and addressed them:
"You should proceed forward; this was merely a conjured city!
Seeing that you were utterly exhausted and wished to turn back midway,"
Therefore, by the power of skillful means, I have temporarily conjured this city;
now that you are diligent and energetic, you shall together reach the place of treasure.
I am likewise so, acting as the guide for all.
Seeing those seekers of the Way who grow weary and desist midway,
unable to cross over birth and death or the perilous paths of affliction,
he therefore employs the power of skillful means to preach nirvana as a place of rest.
"You have extinguished suffering; that which was to be done has all been accomplished.
Since you know you have reached Nirvana, you have all attained Arhatship.
Only then did he assemble the great assembly and preach the True Dharma for them.
By the power of skillful means, the Buddhas distinguish and teach the three vehicles;
yet there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, taught as two for the sake of providing rest.
Now I shall speak the truth to you: what you have attained is not final extinction.
For the sake of the Buddha’s omniscience, you should arouse great diligence;
when you realize omniscience, possessing the ten powers and other Buddha-qualities along with the thirty-two marks, that is indeed true cessation.
The Guides of all Buddhas, for the sake of quiescence, preach nirvāṇa;
once they know that [the disciples] have attained this quiescence, they lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.
— *The Sutra of the Lotus Flower of the Wonderful Dharma*, Scroll Three, with Added Chapters.
The Added Chapters to the Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India, together with Dharmagupta, during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Prophecy Bestowed upon the Five Hundred Disciples. Chapter Eight: The Prophecy Bestowed upon the Five Hundred Disciples.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard from the Buddha this teaching of wisdom and skillful means according to what was appropriate, and having further heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples, and having also heard of the events of his past lives and the great sovereign power of the supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*) of all Buddhas, attained a state never before experienced; his heart was purified and he leaped with joy. He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he did not for a moment turn his eyes away, and he thought to himself:

“The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; what he does is rare and unprecedented. In accordance with the various dispositions of the world, he preaches the Dharma through skillful means and insight, uprooting sentient beings from their attachments everywhere. We are unable to fully proclaim the Buddha’s merits in words; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our deep-seated intentions and original vows.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?

I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, and I have also constantly praised his various merits: his diligent protection and assistance in proclaiming my Dharma; his ability to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly; his complete exposition of the Buddha’s true Dharma; and his great benefit to his fellow practitioners of the holy life. Apart from the Tathāgata, no one is able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse."

"You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming my Dharma; he has also, in the past, protected, upheld, and assisted in proclaiming the true Dharma of ninety billion Buddhas, and among those who proclaimed the Dharma at that time, he was likewise the foremost."

Furthermore, they clearly understand and penetrate the Dharma of emptiness taught by all Buddhas and attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). They are always able to expound the Dharma with meticulous accuracy and purity, free from doubt, and are fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva. Throughout their lifespans, they constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), such that those Buddhas and the people of that world all regard them as being truly śrāvakas.

Pūrṇa, by means of these skillful means, benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings; furthermore, he transformed immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people, causing them to establish themselves in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For the sake of purifying a buddha-field, he constantly performs the work of a Buddha, teaching and transforming sentient beings.
"O Bhikṣus! Pūrṇa was foremost among those who expound the Dharma under the seven Buddhas;
he is now foremost among those who expound the Dharma under me, and he shall be foremost among those who expound the Dharma for all future Buddhas throughout this Bhadrakalpa."
They are likewise foremost in the present, protecting, upholding, and assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha-dharma;
they will also, in the future, protect, uphold, and assist in the proclamation of the immeasurable and boundless Dharma of all Buddhas,
teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, establishing them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and for the sake of purifying their buddha-fields, they shall always—
Diligently exerting himself to transform sentient beings, he will gradually fulfill the path of a bodhisattva;
after the passage of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this very land,
and his name shall be Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata.
Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans,
Buddha, World-Honored One.

That Buddha takes as many trichiliocosms as there are sands in the Ganges River to constitute a single buddha-field. The ground is composed of the seven treasures and is as level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, hills, valleys, streams, ditches, or ravines. Within it, towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures fill the space, while the palaces of the various devas are situated nearby in the void; humans and devas interact, seeing one another. There are no evil realms, nor are there any women; all sentient beings are born by transformation, free from sexual desire. They have attained great supernormal powers, their bodies emit radiance, and they travel through the air with ease. Their resolve and mindfulness are firm, and they possess diligence and wisdom. All are universally golden in color and are adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The sentient beings of that land constantly subsist on two kinds of food: first, the food of Dharma-joy; second, the food of dhyāna-delight.

There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who have attained great supernormal powers and the four types of unimpeded wisdom, and are well able to teach and transform all classes of sentient beings.
As for the assembly of śrāvakas, they are beyond calculation or reckoning; they have all fully attained the six supernatural faculties, the three types of clear knowledge, and the eight liberations.

That buddha-field is thus adorned and perfected with such immeasurable merits. The eon is named Jewel Radiance, and the land is named Good Purity. The lifespan of that buddha is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and the Dharma remains for a very long time. After the buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures will arise and fill the entire land.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“O bhikṣus, listen attentively!
The path traversed by the sons of the Buddha, because they have skillfully studied expedient means, is inconceivable.”
Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior teachings and fears great wisdom,
the Bodhisattvas therefore manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
through countless skillful means, they transform all classes of sentient beings.
Though they claim to be śrāvakas and remain far removed from the Buddha-way,
they deliver immeasurable multitudes, all of whom attain complete accomplishment;
even if their aspirations are small and they are indolent, they shall gradually be led to become Buddhas.
Secretly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva within, while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka,
having few desires and weary of birth and death, they in truth purify their own buddha-field.
They manifest the presence of the three poisons to the multitude, and further display the marks of false views.
My disciples are thus; they deliver sentient beings through skillful means.
If I were to describe in full detail all the various manifestations of my transformations, sentient beings who heard this would harbor doubts in their hearts.
Now this Pūrṇa, under thousands of billions of Buddhas in the past,
diligently cultivated the path he was to travel; he proclaimed and protected the teachings of all Buddhas,
seeking unsurpassed wisdom, and in the presence of those Buddhas—
Among the present disciples, he is foremost; He is widely learned and possesses wisdom.
What he speaks is fearless, Able to bring joy to the multitude.
Never experiencing weariness, He thus assists in the Buddha’s work.
Having already attained great supernormal powers and being endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom,
he knows the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings and constantly preaches the pure Dharma.
Expounding such meanings as these, he instructs trillions of beings.
Causing others to abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma, they purify their own buddha-fields.
In the future as well, they will make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas,
protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the True Dharma, and likewise purifying their own buddha-fields.
Constantly employing various skillful means, they preach the Dharma without fear;
they deliver immeasurable multitudes and achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
They make offerings to all Tathāgatas and protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma-jewel.
Thereafter he attained Buddhahood, His name was called Dharmaprabha;
His land was named Sunirmala, Composed of the seven precious jewels;
The eon was named Ratnaprabha, And the assembly of bodhisattvas was exceedingly vast.
Their number is immeasurable; all possess great supernormal powers and are fully endowed with majestic virtue and strength, filling his land.
His śrāvakas are likewise countless, possessing the three types of clear knowledge and the eight liberations.
Having attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, they constitute the Saṃgha through such qualities.
All sentient beings in that land have completely severed lustful desire;
they are born solely by transformation, their bodies adorned with the primary and secondary marks.
Feeding on the joy of the Dharma and the rapture of dhyāna, they have no further thought of other food;
there are no women there, nor are there any evil realms.
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa has brought all his merits to full completion.
"When this pure land is attained, the assembly of sages and saints will be exceedingly numerous;
such immeasurable matters as these, I now describe only in brief.
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats who had attained mastery of mind thought to themselves:

“We are filled with joy at having attained what we have never experienced before; would it not be most wonderful if the World-Honored One were to grant each of us a prediction of enlightenment, just as he has for the other great disciples?
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
“These twelve hundred arhats, I shall now, in your presence, grant them the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in due order.”

Within this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand koṭis of buddhas; thereafter, he will attain buddhahood, known by the name Samantaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Those five hundred arhats—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Kālodāyin, Udāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakula, Cunda, Śāgata, and the rest—all shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and they shall all share the same title: Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya Shall see immeasurable Buddhas;
After incalculable kalpas have passed, He shall attain equal and perfect enlightenment.”
Constantly emitting great radiance, Fully endowed with all supernormal powers, His fame pervades the ten directions, And he is revered by all.
He constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path; Therefore, he is named Samantaprabha.
That land is pure and serene; bodhisattvas there are all courageous and valiant.
Together they ascend wondrous pavilions and travel through the lands of the ten directions, offering supreme articles of worship to all the Buddhas.
Having made these offerings, his heart filled with great joy, he returned to his own country in an instant; such was his supernormal power.
The Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas, and the True Dharma remained for twice that duration.
The Semblance Dharma shall again be twice as long; when the Dharma is extinguished, devas and humans will grieve.
Those five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become Buddhas, all sharing the same name, Samantaprabha, as they receive their predictions in turn.
After my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha;
the world he transforms shall be just like mine today,
with its lands’ majestic purity and all his supernormal powers.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma,
and the duration of their lifespans in kalpas, are all as previously described.
Kāśyapa, you already know that there will be five hundred masters of self-mastery.
"The other śrāvakas shall likewise be so; for those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim [the teaching] for them.

At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with joy and exultation. They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and repented, reproaching themselves:
“World-Honored One!
We have always harbored this thought, believing ourselves to have already attained ultimate parinirvāṇa; only now do we realize that we were like those lacking wisdom.”
Why is this? Although we ought to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, we have instead become content with our own meager wisdom.
World-Honored One!

It is like a man who went to the house of a close friend and fell asleep after drinking wine; at that time, the friend had business to attend to in the government office, so he tied a priceless jewel inside the man's garment and departed with him.
That person, lying drunk, was entirely unaware;

having risen, he wandered to another country where, for the sake of food and clothing, he sought with diligent effort amidst great hardship, and if he obtained even a little, he considered it sufficient.
Later, a close friend encountered him and spoke these words: "Alas, O man! Why have you come to such a state for the sake of food and clothing?

In the past, desiring to bring you peace and happiness so that you might indulge in the five desires, I tied a priceless jewel into the lining of your garment on such-and-such a day and month of such-and-such a year. It remains there even now, yet you did not know of it; instead, you have lived by toiling in hardship and suffering with anxiety—this is truly foolish."
"You may now use this treasure to trade for whatever you require; it shall always fulfill your wishes, leaving you never lacking or in want. The Buddha is likewise:

when he was a bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to resolve upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*). Yet we soon forgot it, neither knowing nor perceiving it; having attained the path of an arhat, we considered ourselves liberated, finding it difficult to provide for our livelihood and being content with little. Nevertheless, the vow for omniscience remains within us, not lost.
Now the World-Honored One has awakened us by speaking these words:

"O Bhikṣus! That which you have attained is not ultimate extinction. For a long time I have caused you to plant roots of goodness for Buddhahood; it was only through skillful means that I showed you the appearance of nirvāṇa, yet you believed you had truly attained final liberation."
"World-Honored One!

It is only now that I know he is truly a bodhisattva who has received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, I am filled with great joy, having attained what I never had before."
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Having heard the unsurpassed sound Of the prophecy of peace and security, We experience a joy never known before;
We pay homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom.”
Now, before the World-Honored One, I repent of all my transgressions;
regarding the immeasurable Jewel of the Buddhas, I have obtained but a small portion of nirvana,
yet like a foolish person lacking wisdom, I considered myself sufficient.
For example, it is like a poor man who goes to the house of a kinsman;
that house is exceedingly wealthy and has prepared all manner of delicacies.
[The kinsman] fastens an invaluable jewel within the lining of his inner garment.
He silently accepted it and departed, while at that time [the owner] lay down and was unaware.
Once this man had risen, he traveled on to another country, seeking food and clothing to sustain himself; his livelihood was extremely difficult.
Having obtained but a little, he considers it sufficient; he does not further desire anything better.
Unaware that within his inner garment there is a priceless jewel, a kinsman who possesses that jewel later encounters this poor man.
Having rebuked him with harsh words, he showed him the jewel he had tied [in his garment].
When the poor man saw this jewel, his heart was filled with great joy;
possessing all manner of wealth, he indulged himself in the five desires.
We are also like this: throughout the long night, the World-Honored One has constantly looked upon us with compassion and taught us, causing us to plant the unsurpassed aspiration;
yet because we were ignorant, we neither perceived nor understood it.
Having attained a small portion of nirvāṇa, I was self-sufficient and sought nothing more.
Now the Buddha has awakened me, saying that this is not true extinction;
only by attaining the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom is one then truly extinguished.
"Now that I have heard from the Buddha The prophecy concerning these matters of adornment, And the successive bestowal of predictions, My body and mind are filled with universal joy.
Chapter Nine: The Bestowal of Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training. At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought:
"Whenever we reflect upon it ourselves, we think: 'If we were to receive a prediction of our future enlightenment, would that not be most delightful?
Thereupon, they rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"

"We too should have a share in this. The Tathāgata is our sole refuge; furthermore, we are known and recognized by all the world—devas, humans, and asuras. Ānanda has constantly served as his attendant and protects the treasury of the Dharma, and Rāhula is the Buddha’s son. If the Buddha would grant us the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, our own wishes would be fulfilled and the hopes of the multitude would be satisfied."

At that time, two thousand śrāvaka disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training, all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, and approached the Buddha. With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One; then, as Ānanda and Rāhula had vowed, they stood to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“In a future age, you shall become a buddha, titled Śāgarabuddhi-vaśavartī-abhijñārāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
You shall make offerings to sixty-two billion buddhas and protect and uphold their Dharma-treasury; thereafter, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
He will transform and guide twenty quadrillion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattvas, causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The land shall be named Constantly Erected Supreme Banner; its soil is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground, and the eon shall be named Pervasive Wondrous Sound.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall last for immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, such that even if one were to calculate and reckon for thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it could not be fully known.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as the True Dharma. Ānanda!

This Buddha, King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Ocean Wisdom, is praised together by immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who extol his merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I now declare within this assembly: Ānanda, the upholder of the Dharma, shall make offerings to all Buddhas, and thereafter attain perfect enlightenment."
He is named Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijñārāja Buddha; his land is pure and is called Constantly Erecting the Supreme Banner,
where he teaches and transforms bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha possesses great majestic power, His fame fills the ten directions;
His lifespan is immeasurable, Out of compassion for sentient beings.
The True Dharma shall last twice as long as his lifespan, And the Semblance Dharma twice as long again.
“Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, countless in number,
shall plant the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way within this Dharma of the Buddha.
At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly who had newly resolved their minds all thought to themselves:
“We have not even heard that the great bodhisattvas receive such a prediction; by what causes and conditions do these śrāvakas receive such a definitive assurance?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
“O sons of good family!

I and Ānanda, together with others, simultaneously resolved our minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja. While Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning, I was constantly diligent and energetic; therefore, I have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, Ānanda shall protect and uphold my Dharma, as well as the Dharma-treasury of all future Buddhas, and he shall teach and bring to maturity the assembly of Bodhisattvas. Because his original vow was such, he has received this prediction.

In the presence of the Buddha, Ānanda personally heard his own prophecy and the adornments of his buddha-field; his aspirations being fully realized, his heart was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before.

Immediately, he recollected the dharma-treasuries of immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of past buddhas, penetrating them without obstruction just as he had now heard, and he also recognized his own original vows.
At that time, Ānanda spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous, Causing me to remember the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, Just as I have heard them today.”
"I now have no further doubts; I abide securely in the Buddha-way.
Acting as an attendant through skillful means, I shall protect and uphold all the Buddhas' teachings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula:

"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Ratnapadmacaraṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
He shall make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in ten worlds, and shall always be the eldest son of those Buddhas, just as he is now.

The adornments of the land, the lifespan in kalpas, the disciples transformed by him, and the duration of the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma of this Buddha Padmaprabha will be no different from those of the Tathāgata Sāgaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña.
"He shall also be the eldest son of this Buddha, and after that time has passed, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son; Now, when I have attained Buddhahood, He shall likewise be my eldest son."
Now that I have attained the Buddha-way, you shall receive the Dharma as my Dharma-son;
throughout future ages, you shall behold immeasurable billions of Buddhas and serve as their eldest son, single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way.
Rāhula’s secret practice is known only to me;
though he now appears as my eldest son to demonstrate this to all sentient beings,
his immeasurable billions of merits are beyond counting.
"Abiding securely in the Buddha-dharma, they seek the unsurpassed path.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the two thousand disciples—both those in training and those beyond training—had minds that were supple, tranquil, pure, and single-mindedly contemplating the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these two thousand persons, those in training and those beyond training?
"Indeed, I have seen them."

“Ānanda! These people shall make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in fifty worlds; they shall reverently honor, respect, and uphold the treasury of the Dharma. Finally, at the same time, they shall each attain Buddhahood in lands throughout the ten directions, all bearing the same name: Ratnaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. Their lifespans shall be one kalpa, their lands shall be equally adorned, and their assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as their True Dharma and Semblance Dharma, shall all be identical.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"These two thousand śrāvakas, who now stand before me,
have all been granted the prediction that they shall become Buddhas in the future."
The Buddhas whom they have made offerings to, as numerous as the atoms described above,
shall protect and uphold their Dharma-treasury and later attain perfect enlightenment.
Each, in the lands of the ten directions, shall possess the very same name.
Simultaneously seated at the site of enlightenment, they shall realize unsurpassed wisdom.
All shall be named Ratnalakṣaṇa; their lands and disciples, as well as their True Dharma and Semblance Dharma, shall all be equal and without distinction.
"By means of all their supernormal powers, they shall deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions;
their fame shall spread everywhere, and they shall gradually enter nirvana.

At that time, two thousand disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training, hearing the Buddha’s bestowal of predictions, were filled with joy and exultation, and spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One, Lamp of Wisdom, Having heard the sound of my prophecy, My heart is filled with joy, Like being sprinkled with nectar.

Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Master (The Added Chapter on the Dharma-Master from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*) At that time, the World-Honored One, because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!

You see within this great assembly the immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and those who seek the path of the Buddha. For all such beings as these, who have heard even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before the Buddha, or have even for a single moment rejoiced in it, I bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there are those who hear even a single verse, a single phrase, or even a single thought of sympathetic joy regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I likewise grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Furthermore, if there should be anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and regards this scripture with reverence as if it were the Buddha, making various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music, and even joining their palms in reverent salutation.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas; having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have been born into this human world out of compassion for sentient beings.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!
If someone should ask:
'Which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in a future age?'"
"One should show these people that they will certainly attain Buddhahood in a future age. Why is this?"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, should accept, uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe it, and should offer various kinds of worship to the scripture with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, flags, robes, and music, joining their palms in reverent homage—such a person is worthy of being venerated by all the world; they should be honored with the same offerings as a Tathāgata. You should know that this person is a great bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, out of compassion for sentient beings, has made a vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; how much more so those who are able to fully accept, uphold, and offer various kinds of worship to it.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person,
having relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will, out of compassion for sentient beings after my parinirvāṇa, be born in an evil age to widely expound this sutra.

If there are good sons or good daughters who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to secretly preach even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of a single person, you should know that such a person is an envoy of the Tathāgata, one sent by the Tathāgata, and one who performs the work of the Tathāgata; how much more so if they preach it extensively for others amidst the great assembly.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!
If there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him, his transgression would still be light;
but if someone, with even a single harsh word, reviles those—whether lay or ordained—who read and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, their transgression is exceedingly grave.”

Bhaiṣajyarāja! You should know that anyone who reads and recites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is adorned with the adornments of the Buddha; such a person is borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata. To whatever place they go, one should turn toward them, pay homage with single-minded palms joined, and offer them respect, worship, reverence, and praise. One should provide offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and delicacies, performing various musical performances as the supreme offerings among humans. One should scatter celestial jewels and present heaps of heavenly treasures as offerings.
Why is this? Because such a person joyfully expounds the Dharma, and upon hearing it for even a brief moment, one immediately attains ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way And achieve spontaneous wisdom,
One should always diligently make offerings To those who receive and uphold the *Lotus Sūtra*."
Those who wish to quickly attain The wisdom of all modes,
Should receive and uphold this sutra, And make offerings to those who uphold it.
If there are those able to receive and uphold The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*;
You should know that these are the messengers sent by the Buddha, who take pity on all sentient beings.
Those who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* have left the pure lands and been born here out of compassion for the masses.
You should know that such a person, possessing mastery over where they wish to be born,
will be able to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in this evil world.
One should honor them with celestial flowers and incense, as well as celestial jewel-encrusted garments.
With a heap of exquisite celestial jewels, one should make offerings to the teacher of the Dharma.
In the evil age after my parinirvāṇa, those who are able to uphold this sutra should be saluted with palms joined in reverence, just as one would make offerings to the World-Honored One.
With the finest delicacies and various sweet foods, as well as diverse garments,
one should make offerings to these sons of the Buddha, hoping to hear [this teaching] for even a brief moment.
If, in future ages, there are those who can receive and uphold this sutra;
I have dispatched them among human beings to perform the deeds of a Tathāgata.
Even if one were to harbor unwholesome thoughts for an entire kalpa,
and with a frowning countenance revile the Buddha, they would incur immeasurable and grave offenses.
If there are those who read, recite, or uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
and one should utter evil words against them for even a moment, their sin shall exceed that [previous offense].
Suppose there is someone seeking the Buddha-way who, for the duration of an eon,
stands before me with palms joined and praises me with countless verses;
by virtue of these praises of the Buddha, they shall attain immeasurable merit.
To praise and extol those who uphold this sutra brings merit even greater than that;
for eighty billion kalpas, one might offer the most exquisite forms and sounds,
as well as fragrances, flavors, and textures, to those who uphold this sutra.
Having made such offerings, if one should hear [this teaching] for even a moment, one should rejoice within oneself, thinking: "I have now obtained a great benefit.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja!
"I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras I have preached—those already preached, those being preached now, and those yet to be preached—among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand."
Bhaiṣajyarāja!

This sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others. It is protected by the World-Honored Buddhas and has never been openly proclaimed since the distant past.
Regarding such a sutra as this, even while the Tathāgata is currently present in the world, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa!

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s extinction, those who are able to write it down, uphold it, read and recite it, make offerings to it, and explain it to others, will be covered by the Tathāgata with his own robe. Furthermore, they will be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions. Such persons possess the power of great faith, the power of resolute vows, and the power of all roots of goodness. You should know that these persons dwell together with the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata himself will stroke their heads with his hand.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!

In whatever place this [sūtra] is preached, read, recited, or written, or wherever the scroll of the sūtra may reside, one should erect a stūpa made of the seven treasures, making it as high, broad, and magnificently adorned as possible; there is no need to enshrine relics therein."

Why is this?
