Because within this [stūpa] already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata; this stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners, pennants, music, and songs. If there are those who see this stūpa, prostrate before it, or make offerings to it, you should know that they are all drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Bhaiṣajyarāja!
There are many people, both householders and those who have left the home life, who practice the bodhisattva path.

If they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.

If there are those who hear this sutra, they will be able to practice the bodhisattva path skillfully. Any sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way, whether they see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it—know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!

It is like a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau. Seeing only dry earth, they know the water is still far off; yet, without ceasing their efforts, they see moist soil appear, and eventually reach mud. Their mind becomes certain, knowing that the water must be near.”

It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they have not yet heard, not yet understood, and not yet practiced this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one hears, understands, contemplates, and practices [this], one will certainly know that one is drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this so?
All the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas belongs to this sutra.

This sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true reality; it is the treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, profound, firm, remote, and inaccessible to anyone else, now revealed by the Buddha’s teaching to bring bodhisattvas to fulfillment.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!
If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, become startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
If there are śrāvakas who, upon hearing this sūtra, become startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those possessed of overweening pride."
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the fourfold assembly, how should they preach it?”

These good sons and good daughters, having entered the Tathāgata’s chamber, donned the Tathāgata’s robe, and sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat, should then extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.
The dwelling of the Tathāgata is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
the robe of the Tathāgata is the mind of gentleness and patience;
the seat of the Tathāgata is the emptiness of all dharmas.
Abiding therein, you should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!

In other lands, I shall dispatch emanated beings to assemble for him a congregation to hear the Dharma; I will also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to his preaching of the Dharma. These emanated beings, having heard the Dharma, will believe and accept it, following it in accordance without opposition."
If a Dharma-preacher is in a secluded place, I shall at that time extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others to listen to their preaching of the Dharma.

Although I am in another land, I shall from time to time cause the preacher of the Dharma to see my body; if they should forget or lose any phrases or clauses of this sutra, I will speak them again for them so that they may be complete.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"To abandon all indolence, One should listen to this sutra.
This sutra is difficult to hear, And those who believe and accept it are also rare."
Just as a person thirsty for water digs into a high plateau,
If they still see dry earth, they know the water is yet far off;
When they gradually see moist soil and mud, They know with certainty that the water is near.
Bhaiṣajyarāja!
You should know that such people as these, having not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, are very far removed from the Buddha’s wisdom;
yet if they hear this profound sūtra, they will definitively understand the Dharma of the śrāvakas.
This is the king of all sutras; having heard it, one should contemplate it with careful attention.
Know that such persons as these draw near to the Buddha’s wisdom.
If anyone were to preach this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Clad in the robes of the Tathāgata, seated upon the Tathāgata’s throne,
he dwells among the assembly without fear, expounding the Dharma in detail;
with great compassion as his dwelling and gentleness and forbearance as his robe.
Taking the emptiness of all phenomena as one’s seat, one dwells therein and preaches the Dharma.
When preaching this sutra, if someone should revile one with harsh words or strike one with knives,
staves, tiles, or stones, one should endure it by recollecting the Buddha.
In my thousands of millions of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body,
preaching the Dharma for sentient beings throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas;
if, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who can preach this sutra, [they shall likewise attain such a body].
I dispatch four groups of emanations— bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
as well as upāsakas and upāsikās— to make offerings to the Dharma Master,
to guide all sentient beings, and to assemble them so that they may hear the Dharma.
If someone intends to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones,
I shall dispatch emanated beings to provide them with protection.
If a person who preaches the Dharma is alone in a secluded place, [I shall likewise protect them].
In a place of solitude where no human voice is heard, one reads and recites this sutra;
at that time, I shall manifest for them a body of pure radiance.
Should they forget any passages or lines, I shall explain them to them so that they may master them.
If a person possesses these virtues, whether they preach for the fourfold assembly,
recite the sutras in a secluded place, or do so anywhere, they shall all behold my body.
If a person dwells in a quiet retreat, I shall dispatch the celestial kings and dragon kings [to protect them].
Yakṣas, spirits, and other such beings shall serve as the assembly for listening to the Dharma.
This person delights in preaching the Dharma, analyzing it without obstruction;
because all Buddhas protect and keep them in mind, they are able to bring joy to the great assembly.

If one draws near to a Dharma Master, One will swiftly attain the path of a Bodhisattva; By following and learning from such a teacher, One shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa *The Enriched Version of the Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa At that time, before the Buddha, there appeared a stupa made of the seven treasures. It was five hundred *yojanas* in height and two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth. It emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air, adorned with various precious substances. It had five thousand railings and ten million chambers, decorated with countless banners and streamers. Precious necklaces and billions of jeweled bells hung down from its top.
From all four directions, the fragrance of tāmarakha- and candana-sandalwood issued forth, pervading the entire world;
those various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, agate, pearl, and ruby—and reached as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings;
the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down celestial māndārava flowers as an offering to the jeweled stupa.

The remaining multitudes of tens of billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans made offerings to the precious stupa with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music;
they paid homage, revered it, and praised it.
At that time, a great voice issued forth from within the precious stūpa, exclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent!
World-Honored One Śākyamuni!"

He was able to preach for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas through the great wisdom of equanimity and is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas. It is so, it is so!
“Śākyamuni World-Honored One!
All that has been spoken is indeed true.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the great jeweled stupa abiding in mid-air and hearing the sounds issuing from within it, all attained the joy of the Dharma. Astonished by this unprecedented marvel, they rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna, who, knowing the doubts in the minds of all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"For what cause and condition has this precious stūpa emerged from the earth,
and why does it emit such a sound from within?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakīrti:

“Within this precious stupa is the entire body of a Tathāgata. In the past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there was a land named Ratnaviśuddhā. Therein dwelt a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna.”
When that Buddha was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this great vow:

"If I attain buddhahood, after my parinirvāṇa, wherever in the lands of the ten directions the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached, may my stupa emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, acting as a witness and praising them, saying, 'Excellent!'"
After that Buddha had attained enlightenment, as he was approaching his final nirvana, he addressed the bhikṣus amidst the great assembly of devas and humans:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a single great stūpa."

"By the power of that Buddha’s supernormal abilities and vows, wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be those who preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, that precious stupa shall emerge before them, and with his entire body within the stupa, he will praise them, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
“Mahāratnapratibhāna!
Now, because it has heard the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has emerged from the earth and uttered this praise: ‘Excellent!’”
"Excellent!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsukhavighuṣṭa, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"We wish to behold this Buddha-body.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Joyous Eloquence:
"This Buddha Many Treasures has a profound and solemn vow:"

"If my jeweled stupa emerges before all Buddhas for the sake of hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and there is anyone who wishes to manifest my body to the fourfold assembly, then all those emanated bodies of that Buddha who are preaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions shall gather together in one place; only then shall my body appear."
“Mahāpratibhāna! Those emanations of mine, the Buddhas who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions, should now assemble.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We also wish to see the various Buddhas who are emanations of the World-Honored One, so that we may pay them homage and make offerings.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, and immediately they saw the Buddhas in lands to the east as numerous as the sands of five hundred *nayuta* kotis of *Ganges* rivers. In all those lands, the ground was made of crystal, adorned with jeweled trees and jeweled robes; countless thousands of millions of *kotis* of bodhisattvas filled them, with jeweled canopies spread everywhere and jeweled nets draped above.

The Buddhas of those lands preach all dharmas with great and wondrous voices, and one sees immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—wherever the light from the white tuft between his brows shines—it was likewise so.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed their respective assemblies of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!"
"I should now go to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, and also to make offerings to the precious stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.

At that moment, the Sahā world was instantly transformed into purity: its ground became of lapis lazuli, adorned with jewel-trees; golden cords demarcated the eightfold paths; all villages, hamlets, towns, and cities were gone, as were the great oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, and marshes. Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground, which was covered by nets and canopies of jewels.
Precious bells were suspended from above, and while this assembly remained, all other devas and humans were moved to other lands.

At that time, each of the Buddhas took a great Bodhisattva as his attendant and arrived at the Sahā world, each reaching beneath a precious tree. Each of these precious trees was five hundred yojanas high, adorned in successive layers with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Beneath each of the precious trees there was a lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.

At that moment, each of the Buddhas sat cross-legged upon such a throne. In this manner, they spread throughout the entire trichiliocosm, yet even within the single direction occupied by the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha, they were still not yet exhausted.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to accommodate the Buddhas who had been manifested as his emanations, further transformed two hundred *koṭi-nayuta* worlds in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and *asuras*.

He also moved the various devas and humans to other lands. These transformed lands likewise had floors of lapis lazuli and were adorned with jeweled trees five hundred *yojanas* high; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were arranged in successive layers of beauty. Beneath each tree was a precious lion throne five *yojanas* high, adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, or mountain kings such as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, or Mount Sumeru;

rather, it was all a single Buddha-land, with a ground of jewels that was level and even, covered everywhere by jeweled lattices and canopies, hung with banners and parasols, burning great precious incense, and strewn with celestial jewel flowers upon the earth.

For the sake of the Buddhas who were to come and sit therein, Śākyamuni Buddha further transformed two million *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras. He then moved the devas and humans to other lands within the realms he had manifested. These lands also had floors of lapis lazuli and were adorned with jeweled trees five hundred *yojana*s in height; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were arranged in orderly splendor. Beneath each tree was a precious lion throne five *yojana*s high, likewise embellished with great jewels.

Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, or mountain kings such as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, or Mount Sumeru; rather, it was all a single Buddha-field with a ground of jewels, level and even. Canopies of interlaced jewels covered it everywhere, with banners and parasols suspended above, great precious incense being burned, and celestial jewel-flowers strewn across the ground.

At that time, the Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni from the east—in lands as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers—each preaching the Dharma, came and assembled here;
likewise, in succession, the Buddhas of the ten directions all came and assembled, sitting in the eight directions.

At that time, in each of the ten directions, there were four million billion nayutas of lands, all of which were filled with Buddhas, Tathāgatas. At that moment, each of these Buddhas sat beneath a jeweled tree upon a lion throne and sent forth his attendant to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha. Each attendant brought a handful of precious flowers and was told by their respective masters: "Good son! Go to the world of Sahā and pay homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni."
Go to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to where the Buddha Śākyamuni is, and speak these words on my behalf:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you physically strong and at ease?"
"And are the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas all at peace?
With these precious flowers, he scattered them as an offering to the Buddha and spoke these words:
"That certain Buddha desires to open this precious stūpa."
The Buddhas dispatched their messengers in this same manner.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, seeing that all the emanated Buddhas had already assembled and were each seated upon lion thrones, and hearing that all the Buddhas desired to open the precious stupa together, immediately rose from his seat and stood in mid-air. All four assemblies rose and joined their palms, gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stupa with his right finger, producing a great sound like that of a massive city gate being swung open after its bolt has been withdrawn.
Immediately, the entire assembly saw the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna seated upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa, his entire body intact and undispersed as if he had entered meditative absorption;
they also heard him say:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Śākyamuni Buddha! Please quickly preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; it is for the sake of hearing this sūtra that I have come here.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddha who had entered parinirvāṇa immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago, speak such words, marveled at what they had never before experienced, and scattered heaps of celestial jewel-flowers over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words: “Śākyamuni Buddha!
"You may sit upon this seat.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stūpa and sat upon half of that seat, assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
At that time, the great assembly, seeing two Tathāgatas seated in the full lotus posture upon lion thrones within the seven-jeweled stūpa, each had this thought:
“The Buddha’s seat is high and remote; we pray only that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, may cause us all to dwell together in the void.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha, using his supernormal powers, received the great assembly, and they all came to abide in the void. With a great voice, he proclaimed to the fourfold assembly:

“Who among you is able to expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* extensively in this Sahā world-system? Now is precisely the right time. Before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa, and the Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to those who remain.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses: "The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, though long since entered parinirvāṇa, remains within the jeweled stupa,
yet comes for the sake of the Dharma."
Why do you all not diligently practice for the sake of the Dharma?
Since the parinirvāṇa of this Buddha, throughout incalculable kalpas, you have heard the Dharma here and there,
for it is so difficult to encounter.
That Buddha’s original vow was:
"After my parinirvāṇa, wherever I may go, I shall always listen to the Dharma;
furthermore, immeasurable Buddhas who are my emanations, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall come desiring to hear the Dharma."
And seeing that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has entered parinirvāṇa, each of them has relinquished their wondrous lands and their assemblies of disciples;
together with devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, they have come here for the sake of causing the Dharma to abide long, setting aside all matters of worldly offerings.
For the sake of the seated Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers, they moved immeasurable multitudes and caused the lands to be pure.
Each of the Buddhas proceeded beneath the jeweled trees, which were adorned with lotuses like refreshing ponds.
The Buddha sat upon it, his radiance providing magnificent adornment, like a great torch burning in the midst of the night’s darkness.
From his body issued a wondrous fragrance that pervaded the lands of the ten directions; all sentient beings who were touched by its scent were overcome with joy beyond measure.
It is like a great wind blowing against the branches of small trees;
by such skillful means, he causes the Dharma to endure for a long time.
He then addressed the great assembly:
"After my parinirvāṇa,
who will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra?
Now, before the Buddha, let them each speak their own vow."
Although that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he lets out a lion’s roar by virtue of his great vow;
you should understand this intention regarding Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata, my own person, and all the emanated Buddhas who have gathered here.
O sons of the Buddhas!
Whoever is able to protect the Dharma should make a great vow so that it may endure for a long time;
whoever is able to protect this Dharma of the sutra thereby performs an act of worship.
I and Prabhūtaratna—
this Buddha Prabhūtaratna, who dwells within the jeweled stupa, constantly travels throughout the ten directions for the sake of this sutra;
I likewise make offerings to all the manifested Buddhas who come, adorning and illuminating all the worlds.
If one preaches this sutra, then one sees me, as well as the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and all the emanation Buddhas.
O sons of good family!
Reflect deeply upon this: it is a difficult task, and you should therefore resolve to make great vows.
Although other sutras exist as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, even to expound them would not be considered difficult.
If one were to take up Mount Sumeru and cast it to another direction, across countless Buddha-lands,
that would not yet be difficult;
if one were to move the great trichiliocosm with a single toe and hurl it far to another realm, that too would not yet be difficult.
To stand at the Peak of Existence and expound for the multitude immeasurable other sutras is not yet difficult;
but if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to preach this sutra in an evil age,
that indeed is difficult.
Even if someone were to grasp empty space with their hands and travel about, it would not be difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, for one to write this down themselves or to cause another to write it, that indeed would be difficult.
If one were to take the great earth and place it upon the tip of a toenail, then ascend to the Brahma Heaven,
this would not yet be difficult;
but after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, to read this sutra even for a moment amidst this evil age— this indeed is difficult.
Even if one were to carry dry grass upon one's back and enter into the conflagration at the end of an eon without being burned, that would not yet be difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and explains it for the sake of even a single person,
that indeed will be difficult.
To expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras for others, causing all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers— though one can do such things, it is not yet difficult; but after my parinirvāṇa,
to hear and receive this sūtra, and to inquire into its meaning and intent, [is truly difficult].
This would indeed be difficult.
That immeasurable and innumerable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
should attain arhatship and be endowed with the six supernormal powers— though such a benefit exists, it is not yet considered difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, if one can receive and uphold a sūtra such as this,
that indeed will be difficult.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands, from the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sūtras.
And among them, this sutra is the foremost; if there are those who can uphold it, they then uphold the body of the Buddha.
O sons of good family!
After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra?
Now, before the Buddha, speak your own vow.
This sutra is difficult to uphold; if one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and so shall all the Buddhas.
Such a person is praised by all the Buddhas.
This is indeed valor; this is indeed diligence. This is called upholding the precepts;
for one who practices the dhūtas, the unsurpassed path of the Buddha will be swiftly attained.
Those who, in a future age, are able to read and uphold this sutra are true sons of the Buddha,
dwelling on the ground of pure goodness.
They are the eyes of all devas and humans in this world, amidst an age of fear and dread.
“[He] can speak [this] for even a brief moment;
all devas and humans should make offerings to him.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans:
"In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without weariness or indolence.

During many kalpas, I constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unsurpassed bodhi with a mind that never regressed. Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, I diligently practiced giving with no sense of stinginess, not sparing elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, attendants, nor even my own head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, hands, or feet—I did not begrudge my very life."

At that time, the lifespan of the people of the world was immeasurable. For the sake of the Dharma, he renounced his royal throne and entrusted the administration to his crown prince; then, beating a drum, he issued a proclamation throughout the four quarters seeking the Dharma:
"Whoever can expound the Mahāyāna for me, I shall serve as their attendant for the rest of my life."
At that time, there was a rishi who came and said to the king:
"I possess a Mahāyāna teaching called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If you do not oppose me, I shall expound it for you."

Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately followed the rishi, providing all that was required: gathering fruits, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food; even using his own body as a bed and seat, he remained untiring in body and mind. Thus he served him for a thousand years, diligently attending to him for the sake of the Dharma so that he lacked for nothing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses: "I recall past kalpas, when for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma,
Though I was a king of the world, I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires."
He struck the bell to announce to the four quarters:
"Whoever possesses the Great Dharma, if you will explain it to me, I shall become your servant.
At that time, there was a seer who came and addressed the great king, saying:
"I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world;
if there are those capable of practicing it, I shall expound it for you.
When the king heard the words of the seer, his heart was filled with great joy.
Even as he followed the rishi, providing whatever was desired—
gathering firewood, fruits, and melons— and offering them with respect at the proper times;
because his heart was set upon the sublime Dharma, his body and mind were free from weariness or fatigue.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently sought the Great Dharma;
neither for his own body nor for the pleasures of the five desires did he do so.
Therefore, as a great king, he diligently sought and attained this Dharma.
"Consequently, he attained Buddhahood; therefore, I now speak for your sake.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was none other than myself."
The seer of that time was none other than Devadatta.

It is because of the spiritual friend Devadatta that I have been able to fulfill the six pāramitās, the [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; the purple-golden hue; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four methods of attraction, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and the supernatural powers of the path, whereby I attained equal and perfect enlightenment to extensively deliver all sentient beings—all this is due to the spiritual friend Devadatta.

He addressed the fourfold assembly: "In the future, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, Devadatta shall attain Buddhahood; he shall be named Tathāgata Heavenly King (Devendra), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world shall be named Devamārga."

At that time, the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively expounding the wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds on Pratyekabuddhahood; and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds on unsurpassed Bodhicitta, attaining the patience of non-arising and reaching the stage of non-retrogression.

After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas. A stupa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire body relics, sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth. All the devas and human beings offered worship and made offerings to this wondrous stupa of the seven jewels with various flowers, unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, robes, necklaces, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, music, and songs of praise; they prostrated before it and venerated it. Immeasurable sentient beings attained the state of Arhat, immeasurable sentient beings realized the path of Pratyekabuddha, and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the Bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In future ages, if there are good men or good women who hear this chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it, believe and revere it with a pure mind without giving rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions;
in every place where they are born, they shall always hear this sūtra."
"If one is born among gods or humans, one will experience supreme and wondrous bliss; if one is before the Buddha, one will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower.
At that time, the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa), who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna from the lower regions, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna:
"We should now return to our original land."
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñānakośa:
"Good son, wait but a moment;
here is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī with whom you may meet and discuss sublime meanings. You may then return to your own land."
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel;

the bodhisattvas who had come with him likewise sat upon precious flowers. They emerged spontaneously from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the great ocean, remained suspended in mid-air, and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain.

Descending from their lotuses to the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated themselves at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones. Having completed their salutations, they went to the place of Prajñākūṭa, exchanged greetings with one another, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Bodhisattva Jñānākara asked Mañjuśrī, "Virtuous One!
How many sentient beings were transformed by you during your visit to the dragon palace?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Their number is immeasurable and incalculable; it cannot be proclaimed by mouth nor fathomed by mind. Wait but a moment, and there shall naturally be witness."
Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas emerged from the sea, seated upon precious lotus flowers, and proceeded to Vulture Peak, where they remained suspended in mid-air.
All these bodhisattvas had been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; they were fully endowed with the practices of the bodhisattva path and were collectively discussing the six pāramitās.
Those who had originally been śrāvakas were now expounding the practices of the śrāvakas while in the air, yet they were all now practicing the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness.
Mañjuśrī said to Jñānakūṭa, "Such was the manner of his teaching and transforming beings within the ocean.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa praised him with these verses:
"Of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, you have transformed and delivered immeasurable multitudes;
now this entire great assembly, as well as I, have all witnessed it.
You have eloquently expounded the meaning of the true mark and revealed the Dharma of the One Vehicle."
"Extensively deliver all sentient beings, causing them to swiftly attain Bodhi.
Mañjuśrī said: "Within the ocean, I have always only proclaimed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
Jñānakūṭa asked Mañjuśrī, “This sutra is profoundly deep and subtle,
a jewel among all sutras, rare in the world. Are there perhaps any sentient beings who,
by applying themselves with diligent vigor and practicing this sutra, will swiftly attain Buddhahood?”

Mañjuśrī said: "There is the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara, only eight years of age, yet possessing sharp faculties and wisdom. She well understands the faculties, karmic actions, and practices of sentient beings; she has attained dhāraṇīs and is able to receive and uphold all the profound secret treasuries spoken by the Buddhas. She has deeply entered dhyāna and thoroughly realized all dharmas. In a single kṣaṇa, she gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained the stage of non-retrogression, her eloquence being unimpeded.

She regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were her own infant children. Her merits are fully perfected; what her mind conceives, she expresses through speech—subtle, wondrous, vast, and great. Compassionate, benevolent, and yielding, her will is harmonious and refined; she is capable of reaching Bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa said:

"I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult and painful practices, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the path to bodhi without ever ceasing. He surveyed the trichiliocosm and found not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he had not sacrificed his body and life for the sake of sentient beings before finally attaining the path to bodhi;
I cannot believe that this woman has attained perfect awakening in such a brief moment."
Before his speech was finished, the Dragon King’s daughter suddenly appeared before him. She bowed her head in prostration and withdrew to stand to one side, praising him with these verses:
"Thoroughly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, You illuminate the ten directions;
Your subtle and pure Dharma-body Is endowed with the thirty-two marks."
Adorned with the eighty minor marks, he embellishes the Dharma-body.
Honored and looked up to by devas and humans, all dragons and spirits pay him reverence;
among all classes of sentient beings, there are none who do not revere and follow him.
"There are those who attain Bodhi upon hearing [the Dharma], a fact that only a Buddha can verify and know;
I proclaim the Mahāyāna teaching to deliver suffering sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra spoke to the dragon girl, saying:
"You claim that you will soon attain the unsurpassed path; this is difficult to believe.
Why is this? A woman’s body is defiled and not a vessel for the Dharma; how could she possibly attain unsurpassed bodhi?"

The Buddha-way is profound and vast; it is only after passing through immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practices through diligent toil, and fully cultivating all the pāramitās that one finally achieves it.
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstacles:

first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, one cannot become Śakra Devendra; third, one cannot become a Māra King; fourth, one cannot become a Cakravartin King; and fifth, one cannot attain the body of a Buddha.
"How can a woman's body quickly attain Buddhahood?

At that time, the Dragon King’s daughter possessed a precious jewel, worth as much as the three-thousandfold world system; she held it up and offered it to the Buddha, and the Buddha immediately accepted it.
The dragon girl said to the Bodhisattva Zhijī and the Venerable Śāriputra, "I offered this precious jewel and the World-Honored One accepted it; was this matter not swift?"
He replied, "Very quickly. The woman said:
"By the power of your supernatural faculties, observe my attainment of Buddhahood; it shall be even swifter than this.

At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a male, fully endowed with the practices of a Bodhisattva. She immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal and perfect enlightenment. Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, she universally expounded the wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, as well as humans and non-humans of the Sahā world, all saw from afar that the dragon girl had attained buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly of humans and devas. Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.

Immeasurable sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression; immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of their future enlightenment. The Immaculate World shook in six ways, and in the Sahā World, three thousand sentient beings dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, while three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire great assembly silently accepted this with faith.

Chapter Twelve: Encouragement to Uphold (Addendum to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha:

“We only pray that the World-Honored One need not worry; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra. Although sentient beings in the future evil age will have diminished roots of goodness, will largely increase in overweening pride, will crave gain and offerings, will augment their unwholesome roots, and will distance themselves from liberation—making them difficult to transform—we shall give rise to the power of great patience to read and recite this sutra, to uphold, expound, copy, and provide various offerings for it, without begrudging our own bodies or lives.”
At that time, five hundred arhats within the assembly who had received their prediction of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We too vow that we shall extensively expound this sutra in other lands.”

Furthermore, eight thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training, who had received their prediction of enlightenment, rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and made this vow:
“World-Honored One!...”
We, too, shall extensively proclaim this sutra in other lands. Why is this?

Because in this Sahā world-system, people are for the most part corrupt and evil; they harbor overweening pride, their merit is meager, and because their minds are not sincere, they are turbid with anger and full of guile.

At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those in training and those beyond training—rose from their seats, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and did not for a moment turn their eyes away.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī:
"Why do you look upon the Tathāgata with such a sorrowful countenance?
Does it not occur to your mind that I have failed to mention your name and bestow upon you the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

"Kauṭamī! Previously, I spoke in general that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions. Now, if you wish to know your own prediction: in a future age, within the teachings of sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, you shall become a great Dharma teacher; together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), you shall all be Dharma teachers. Thus, gradually perfecting the bodhisattva path, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
"Kauṇḍinya! This Buddha Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, along with six thousand bodhisattvas, shall successively receive the prediction of their attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, thought to herself:
"World-Honored One!
Among those who have received predictions, you alone have not mentioned my name."
The Buddha told Yaśodharā:

"In future ages, throughout the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices and become a great Dharma teacher. Gradually perfecting the path to Buddhahood, you shall attain enlightenment in the land of Kṣema, where you will be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Sāhasrārciḥparipūrṇalakṣaṇa. The lifespan of this Buddha shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, together with their retinues, were all filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence. They then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One, Guiding Teacher!
"Bringing peace and security to devas and humans, we have heard this prediction; our minds are now fully at ease.
After these bhikṣuṇīs had spoken this verse, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We, too, shall extensively expound this sutra in other lands.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked upon eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

these bodhisattvas were all *avaivartika*, turning the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma and having attained various *dhāraṇīs*. They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and with single-minded palms joined, formed this thought:
"If the World-Honored One had commanded us to uphold and proclaim this sutra, we would have widely disseminated this Dharma in accordance with the Buddha's teaching.
They further thought:
"The Buddha now remains silent and does not issue a command; what should we do?"

At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, let out a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this solemn vow:
“World-Honored One!...”

"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness—all through the majestic power of the Buddha."
“May the World-Honored One,
from afar in another land, behold us and protect us!
Thereupon, all the bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke these verses:
“Please do not worry; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this terrifying and evil age, we shall expound [the teaching] extensively.
There will be those who lack wisdom, who will revile us with harsh words and the like.”
Even when blades and staves are brought against us, we shall endure it all.
In this evil age, there will be bhikṣus whose wisdom is perverted and whose minds are crooked;
having not attained, they claim to have attained, their hearts filled with the pride of self-conceit.
There may be forest-dwellers, clad in rag-robes in secluded places,
who claim to practice the true path while looking down upon those in the world; yet,
because they are greedily attached to gain and offerings, they preach the Dharma to laypeople.
Respected by the world as if they were arhats with the six supernormal powers,
these people harbor evil intentions and constantly dwell on worldly matters;
though they falsely claim the name of forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), they delight in exposing our faults.
And they spoke these words:
"For the sake of craving gain and offerings, they preach the doctrines of external paths;
having composed these sūtras themselves, they deceive and delude the people of the world."
For the sake of seeking fame and renown, they analyze this sutra;
constantly amidst the great assembly, they desire to disparage us,
[speaking ill] before kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders.
As well as other assemblies of bhikṣus, who slandered me and spoke of my evils,
saying, "This man holds wrong views and propounds the doctrines of non-Buddhists"—
out of our reverence for the Buddha, we endured all such evils.
Regarding these words of contempt, "You are all Buddhas," such disparaging speech should be endured by all.
In this defiled age of the evil world, there will be many terrors.
Evil spirits enter their bodies, reviling and insulting us;
yet we, who revere and trust in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience.
For the sake of expounding this sutra, we endure these various hardships.
I do not cherish my own body or life, but only regret the unsurpassed Way;
in future ages, we shall protect and uphold what the Buddha has entrusted to us.
The World-Honored One should know for himself that there will be evil bhikṣus in this turbid world.
Not understanding the Buddha’s skillful means and the teachings he gave according to what was appropriate,
they spoke with harsh words and frowned; repeatedly being expelled and banished,
they were kept far away from the stupas and monasteries— such were their manifold evils.
Because of the Buddha’s entrustment, you should all endure these matters.
To those in various villages and cities who seek the Dharma,
I shall go to each of their places and preach the Dharma with which the Buddha has charged me.
I am the messenger of the World-Honored One, Standing amidst the assembly without fear;
I shall skillfully expound the Dharma, May the Buddha dwell in peace and security.
Before the World-Honored One, And before all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions...
Having made such a vow, the Buddha fully knows my heart.
*The Added-Portion Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma*, Scroll Four;
*The Added-Portion Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India, together with Guptaka, during the Sui Dynasty. Chapter Thirteen: On Peaceful Conduct.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These bodhisattvas are truly rare and extraordinary; out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha, they have made great vows to protect, uphold, recite, and expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the evil world of the future.”
“World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva preach this sutra in the evil age to come?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to expound this sutra in the future evil age, they should abide securely in four dharmas:
first, by abiding securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of conduct and sphere of association, they will be able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī! What is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the ground of patience, being gentle, harmonious, and compliant, without sudden outbursts of violence, and with a mind that is not startled.
Furthermore, not engaging with any phenomena, yet observing all phenomena as they truly are, neither acting nor discriminating—this is called the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is called the "sphere of association" for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials;

nor does he associate with various non-Buddhists, brahmins, Nirgranthas, and others who compose secular writings, hymns, or foreign texts, as well as with Lokāyatas and those who follow the inverse Lokāyata.
Furthermore, he does not associate with those who engage in violent games, such as boxing or wrestling, nor with various performances such as those by the *naṭas*;

nor does he associate with *caṇḍālas*, or those who keep pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs, or who follow the evil vows (*akuśalasaṃvara*) of hunting, fishing, or trapping. If such persons should occasionally come to him, he preaches the Dharma for them without any expectation of reward.
Moreover, he does not associate with śrāvaka bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, nor does he exchange greetings with them.

Whether in a dwelling, on a walking path, or within a lecture hall, he does not dwell together with others; yet if they should come at times, he preaches the Dharma to them as appropriate, without seeking anything for himself.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not take up signs from the body of a woman that give rise to thoughts of desire while preaching the Dharma, nor should he delight in seeing them.
If he enters another's home, he should not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, and the like.

Furthermore, he does not associate closely with the five kinds of impotent persons. He does not enter the homes of others alone; however, if there is a necessary reason for entering alone, he should simply keep his mind single-mindedly on the Buddha.
When preaching the Dharma to women, he should not smile by showing his teeth nor reveal his chest. Even for the sake of the Dharma, he should not form close intimacies, much less for other matters.

He does not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or children, nor does he delight in having the same teacher as them; he always prefers to practice dhyāna in secluded places, cultivating and collecting his mind.
Mañjuśrī! This is called the first stage of close approach.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty according to their true mark—uninverted, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-revolving; like space, they are of a nature of non-existence, where all paths of verbal expression are severed.

Unborn, unarisen, and unproduced; nameless, signless, and truly non-existent; immeasurable, boundless, unimpeded, and unobstructed—it exists only through causes and conditions and arises from inversion. Therefore, it is described as eternal and blissful. To contemplate such characteristics of phenomena is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“If there be a bodhisattva who, in the evil age to come, desires to preach this sutra with a heart free from fear;”
One should enter into the proper spheres of conduct and the spheres of association.
One should always remain far removed from kings, princes, ministers, high officials, and those who engage in violent or reckless amusements.
Nor should one associate with outcasts, non-Buddhist brahmins,
nor with those of overweening pride, nor with those who are greedily attached to the Lesser Vehicle and study only the Tripitaka,
nor with bhikṣus who have broken the precepts, nor with those who are arhats in name only.
And those bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter;
those upāsikās who are deeply attached to the five desires and seek nirvāṇa in this present life—do not associate with any of them.
If such persons come with a sincere heart to the place where the Bodhisattva dwells in order to hear the Buddha-way,
the Bodhisattva then, with a mind free from fear and harboring no expectations, shall preach the Dharma for them.
Widows, virgins, and those who are not male— do not associate with them or treat them as close friends.
Likewise, do not associate with butchers, executioners, hunters, fishermen,
or those who kill for profit, those who live by selling meat, or those who peddle their own sexual favors.
Such persons as these, one should not associate with at all.
Those who engage in violent wrestling and various kinds of frivolous games,
and all such courtesans— one must never associate with them.
Do not preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place alone; when preaching the Dharma, do not engage in jesting or laughter.
If there is no other bhikṣu present, single-mindedly recollect the Buddha; this is what is called [the proper conduct].
Regarding the sphere of practice and the sphere of proximity—
by means of these two spheres, one can preach with ease and joy. Furthermore,
one does not engage in the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, nor in the conditioned or the unconditioned.
Neither discriminating between real and unreal dharmas, nor between male and female;
not apprehending any dharmas, neither knowing nor seeing— this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.
There is no permanence, nor is there arising or ceasing; this is called the place frequented by the wise.
Whether real or unreal, whether born or unborn, one dwells in a secluded place.
Cultivating and gathering the mind, dwelling peacefully and immovable like Mount Sumeru,
one contemplates all phenomena as being entirely non-existent;
they are like space, lacking any solidity.
Neither arising nor emerging, unmoving and non-retrogressive, eternally abiding in a single mark— this is called the "near place.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who enter this sphere of practice and this place of intimacy will have no fear or weakness when preaching this sūtra.
At times, the Bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber and, with right mindfulness, contemplates the Dharma according to its meaning;
emerging from meditative concentration, he teaches, transforms, and expounds this sutra for kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others.
Their minds are peaceful and secure, free from any timidity or weakness.
Mañjuśrī! This is called a bodhisattva dwelling securely in the first dharma, who is able, in future lives, to...
He preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, if one wishes to preach this sūtra, one should abide in the Practice of Peaceful Abiding. Whether preaching it orally or reading it, one should not delight in speaking of the faults of people or of other scriptures; nor should one disparage or treat with contempt other Dharma-preachers, nor speak of the good or evil, the long or the short, of others."
Regarding śrāvakas as well, one does not mention their names to speak of their faults, nor does one mention their names to praise their virtues;
furthermore, one does not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion, because one skillfully cultivates such a mind of peace and happiness.

All who listen shall not have their intentions thwarted; should they pose difficult questions, he shall not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but shall explain them solely through the Mahāyāna, enabling them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Bodhisattvas always delight in preaching the Dharma with peace and security;
upon pure ground, they provide seats and couches, anoint their bodies with oil, and bathe away all dust and impurity.”
Wearing new, clean robes, pure both within and without;
seated upon the Dharma throne, he speaks according to their questions.
To the upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as to kings and princes—
To the ministers, officials, and the common people, he explained the subtle and profound meanings with a serene countenance;
if there were any questions or challenges, he answered according to the principles, elaborating and analyzing them through causes, conditions, and parables.
By these skillful means, he causes all to resolve their minds [on enlightenment]; gradually increasing their merit, they enter the path of the Buddha.
He removes slothful intent and thoughts of indolence, and being free from all sorrow and affliction, he preaches the Dharma with a compassionate heart;
day and night he constantly teaches the unsurpassed Way of the Buddhas.
Through various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables, he reveals the truth to sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
Regarding clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicine, he harbors no expectations for these things.
May they attain the Buddha-way, and cause all beings to do likewise; this is the great benefit, the peaceful and joyful offering.
To be able to expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with a mind free from envy and anger—
There are no afflictions or obstacles, nor is there any sorrow or those who revile;
furthermore, there is no fear of being struck with swords or staffs, nor is there any expulsion,
because one dwells securely in patience.
The wise person who thus skillfully cultivates their mind can abide in peace and happiness as I have described above;
such a person’s merit shall endure for thousands of billions of kalpas.
"Even through calculation and parable, it cannot be fully described.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra must not harbor jealousy or a deceitful mind; nor should they disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way, seeking out their faults."

If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—whether they seek the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva path—you must not trouble them or cause them doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Way; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
"Why is this? Because you are a person of negligence, being indolent regarding the Path.

Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation about dharmas or contend with others; rather, one should give rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings and the thought of a loving father toward all Tathāgatas.

One should conceive of all bodhisattvas as great teachers; one should always, with a profound mind, pay respect and prostrate to the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions. One should preach the Dharma equally to all sentient beings, in accordance with the Dharma, neither too much nor too little; even for those who deeply love the Dharma, one should not speak excessively.

“Mañjuśrī! When the Dharma is about to perish in the final age of the future, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish this third practice of peace and happiness will, when preaching this Dharma, be free from any who can disturb or confuse them; they will obtain good companions with whom to read and recite this sutra together, and a great assembly will also come to listen and receive it. Having heard it, they will be able to uphold it; having upheld it, they will be able to recite it; having recited it, they will be able to explain it; and having explained it, they will be able to write it down.
Or they may cause others to write it, and they will make offerings to the scroll, honoring, respecting, and praising it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, One should abandon envy, anger, and pride,
As well as deceit, guile, and a crooked mind, And always cultivate upright conduct."
Do not despise others, nor engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma;
do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood.
Such is the teaching of the Buddha’s son: he is always gentle and capable of forbearance.
Compassionate toward all, they never give rise to a mind of indolence.
The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Path out of pity for sentient beings;
one should give rise to a heart of reverence, for they are my Great Teachers.
Toward all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one should conceive the thought of them as one's unsurpassed father;
having destroyed the mind of pride, one preaches the Dharma without obstruction.
This third dharma is thus; the wise should guard it.
“With a single mind practicing peaceful conduct, they shall be revered by immeasurable multitudes.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, there will be those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Toward those who are householders or renunciants, they should give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness; toward those who are not bodhisattvas, they should give rise to a mind of great compassion, and they should reflect as follows:

"Such a person will suffer a great loss. Although the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate, they do not hear it, do not know it, do not awaken to it, do not inquire about it, do not believe it, and do not understand it. Even though such a person does not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra, when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wherever they may be, I shall use my power of supernatural faculties and my power of wisdom to draw them in and cause them to abide within this Dharma."

“Mañjuśrī! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, accomplish this fourth dharma, they will be free from fault when preaching this Dharma. They will always be provided with offerings, honored, respected, and praised by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, commoners, brahmins, householders, and others.

The devas of the void, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, will also constantly attend upon them. Whether they are in villages, towns, cities, or in secluded forests, if anyone comes to challenge them with difficult questions, the devas will constantly protect them day and night for the sake of the Dharma.”
It enables all who hear it to attain joy.
Why is this? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Mañjuśrī! In immeasurable lands, even the name of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* cannot be heard, let alone being seen, received, upheld, read, or recited.

Mañjuśrī! It is like a powerful wheel-turning sage king who, wishing to subdue various kingdoms through his majesty and power, finds that the minor kings do not obey his commands; at that time, the wheel-turning king raises various armies and goes forth to campaign against them.

When the king saw that his soldiers had performed meritorious deeds in battle, he was greatly delighted and bestowed rewards according to their merit. He gave them fields, houses, villages, and towns; or clothing and ornaments for the body; or various kinds of rare treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, and amber; or elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, and subjects.
Yet, the bright pearl from within his topknot, he did not give to them.
Why is this? This single jewel is found only upon the crown of the king's head; if he were to give it to him, the king’s entire retinue would surely be greatly astonished and amazed. Mañjuśrī!

The Tathāgata is also like this: having attained the kingdom of Dharma through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he reigns as king over the triple world. Yet the various Māra kings refuse to submit. The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engage them in battle; those who achieve merit therein also bring joy to his heart. Among the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sūtras to gladden their minds, bestowing upon them the wealth of the dharmas of meditative concentration, liberation, the outflows-free state, the faculties, and the powers. He further grants them the city of Nirvāṇa, declaring that they have attained extinction (*parinirvāṇa*), guiding their hearts so that they are all filled with joy—but he does not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them.

Mañjuśrī! Just as a wheel-turning monarch, seeing among his troops those who have achieved great merit, is filled with profound joy and bestows upon them this rare and difficult-to-believe pearl—which he has long kept within his topknot and never gave to others—so too is it with the Tathāgata.

As the Great Dharma King within the triple world, he transforms all sentient beings through the Dharma. When he sees the army of sages and saints battling against the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of afflictions, and the demon of death, achieving great meritorious feats—extinguishing the three poisons, escaping the triple world, and shattering the net of Māra—the Tathāgata likewise experiences great joy.

This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can enable sentient beings to reach all-knowledge; though it is full of enmity and difficult to believe in throughout all worlds, that which was not previously taught is now being taught.

Mañjuśrī! This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas; among all teachings, it is the most profound. It is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king, having long guarded a bright jewel, finally grants it to another.

Mañjuśrī! This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; it stands supreme among all sūtras. Having guarded it throughout the long night without proclaiming it recklessly, I now, for the first time, expound it to you and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all beings,
one is then able to expound the sutras praised by the Buddha."
Whether they are householders or renunciants, and whether they are bodhisattvas or not, one should give rise to compassion for them;
that such people do not hear this sutra and do not believe it is a great loss.
When I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall, by means of various skillful expedients, preach this Dharma for them, causing them to abide within it.
Just as those who have merit in battle are rewarded with various goods— elephants, horses, and chariots— so too shall I bestow upon them the supreme vehicle.
Or ornaments for adorning the body;
or clothing, various kinds of rare jewels, slaves, servants, and wealth—
these he joyfully bestowed as gifts.
If there is one who is brave and capable of performing difficult deeds, the King unties the bright pearl from within his topknot and gives it to him.
As a Dharma King, possessing the great power of forbearance and a treasury of wisdom,
he transforms the world according to the Dharma with great compassion, beholding all people.
Suffering various afflictions and desiring liberation, they wage war against all Māras;
for the sake of these sentient beings, you preach various dharmas,
and through great skillful means, you preach these sūtras.
Having known the sentient beings and gained their capacity, he finally preaches this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for them;
it is like a king untying his topknot and giving the bright pearl to them.
I have constantly guarded [this teaching] and did not reveal it recklessly; now is the very time for me to speak it for your sake.
Those who desire peace and security should approach [this teaching] as they expound this sutra.
Those who read this sutra shall possess these four qualities: they will always be free from sorrow and affliction, and likewise free from illness;
their complexion will be bright and radiant;
they will not be born into poverty, low status, or ugliness; and all sentient beings will delight in seeing them, as if yearning for a sage or a holy one.
The youths of the heavens serve as his attendants;
weapons do not strike him, and poisons cannot harm him.
If someone reviles him with evil words, their mouth shall be closed; he wanders without fear, like a lion king.
The light of wisdom shines like the sun;
even within dreams, one sees only wondrous things— beholding all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones,
surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣus as they preach the Dharma.
In numbers like the sands of the Ganges, they respectfully join their palms; they see themselves before them as these Buddhas preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, they see all the Buddhas, their bodies golden in color, emitting immeasurable light that illuminates everything.
With the voice of Brahmā, they expound all dharmas.
Seeing their own bodies situated therein, they join their palms to praise the Buddha; hearing the Dharma with joy, they make offerings.
Having attained dhāraṇī and realized non-retrogressive wisdom,
the Buddha, knowing his mind had deeply entered the path of the Buddhas, immediately bestowed upon him the prediction that he would attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
"You, son of good family!
You have attained immeasurable wisdom and the Great Way of the Buddha; your buddha-field is adorned and pure, vast and beyond compare."
There were also the fourfold assembly, with palms joined, listening to the Dharma. Furthermore,
he saw his own self in mountain forests, practicing wholesome dharmas, realizing all true marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
entering deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings;
hearing the Dharma and preaching it for others, one always has such auspicious dreams.
Furthermore, one dreams of becoming a king, yet renouncing the palace, the throne, and one's kin.
Accompanied by the five supreme and exquisite sensual pleasures, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment;
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon the lion throne,
he sought the Way for seven days and attained the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having attained the Unsurpassed Way, he arose and turned the wheel of Dharma,
preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas;
he expounded the subtle Dharma free from outflows, delivering immeasurable sentient beings.
In the future, when entering parinirvāṇa, like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended,
if one should preach this supreme Dharma during the evil ages of the future,
that person will obtain great benefit, such as all the merits mentioned above.

Chapter 14: The Emergence from the Earth. An Additional Chapter of the Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma. Chapter Fourteen: The Emergence from the Earth. At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from other lands—more numerous than the sands of eight Ganges Rivers—rose within the great assembly, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If you would permit us, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, to diligently apply ourselves with vigor in this Sahā world to protect, uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings to this sutra, we shall extensively expound it in this land.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: “Cease!
Sons of good family!”
"You need not protect and uphold this sutra. Why is this?

In my Sahā world, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers; each of these bodhisattvas has a retinue as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. These individuals will be able to protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra after my parinirvāṇa."

When the Buddha spoke these words, the earth throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of the Sahā universe quaked and split open. From within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously leaped forth. These bodhisattvas were all golden in color, possessed the thirty-two marks, and emitted immeasurable radiance; they had previously been dwelling in the space beneath this Sahā world, within the void of this realm.

When these bodhisattvas heard the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, they set out from below; each and every one of these bodhisattvas was a leader among the great assemblies, each bringing with them a retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [Ganges-sand] beings—not to mention those who brought fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* retinues—and even those who brought as few as one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, half a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, a quarter, or even down to a ten-millionth part of a *nayuta* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.

How much more so for those with retinues of thousands of millions of nayutas; how much more so for those with retinues of hundreds of millions; how much more so for those with thousands of millions, hundreds of thousands, or even ten thousand; how much more so for those with one thousand, one hundred, or even ten; how much more so for those who lead five, four, three, two, or one disciple; and how much more so for those who are solitary and delight in the practice of seclusion—such as these are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.

Once these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded to the wondrous stupa made of the seven treasures in the sky, where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were located. Upon arrival, they bowed their heads at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones; they likewise went before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees, prostrating themselves and circumambulating them three times to the right. With palms joined in reverence, they praised them with the various modes of praise used by bodhisattvas, and then withdrew to one side, joyfully gazing up at the two World-Honored Ones.
From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first emerged, they praised the Buddha with various kinds of bodhisattva eulogies for a period of fifty intermediate kalpas.

During this time, Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent; yet, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused the great multitude to perceive these fifty intermediate kalpas as being like half a day.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the fourfold assembly also saw all those bodhisattvas filling the voids of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands. Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders:

the first was named Upward-Going (Urdhvagama), the second Boundless-Practice (Anantacaryā), the third Pure-Practice (Śuddhacaryā), and the fourth Established-Practice (Pratiṣṭhitacaryā). These four bodhisattvas were the foremost leaders and guides within that multitude; standing before the great assembly, they each joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after his well-being, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Are you free from much illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is it not difficult for those who are to be delivered to receive your teachings?
And do you not cause the World-Honored One any fatigue?
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
“World-Honored One, you are at ease, with little illness and little affliction; in teaching and transforming sentient beings, you have attained freedom from weariness.”
"Furthermore, are these sentient beings easy to transform?
Will you not cause the World-Honored One to experience weariness?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas:
"So it is, so it is! O sons of good family!
The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction; all sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered, and there is no weariness."

Why is this? These sentient beings have, from lifetime to lifetime since the distant past, constantly received my transformation. They have also made offerings to and revered past Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness. Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say, these beings immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—with the exception of those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna. Even for such people as these, I now cause them to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
“Excellent, excellent!
Great Hero, World-Honored One!”
These sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered.
They are able to inquire about the profound wisdom of the Buddhas; having heard it, they believe and practice it—we rejoice in them.
Then the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas:
"Excellent, excellent, sons of good family!"
"You all are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, all had this thought:
