"Since the distant past, we have never seen nor heard of such a great multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these, who have leaped forth from the earth to stand before the World-Honored One, joining their palms, making offerings, and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, and wishing to resolve his own doubts as well, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse:
“Immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis— This great assembly of bodhisattvas, Such as has never been seen before;”
I pray that the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings will explain: from where have they come, and by what causes and conditions have they gathered?
They possess massive bodies and great supernormal powers, and their wisdom is inconceivable.
Their resolve is exceedingly firm, and they possess the power of great forbearance;
they are a joy for all sentient beings to behold—from where have they come?
Each of these bodhisattvas, along with the retinues they bring with them—
Their number is immeasurable, like the sands of the Ganges;
there are great Bodhisattvas who lead sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges—
such a great assembly, with one mind seeking the Buddha-way.
These great masters, as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers,
have all come together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra;
there are another fifty thousand Ganges Rivers' worth, their number exceeding even that.
Forty thousand and thirty thousand, twenty thousand down to ten thousand,
one thousand, one hundred, and so forth, even down to a single Ganges-sand,
half, a third, or a fourth part, and a ten-millionth part of that;
Tens of millions and nayutas, tens of billions of disciples,
even down to fifty million, their number exceeding that;
from one million down to ten thousand, one thousand, and one hundred.
Fifty and ten, down to three, two, and one—
those who are alone without retinue and delight in dwelling in solitude have all come to the presence of the Buddha, their number exceeding even those mentioned above.
If one were to count these great assemblies by casting tally-sticks,
even after more than *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still could not know them all.
These bodhisattvas of great majestic power are possessed of such diligence.
Who preached the Dharma for them, transforming and bringing them to maturity?
From whom did they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment]?
Which Buddha-dharma did they extol?
Which sutras do they uphold and practice?
What Buddha-way do they cultivate?
Such bodhisattvas possess the great power of supernatural penetrations and wisdom.
The earth in the four directions quakes and splits open, and all emerge from within it.
World-Honored One, since my past, I have never seen such a thing;
I pray you tell us whence they come and the names of their lands.
I have constantly traveled through various lands, yet I have never seen such an assembly as this.
Among these people, I do not recognize even a single individual;
they have suddenly emerged from the earth—pray, tell me the causes and conditions for this?
In this great assembly today, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions;
all these bodhisattvas wish to know this matter—
the causes and conditions regarding the beginning and end of these multitudes of bodhisattvas.
"O World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.

At that time, the various Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha and had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands in other directions sat cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees in the eight directions.

The attendants of those Buddhas each saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas springing forth from the earth in the four quarters of the trichiliocosm and dwelling in mid-air; they each addressed their respective Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes of bodhisattvas come?
At that time, each of the Buddhas addressed their own attendant:
“Good sons! Wait but a moment.

There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya, who has been prophesied by Śākyamuni Buddha to be the next to attain buddhahood. He has already asked about this matter, and the Buddha is now answering it; you shall yourselves hear it through him.”
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent! Ajita!"

That you are able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter as this—you all should be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firm intent; for the Tathāgata now wishes to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas, the sovereign power of supernatural penetrations of all Buddhas, the lion-like prowess of all Buddhas, and the majestic, mighty power of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter.
Do not harbor doubt or regret, for the Buddha's wisdom is inconceivable."
Now, exerting the power of faith, abide in the goodness of patience;
the Dharma never heard before, you shall now hear it all.
I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear.
The Buddha never speaks words that are not true; his wisdom is immeasurable.
The supreme Dharma he has attained is profoundly deep and beyond conceptual discrimination;
I shall now explain it as it is—listen with a single-minded focus.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“I now proclaim this to you all within this great assembly.”

Ajita! These great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable—who have emerged from the earth and whom you have never seen before, were all taught, instructed, and guided by me after I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sahā world; I tamed their minds and caused them to resolve upon the path.
All these bodhisattvas dwell in the space beneath this Sahā world, reciting, mastering, contemplating, analyzing, and correctly recollecting various sūtras.

Ajita! These sons of good family do not delight in being among the multitude or in much speaking; they always delight in solitary places, practicing with diligence and vigor without ever resting. They do not rely upon humans or devas for their dwelling, but always delight in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, and they also always delight in the teachings of all Buddhas, single-mindedly and vigorously seeking supreme enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Ajita, you should know:
Since incalculable kalpas past, I have cultivated the wisdom of the Buddha."
All of these have been transformed by me, causing them to resolve upon the mind of the Great Way. They are my children, who rely upon this world;
they constantly practice the dhūta austerities and take delight in secluded places.
Having abandoned the clamor of the great assembly, they take no pleasure in much speaking.
Such sons as these study my Way and Dharma;
day and night they are always diligent for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
In the Sahā world, dwelling in the space below,
his resolve and power are firm; constantly and diligently seeking wisdom,
he preaches various sublime dharmas with a mind free from fear.
In the city of Gayā, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree,
I attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
it was then that I transformed them, causing them to first resolve their minds upon the Way.
Now all abide in non-retrogression, and shall all attain Buddhahood.
I now speak these words of truth: you should believe them with one mind.
From long ago, I have been teaching and transforming this assembly.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, along with countless other bodhisattvas, felt doubt and wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence, and they thought to themselves:

"How is it that in such a short time, the World-Honored One has taught and transformed such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of great bodhisattvas, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. From that time until now, only slightly more than forty years have passed.”
World-Honored One!

How is it that in such a short time you perform such great Buddha-work, and by means of the Buddha’s power and the Buddha’s merit, you teach and transform such an immeasurable multitude of great Bodhisattvas so that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“World-Honored One!

As for this great assembly of bodhisattvas, even if someone were to count them for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they could not exhaustively enumerate them nor reach their limit. For a long time past, these beings have planted roots of goodness under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, accomplished the bodhisattva path, and constantly cultivated pure conduct.”
World-Honored One!
Such a matter is difficult for the world to believe.
It is like a person, handsome in appearance with black hair and twenty-five years of age, pointing to a hundred-year-old man and saying, "This is my son."
That a hundred-year-old man would point to a youth and say, "This is my father; he begot and raised us"—such a thing is difficult to believe. It is the same with the Buddha:

although it has not been long since he attained the Way, this great assembly of bodhisattvas has, for the sake of the Buddha-way, practiced with diligent vigor for immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas. They have skillfully entered, emerged from, and dwelt within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samādhis; they have attained great supernormal powers and long cultivated pure conduct. They are well able to gradually accumulate all wholesome dharmas, are adept at question and answer, are jewels among men, and are exceedingly rare throughout all worlds.

Today the World-Honored One has only now said that when he first attained the Way of the Buddha, he first caused them to resolve their minds, teaching and guiding them to turn toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

World-Honored One, it has not been long since you attained Buddhahood, yet you have already been able to perform such a deed of great merit. Although we believe what the Buddha has taught according to his skillful means, and though the words spoken by the Buddha have never been false and all that he knows is fully understood by him;

nevertheless, there may be bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, might hear these words and either fail to believe and accept them, or give rise to the karmic causes and conditions for the sin of destroying the Dharma.

"Indeed, World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain this for us to dispel our doubts, so that good sons of future generations, upon hearing of this matter, shall likewise not give rise to doubt."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha formerly left the Śākya clan And went forth near Gayā;
He sat beneath the Bodhi tree— Not long has it been since then."
These sons of the Buddhas are immeasurable in number;
having long practiced the path of the Buddhas, they abide in the power of supernatural knowledges and wisdom.
Having skillfully studied the bodhisattva path, they remain unstained by worldly dharmas.
Like lotuses in the water, they have emerged from the earth;
with hearts full of reverence, they stand before the World-Honored One.
This matter is inconceivable—how can it be believed?
The Buddha attained the Way but recently, yet that which he has accomplished is vast;
we pray that you will dispel our many doubts by explaining them according to reality.
It is like a man in his prime, only twenty-five years of age.
If one were to show people a hundred-year-old son with white hair and wrinkled face,
saying, "These are my sons," and the son likewise said,
"This is my father," that the father is young while the son is old would be something the whole world would not believe.
The World-Honored One is likewise; though he attained the Way but recently,
these bodhisattvas are firm in resolve and free from timidity,
having practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable kalpas.
Skillful in answering difficult questions, their minds are free from fear;
firm in the resolve of patience, upright and possessed of majestic virtue,
they are praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions and are well able to analyze and explain the teachings.
Not delighting in the company of crowds, always preferring meditative concentration,
they dwell in the lower void for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
Having heard this from the Buddha, we have no doubt regarding this matter.
I pray that for the sake of the future, the Buddha will expound this so that they may attain understanding.
If there are those who harbor doubts and do not believe in this sutra, they shall immediately fall into the evil realms; I pray that you will now explain it for them.
"How did these immeasurable bodhisattvas, in such a short time, become inspired to seek enlightenment and dwell on the stage of non-retrogression?
Chapter Fifteen: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata At that time, the Buddha addressed all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly:
“O sons of good family!
You should all have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
He then addressed the great assembly again:
“You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
He further addressed the great assembly:
“You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.”
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that you will speak of this; we shall faithfully accept the words of the Buddha."
Having made this request three times, they spoke again:
"We pray that you will explain it; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas would not cease their triple entreaty, addressed them, saying:
"Listen attentively!

Regarding the power of the Tathāgata’s secret supernatural faculties, all the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—believe that the present Śākyamuni Buddha has departed from the palace of the Śākyas, traveled not far from the city of Gayā, and is seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
However, good son!

It has actually been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas since I truly attained Buddhahood. Suppose there were five hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of trichiliocosms, and someone were to grind them into fine dust; then, passing beyond five hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of worlds to the east, he were to drop a single grain of that dust, and continue dropping one grain after another as he traveled eastward until all the dust was exhausted.
"Good sons! What do you think? Is it possible to conceive of, calculate, or know the number of these worlds?"
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These worlds are immeasurable and boundless; they cannot be known by calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind. All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even with their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), are unable to contemplate and know their limit.”
"We abide on the stage of *avaivartika*, yet we do not penetrate these matters either.
World-Honored One!
Such worlds are immeasurable and boundless."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas:
"Good sons! I shall now clearly declare to you:

if all the worlds—both those where atoms have been placed and those where they have not—were entirely reduced to dust, and each single atom represented one kalpa, the time since I attained Buddhahood would still exceed these hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

Since that time, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings, and I have also guided and benefited living beings in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya lands in other places.
"O sons of good family!
Within this interval, I have spoken of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others, and have further said that they entered parinirvāṇa; all such things were distinguished by me through skillful means."
"O sons of good family!

If there are sentient beings who come to me, I observe with my Buddha-eye whether their faculties, such as faith and the rest, are sharp or dull. According to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I manifest various names and different ages in various places; I also manifest the statement that I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, I preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, enabling sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy."
"O sons of good family!

When the Tathāgata sees that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings and possess meager virtue and heavy defilements, he speaks for their sake, saying: 'I left home at a young age and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Yet, in truth, it has been this long since I actually attained Buddhahood; I merely employ skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, leading them into the Buddha-way, and thus speak in such a manner."

"Good sons! All the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of liberating sentient beings. Whether he speaks of his own person or the persons of others, whether he manifests his own body or the bodies of others, or whether he reveals his own affairs or the affairs of others—all that he says is true and not false."

Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death, neither falling back nor emerging; there is no one remaining in the world, nor anyone who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different. Not as the triple world perceives it, does he perceive the triple world. Such matters the Tathāgata sees clearly and without error. Because sentient beings possess various natures, various desires, various conducts, and various thoughts and discriminations, he—wishing to cause them to produce roots of goodness—employs various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of speech to preach the Dharma in manifold ways, never for a moment ceasing his buddha-work.
"In this way, since I attained Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and I abide eternally without extinction.
'O sons of good family!'"

The lifespan I attained while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted; it is twice as long as the number mentioned above. Nevertheless, although this is not my actual parinirvāṇa, I now proclaim that I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata employs these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. Why is this?

If the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time, those of meager virtue would fail to plant roots of goodness; being poor, lowly, and base, they would become greedily attached to the five desires and fall into the net of discursive thoughts and false views. If they were to see that the Tathāgata always remains and never perishes, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence, and would be unable to conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter or develop a heart of reverence. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks by way of skillful means.
Bhikṣus, you should know!
The appearance of Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter. Why is this?
Those of little merit may, after the passing of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, sometimes see a Buddha and sometimes not; for this reason, I say to you, "O Bhikṣus!"
"The Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.

When these sentient beings hear such words, they will certainly conceive the thought that he is hard to meet; with hearts full of longing and yearning for the Buddha, they will then plant roots of goodness.
Therefore, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass away, he speaks of "extinction" (parinirvāṇa).
Furthermore, son of good family, such is the nature of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, all that they do is real and not false.

For example, suppose there is a skilled physician, wise and discerning, who is thoroughly proficient in prescriptions and medicines and adept at curing all manner of ailments. He has many sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or even a hundred—and on account of some business matter, he travels far away to another country. Later, his sons drink a potent poison; when the drug takes effect, they become dazed and delirious, writhing upon the ground.

At that time, their father returned home. Among the sons who had drunk the poison, some had lost their original minds while others had not; seeing their father from afar, they all rejoiced greatly, prostrating themselves and inquiring after his well-being:
"We have returned safely and in peace. We were foolish and mistakenly took this poisonous medicine; we pray you will rescue and heal us, and grant us our lives once more."

Seeing his sons suffering in this manner, the father sought out excellent medicinal herbs according to the methods of various scriptures—herbs that were fully endowed with color, fragrance, and fine flavor. He ground and sifted them, compounded them, and gave them to his sons to take, saying:

"This is a great and excellent medicine, fully endowed with color, fragrance, and fine flavor. You may take it; it will swiftly eliminate your suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have these many ailments."
Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds, seeing that this excellent medicine was both fine in color and fragrance, immediately took it and were completely cured of their illness;

as for the others who had lost their minds, although they rejoiced upon seeing their father arrive, greeted him, and sought treatment for their disease, when he gave them the medicine, they refused to take it.
Why is this? Because the poisonous vapor has penetrated deeply and caused him to lose his original mind, he finds even these fine colors and fragrant medicines to be unpleasant.
The father then had this thought:

"This child is pitiable; his heart has been pierced by poison and his mind is completely inverted. Although he sees me and joyfully seeks treatment, he is unwilling to take such excellent medicine as this. I must now employ skillful means to cause him to take this medicine."
He then spoke these words:
"You should know! I am now old and infirm, and the time of my death has arrived. This excellent medicine remains here; you may take it and drink it, and do not worry that you will not be cured."
Having given these instructions, he went to another country and sent a messenger back with the news: "Your father has died.
At that time, when the sons heard that their father had passed away, they were filled with great grief and distress, and they thought to themselves:
"If our father were still alive, he would have compassion for us and been able to protect us; now he has abandoned us and died far away in another land."

Reflecting that he was now orphaned and exposed with no one left to rely upon, he was constantly filled with sorrow and his mind finally awakened; he then realized that this medicine was beautiful in color, flavor, and fragrance, so he immediately took it and his poisonous illness was completely cured.
When the father heard that his son had fully recovered, he returned at once so that they might all see him.
"Good sons! What do you think?
Is there anyone who could say that this skilled physician has committed a falsehood?"
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said: "I am also like this.

Although it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas since I attained Buddhahood, for the sake of sentient beings, I have used the power of skillful means to say that I shall enter parinirvāṇa; yet there is no one who can truly find fault in me by saying my words are false."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, The number of kalpas that have passed Is immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads, Billions of asaṃkhyeya aeons."
Constantly preaching the Dharma to transform and teach countless billions of sentient beings,
causing them to enter the Buddha-way; since that time, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, you have skillfully manifested nirvana.
Yet in truth I do not enter parinirvāṇa, but dwell eternally here preaching the Dharma.
I dwell perpetually here, and by means of various supernormal powers,
cause deluded sentient beings to fail to see me even though they are near.
When the multitude sees my parinirvāṇa, they extensively make offerings to my relics;
all harbor longing and admiration, giving rise to hearts of thirsty aspiration.
Once sentient beings have been brought to faith and submission, their natures become upright and their minds supple.
Single-mindedly desiring to see the Buddha, they did not spare their own bodies or lives.
At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
I then spoke to the sentient beings, saying: "I am always here and do not perish."
By the power of skillful means, I manifest both extinction and non-extinction;
in other lands where there are sentient beings who revere, believe,
and delight [in the Dharma], I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma among them.
"You have not heard this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
Seeing all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction,
I do not manifest my body before them, so as to cause them to give rise to longing and yearning."
Because his heart was filled with longing and devotion, he then came forth to preach the Dharma for him.
Such is the power of his supernormal faculties that, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
he has always remained on Vulture Peak Mountain as well as in other various dwelling places.
When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, when all is consumed by the great fire,
my land remains peaceful and secure, ever filled with devas and humans;
its gardens, groves, and various halls and pavilions are adorned with every kind of jewel.
The jeweled trees abound with flowers and fruit, where sentient beings roam and delight;
the devas beat celestial drums and constantly perform various musical arts,
raining down māndārava flowers which they scatter upon the Buddha and the great assembly.
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as utterly consumed by fire;
they are filled with such pervasive grief, fear, and suffering.
These sentient beings of sinful karma, due to the conditions of their evil deeds, [perceive this].
After incalculable kalpas have passed, those who have not heard the names of the Triple Gem—
yet who cultivate merit and are gentle, mild, and upright—
all shall behold my body here, preaching the Dharma.
At times, for the sake of this assembly, I speak of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan;
to those who see the Buddha only after a long time, I speak of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Such is the power of my wisdom, and the light of my insight shines immeasurably.
A lifespan of countless eons, attained through long-cultivated practice—
O wise ones among you, do not harbor doubts regarding this;
you should sever them so they are forever exhausted, for the Buddha’s word is true and not false.
Just as a skilled physician, for the sake of treating a mad son,
speaks of death when he is actually alive— yet no one can say this is a falsehood;
so too am I the Father of the World, rescuing all who suffer from their ailments.
For the sake of ordinary people who are deluded by inversion, though it truly exists, I speak of its cessation.
Because they constantly perceive a self, they give rise to a mind of arrogance and license;
being heedless and attached to the five desires, they fall into the evil realms.
I always know sentient beings—those who practice the Path and those who do not—and according to how each may be delivered, I preach various teachings for them.
I constantly reflect upon this: by what means can I cause sentient beings...
"May they enter the Unsurpassed Way and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body? Chapter Sixteen:

Distinguishing Merit The Added Chapter on the Lotus Sutra, Chapter Sixteen: Distinguishing Merit At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan and the vast duration of kalpas in this manner; immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings attained great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"Ajita! When I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
Furthermore, there were a thousand times as many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining;
again, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system who attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech;
and again, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system who attained the immeasurable revolving dhāraṇī of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm who were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two thousand medium-sized lands who were able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma;
furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm who would attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after eight births.
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in four sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment after four births;
furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in three sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment after three births;
furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment after two births.
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in one four-continent world-system, who were destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single lifetime;
and there were sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms in eight world-systems, all of whom resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha spoke these words concerning how these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained the great benefit of the Dharma, mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down from the sky, scattering over the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of jewel trees, as well as over Śākyamuni Buddha seated upon the lion throne within the stūpa made of the seven jewels, and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who had long since entered parinirvāṇa; they also scattered over all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, fine powdered sandalwood and aloeswood incense rained down, and celestial drums spontaneously resounded in the sky with profound and wondrous sounds.

Furthermore, a rain of a thousand kinds of celestial garments fell, with various necklaces—pearl necklaces, maṇi-jewel necklaces, and wish-fulfilling jewel necklaces—hanging down, pervading the nine directions. Countless precious incense burners burned priceless incense, which spontaneously reached every seat in the great assembly to make offerings to each of the Buddhas.
There were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies that rose in succession up to the Brahma Heaven; these bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha has preached a rare Dharma, Never heard before;
The World-Honored One possesses great power, And his lifespan is immeasurable.”
Countless sons of the Buddhas, having heard the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition on those who have attained the benefit of the Dharma, were filled with joy throughout their bodies;
some dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, while others attained dhāraṇīs.
Some possess unimpeded eloquence and the dhāraṇī of ten billion revolutions;
others, as numerous as the atoms within a great trichiliocosm,
each and every one are able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm,
each of whom is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
Moreover, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm.
The others each have eight births remaining before they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there are those with four, three, or two;
as many as there are atoms in these four continents, so many bodhisattvas will attain Buddhahood according to their respective numbers of births.
Or in a single four-continent world-system, there may be bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust,
who have but one birth remaining before they shall attain all-knowledge.
When such beings hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is so exceedingly long, [they rejoice].
They attain immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure karmic fruition. Furthermore,
sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within eight worlds,
upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on his lifespan, all resolve to attain the Unsurpassed Mind.
The World-Honored One has preached immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas,
bringing great benefit to many; like the boundlessness of space,
he rains down mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers.
Śakras and Brahmās, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, come from countless Buddha-lands;
they rain down sandalwood and aloeswood, falling in profusion and disorder like birds swooping down from the sky, scattering as offerings before all the Buddhas.
In the midst of the void, celestial drums spontaneously produce wondrous sounds;
ten million kinds of heavenly garments swirl down from above.
Miraculous incense burners made of various jewels burn priceless incense.
Spontaneously pervading everywhere, they make offerings to all the World-Honored Ones.
The great assembly of Bodhisattvas holds banners and canopies of the seven treasures,
of ten trillion exquisite and sublime varieties, which extend in succession as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha, jeweled banners hang with excellent pennants;
likewise, with ten million verses, they sing praises of all the Tathāgatas.
Such various matters as these have never before occurred.
Hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, all are filled with joy.
The Buddha’s name is renowned throughout the ten directions;
he extensively benefits sentient beings, so that all may possess roots of goodness to assist their unsurpassed resolve.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

“Ajita! If there are sentient beings who, hearing that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding, the merit they obtain will be without limit.”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practice the five *pāramitās*—the *dāna-pāramitā*, the *śīla-pāramitā*, the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, the *vīrya-pāramitā*, and the *dhyāna-pāramitā*—for eighty million *nayuta* *kalpas*, excluding the *prajñā-pāramitā*, these merits compared to the former merits do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part; they are beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
"If a son of good family possesses such merit as this, it is impossible for him to fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, For eighty million billion [eons]..."
For *nayuta* eons, one practices the five *pāramitās*;
throughout these eons, one gives alms and makes offerings to the Buddhas,
as well as to the *pratyekabuddhas* and their disciples, and to the assembly of all bodhisattvas.
Rare and exquisite foods and drinks, superior garments and bedding,
sandalwood monasteries, and gardens for adornment—
such acts of giving as these were all of the most subtle and wondrous kind.
Exhausting the number of these kalpas, one dedicates them toward the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, if one upholds the prohibitive precepts, pure and without flaw or leakage,
seeking the unsurpassed way, this is what all Buddhas praise.
If one further practices patience and abides in the stage of gentleness,
even when various evils are inflicted upon them, their mind remains unshaken;
yet those who have attained some dharma may harbor overweening pride.
For this reason, even when slighted or provoked by others, one is able to endure it thus. Furthermore,
if one applies diligent vigor, with a will and mindfulness always firm and steadfast,
for immeasurable billions of eons, one remains single-mindedly without indolence.
Furthermore, throughout incalculable eons, dwelling in secluded places,
whether sitting or walking, he removed sleep and constantly restrained his mind;
by these causes and conditions, he was able to give rise to all meditative concentrations.
For eighty billion koṭis of kalpas, may I abide with a mind undisturbed.
By the merit of this single-mindedness, I vow to seek the unsurpassed path;
may I attain all-knowledge and exhaust the limits of all meditative concentrations.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout hundreds of thousands, ten millions, and billions of kalpas,
practice these various meritorious deeds as described above,
and hear me speak of this lifespan, they shall attain it.
Even a single thought of faith brings merit exceeding that;
if a person is entirely free from all doubts and regrets,
and with a profound heart believes for even a moment, their merit shall be just like this.
Those bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas,
upon hearing me speak of this lifespan, will be able to believe and accept it;
such persons as these shall receive this sutra upon the crown of their heads.
May I, in the future, live long to deliver sentient beings,
Just as the World-Honored One today, the King among the Śākyas,
Roars the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment, Preaching the Dharma with utter fearlessness.
In future ages, when we sit at the site of enlightenment as objects of universal veneration,
our lifespan shall be proclaimed in this same way.
Should there be those with profound resolve, pure and upright in nature, [they shall likewise hear it].
Those who have heard much and are able to maintain it in memory,
who understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning— such persons as these have no doubt regarding this. Furthermore, Ajita!

If there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words, the merit they obtain will be without limit; they will be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata. How much more so for those who extensively hear this sutra, or cause others to hear it, or uphold it themselves, or teach others to uphold it, or write it themselves, or teach others to write it, or offer to the sutra scrolls flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, pennants, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps—the merit of such persons will be immeasurable and boundless, and they will be able to generate the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Ajita! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing me speak of the long duration of my lifespan, should believe and understand it with a profound mind, they will see the Buddha constantly on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma;

and they will also see this Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli, level and even, with the eight paths demarcated by Jāmbūnada gold, rows of jewel trees, and all the terraces and towers made entirely of jewels, wherein the assembly of bodhisattvas all dwell. If there are those who can contemplate in this way, you should know that this is the mark of deep faith and understanding.

Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, you should know that this already constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding; how much more so for those who read, recite, receive, and uphold it—such persons shall be as if they were bearing the Tathāgata upon their heads.
Ajita! These sons and daughters of good family need not further erect stūpas and temples or construct monasteries for my sake, nor provide the four requisites as offerings to the Saṃgha.

Why is this? Because those good men and good women who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra have already erected stupas and constructed monasteries to provide for the Sangha; they have thereby raised stupas of the seven treasures from the Buddha’s relics, vast and high, tapering gradually until reaching the Brahma Heaven, adorned with hanging banners, canopies, and various jeweled bells, and having offered flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and burning incense, along with various drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and all manner of dances and performances, chanting and praising with wondrous voices—they have already performed such offerings throughout immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

“Ajita! If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who hear this sutra and are able to receive and uphold it—whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it—they shall be as if they have erected monasteries, constructing thirty-two halls of red sandalwood, each eight *tāla* trees in height, lofty, spacious, and magnificent. Within them shall dwell hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, and these monasteries shall be filled with gardens, groves, bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves; with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—all such articles of pleasure shall abound therein. Such monasteries, halls, and pavilions, numbering in the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions, shall be immeasurable in their quantity; by this, they will offer present worship to me and the community of bhikṣus.”

Therefore, I say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain it to others; or who write it themselves, or teach others to write it; or who make offerings to the scripture—such persons need not further erect stupas or temples, nor build monasteries to provide for the Sangha. How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; their merit shall be most supreme, immeasurable, and boundless.

Just as space is immeasurable and boundless to the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, so too are this person’s merits immeasurable and boundless; they will swiftly reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If a person reads and recites, receives and upholds this sutra, and explains it for others; or if they write it themselves or instruct others to write it; and furthermore, if they can erect stupas and build monasteries, making offerings to and praising the assembly of *śrāvaka* monks; and also praise the merits of the bodhisattvas with hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of methods of praise;

and further, for the sake of others, explain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through various causes and conditions according to its meaning; and moreover, if they can maintain the precepts purely, dwell together with those who are gentle, practice patience without anger, possess firm resolve and mindfulness, always value sitting in meditation to attain profound concentrations, be diligent and courageous, gather all wholesome dharmas, possess sharp faculties and wisdom, and skillfully answer difficult questions—[they shall attain such merit].

Ajita! If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and who further possess such virtuous merits as these, you should know that these people have already proceeded toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and are seated beneath the tree of enlightenment.
Ajita! Wherever this son of good family sits, stands, or walks, a stūpa should be erected there; all devas and humans should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses: "If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to uphold this sutra,
the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable, just as has been described above."
This constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings:
by erecting a stupa for the śarīra, adorned with the seven treasures,
its pinnacle exceedingly high and broad, tapering gradually until it reaches the Brahma-heaven.
Thousands of millions of precious bells, stirred by the wind, produce wondrous sounds. Furthermore,
throughout immeasurable kalpas, one makes offerings to this stupa with flowers,
incense, various necklaces, celestial robes, and manifold music.
Yet with fragrant oil and ghee lamps, constantly illuminating all around;
in this evil age, at the end of the Dharma, those who can uphold this sutra have already performed the aforementioned offerings in their entirety.
If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present in person.
One might construct a monastic residence out of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood for offerings,
with thirty-two halls, each eight tāla trees in height.
Exquisite food and fine garments, beds and couches all provided in abundance;
dwellings for hundreds of thousands of beings, gardens, groves, and various flowing ponds;
walking paths and meditation caves—all of these were adorned with every kind of excellence.
If there are those with a mind of faith and understanding who receive, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe [this sutra],
or further teach others to transcribe it, and make offerings to the scripture scrolls by scattering flowers,
incense, and powdered incense, such as sumana and campaka;
With *ati-muktaka* flowers and scented oil, one should constantly maintain the lamps;
those who make such offerings shall attain immeasurable merit,
as boundless as space, and their blessings shall be likewise.
How much more so for one who upholds this sutra, while also practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts,
delighting in patience and meditative concentration, being free from anger and harsh speech;
who shows reverence to stupas and temples, and treats all bhikṣus with humility.
Far removed from the mind of self-exaltation, One constantly contemplates wisdom;
When questioned or challenged, one does not become angry, But explains according to the truth.
If one can practice such conduct, The merit shall be immeasurable.
If one sees this Dharma-master who has accomplished such virtues,
one should scatter celestial flowers upon him, cover his body with celestial robes,
bow with the head touching his feet, and give rise to the thought of regarding him as a Buddha.
Furthermore, one should reflect thus: "Before long I shall go to the Tree of Enlightenment and attain the untainted and unconditioned state; there I shall extensively benefit all humans and devas.
Whether staying, walking, or sitting or lying down,"
Even if one were to recite but a single verse, a stūpa should be erected for this,
adorned to be most exquisite and provided with all manner of offerings;
when a Son of the Buddha dwells on this stage, it is then the very enjoyment of the Buddhas.
Always remaining therein, Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
*The Added-Chapter Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma*, Scroll Five;
*The Added-Chapter Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Sui Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta together with Gupta.
Chapter Seventeen: The Merit of Rejoicing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?”
And he spoke in verse:
“After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and can rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

“Ajita! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, as well as other wise persons—whether old or young—who, having heard this sutra and rejoiced in it, depart from the Dharma assembly for another place; whether they be in a monastery, in a secluded spot, or in a city, a street, a village, or a field—and according to what they have heard, expound it to their parents, kinsmen, good friends, and acquaintances to the best of their ability; and these people, having heard it, rejoice and in turn teach others, and those others, having heard it, likewise rejoice and teach others, continuing in this manner until the fiftieth person.”
Ajita! I shall now describe the merit of rejoicing belonging to that fiftieth son or daughter of good family; you should listen well.
If there were sentient beings in four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth:
those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether they have form or are formless, possess perception or are without perception, or are neither with nor without perception; whether they have no feet, two feet, or four feet—
As for those with many feet and others such as these who are counted among the class of sentient beings,
if there is someone seeking merit who provides them with whatever articles of entertainment they desire, giving to each and every sentient being gold,
silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and all [other treasures] sufficient to fill Jambudvīpa—
Exquisite treasures, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems—
the Great Donor gave such gifts for a full eighty years, after which he thought to himself:
"I have already provided these sentient beings with all manner of objects for their enjoyment, according to their every desire.
Yet these beings are all aged and decrepit, over eighty years of age, with white hair and wrinkled faces; death will soon come for them. I shall now instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma."

He immediately gathered these sentient beings and proclaimed the transformative teaching of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; at once, they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, exhausting all outflows (āsrava), attaining mastery in profound meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi), and being endowed with the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa).
"What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by this great donor not indeed vast?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The merit of this person is exceedingly great, immeasurable and boundless;
if such a donor were merely to bestow all instruments of happiness upon sentient beings, their merit would be immeasurable—how much more so if they cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship!”
The Buddha told Maitreya:

“I now speak to you clearly: if a person were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon the sentient beings of the six realms across four million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, and further cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship, the merit thereby obtained would not equal the merit of this fiftieth person who rejoices upon hearing a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. A hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionth part of the latter’s merit does not approach the former; it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.”

Ajita! Thus, the merit of even the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in succession and rejoices is already immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*); how much more so for those who first hear it within the assembly and rejoice—their merit is even more supreme, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, beyond all comparison.
Furthermore, Ajita!

If a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery and listens to it for even a brief moment—whether sitting or standing—by virtue of this merit, in their next rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephants, horses, carriages, precious palanquins, and celestial palaces.

Furthermore, if there is someone who sits at a place where the Dharma is being preached, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen, or offers them half of their seat to sit upon, by virtue of this person's merit, in their next rebirth they will obtain the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā, or the seat of a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Ajita!

Furthermore, if there is someone who says to another person, "There is a sutra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; let us go together to hear it," and that person follows this instruction and hears it for even a brief moment, the merit of this person will be such that, upon changing bodies, they will be born in the same place as Bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs. They will have sharp faculties and wisdom; for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall never be mute or speech-impaired; their breath shall not be foul; their tongue shall always be free from disease, as shall their mouth; their teeth shall not be stained or black, nor yellow, nor sparse, nor missing, nor crooked, nor curved; their lips shall not hang down, nor be drawn back, nor be coarse or rough, nor have sores or calluses, nor be defective, nor be distorted, nor be thick or large, nor be dark or black; they shall be free from all things loathsome.
The nose is neither bulbous nor crooked;
the facial complexion is neither dark nor narrow and long, nor is it sunken or distorted, for there is not a single unpleasing feature.

The lips, tongue, and teeth are all perfectly beautiful; the nose is long, high, and straight; the countenance is full and round; the eyebrows are high and long; the forehead is broad and level—thus he is endowed with the marks of a superior person. In every lifetime where he is born, he sees the Buddhas, hears the Dharma, and faithfully accepts their instructions.
Ajita! Observe this:

if one merely exhorts a single person to go and listen to the Dharma, the merit is such as this; how much more so for one who listens with a single mind, recites it, and, within the great assembly, analyzes it for others and practices according to what has been taught?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses: "If a person, at a Dharma assembly, Hears this sutra,
even as much as a single verse, And with sympathetic joy explains it to others;”
Thus, through successive transmission, reaching the fiftieth person,
the merit obtained by that final individual shall now be analyzed.
Suppose there were a great donor who provided for an immeasurable multitude.
Having reached a full eighty years, one follows the desires of the heart;
yet seeing those signs of decay— the white hair and wrinkled face,
the gaps between the teeth and the withered form— one reflects that death will not be long in coming.
I should now instruct them so that they may attain the fruits of the Path;
thus, as an expedient means, I shall preach the true Dharma of Nirvana.
All worlds are not solid, being like foam, bubbles, or flames.
"You all should likewise quickly give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Upon hearing this Dharma, all people attained arhatship,
becoming fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three insights, and the eight liberations."
Finally, the fiftieth person hears a single verse and rejoices;
the merit of this person surpasses that of the former, beyond all comparison.
Thus, through successive transmission, even the merit of the last person remains immeasurable.
How much more so for those at the Dharma assembly who hear it for the first time and rejoice;
if one encourages even a single person to go and listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
saying, "This sutra is profound and subtle, difficult to encounter in ten million kalpas."
He immediately received the instruction and went to listen;
even hearing it for but a moment, the karmic reward of such a person shall now be explained in detail:
in every lifetime he will have no afflictions of the mouth, and his teeth will not be spaced, nor yellow, nor black.
The lips are neither thick nor upturned, nor are they deficient; there is no feature that could be deemed loathsome.
The tongue is neither dry, black, nor short; the nose is high, long, and straight.
The forehead is broad and level; the face and eyes are entirely dignified and handsome.
They will be pleasing to behold by others; their breath shall be free from foul odors, and the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus shall constantly issue from their mouths.
If they intentionally go to a monastic dwelling wishing to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [they shall attain these qualities].
Having heard this for a brief moment with joy, I shall now describe its merit:
in future lives among gods and humans, one will obtain exquisite elephants,
horses, and chariots, as well as precious palanquins and celestial palaces to ride upon.
If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras,
through the causal conditions of this merit, one shall obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin King;
how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus and explains its underlying meaning and intent!
"Practicing according to what has been taught, one’s merit shall be beyond measure.

Chapter 18: The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher *The Added Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Preacher from the Lotus Sutra* At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Diligent:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this *Lotus Sutra*, that person shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye, twelve hundred merits of the ear, eight hundred merits of the nose, twelve hundred merits of the tongue, eight hundred merits of the body, and twelve hundred merits of the mind. Adorned with these merits, their six sense organs shall all be rendered pure."

These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents, see all the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas within and without the trichiliocosm; from below as far as the Avīci Hell, up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), they also see all sentient beings therein, as well as their karmic causes and conditions, their retributions, and their places of birth—all they see and all they know.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: “If,
in the midst of a great assembly, With a mind free from fear,
one preaches this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Listen now to its merits.”
This person attains eight hundred eyes of supreme merit;
because they are thus adorned, their vision is exceedingly pure.
With the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the three thousandfold world system.
The inner and outer Mālu Mountains, Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains,
along with all other mountain ranges and forests, the great oceans, rivers, and streams,
reaching down to the Avīci Hell and up to the Peak of Existence—
Within it, all sentient beings are seen by everyone;
though they have not yet attained the divine eye, the power of their physical eyes is such as this.
"Furthermore, Constantly Diligent One!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they shall attain twelve hundred merits of the ear. With these purified ears,
they shall hear throughout the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below to the Summit of Existence above.
Among these, there were all manner of internal and external languages and sounds:
the sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots; the sounds of weeping and lamentation;
the sounds of conchs, drums, bells, and gongs; the sounds of laughter and speech; and the voices of men and women.
The voices of boys and the voices of girls; the voice of the Dharma and the voice of non-Dharma;
the voice of suffering and the voice of pleasure; the voices of ordinary persons and the voices of noble ones;
the voice of joy and the voice of displeasure; the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and garuḍas.
...the voices of kinnaras, the voices of mahoragas, the sounds of fire, the sounds of water, the sounds of wind, the sounds of hell-beings,
the sounds of animals, the sounds of hungry ghosts, the voices of bhikṣus, the voices of bhikṣuṇīs,
the voices of śrāvakas, the voices of pratyekabuddhas, the voices of bodhisattvas, and the voices of Buddhas— in short, [all these].

To speak of it: within this trichiliocosm, all sounds—whether internal or external—that exist, he hears and knows them all with the pure, ordinary ear born of his parents, even though he has not yet attained the divine ear;
thus he discriminates among these various sounds without impairing his faculty of hearing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The ears born of one's parents are pure and free from turbidity;
with these constant ears, one hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world-system."
The sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums;
the sounds of zithers, lutes, and harps; the sounds of flutes and pipes;
and the sounds of pure, beautiful songs—he hears them yet remains unattached.
The sounds of countless varieties of people, he hears and understands them all;
He also hears the voices of the devas, their subtle and wondrous songs;
And he hears the voices of men and women, as well as the voices of boys and girls.
Within the treacherous mountains, rivers, and deep valleys, the cries of the kalaviṅka, the jīvañjīvaka,
and all other such birds are heard; likewise, the manifold sounds of agonizing torment and the various sufferings of the hells are heard.
The hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, utter cries as they search for food and drink;
the various asuras, dwelling on the shores of the great ocean,
produce great sounds when conversing among themselves.
A speaker of the Dharma who dwells securely in this world hears these various sounds from afar without their harming the faculty of hearing;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they hear the calls of birds and beasts as they cry out to one another.
The person who preaches the Dharma hears all of this here.
As for the various Brahma heavens— the Ābhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna,
and even up to the Bhavāgra— hears the sounds of their speech.
The Dharma Master, dwelling here, hears them all.
All the assemblies of bhikṣus, as well as the bhikṣuṇīs—
whether they are reading and reciting the scriptures or expounding them for others— [he hears].
The Dharma Master abides here, and all shall hear him.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who read and recite the sutras and teachings,
or explain them for others, or compile and interpret their meanings.
All such sounds and voices, he hears them all.
The Great Holy Sages, the Buddhas who transform sentient beings,
amidst great assemblies, expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shall hear them all:
every sound within and without the trichiliocosm,
from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above.
They all hear those sounds, yet their faculty of hearing remains unimpaired;
because their ears are keen and sharp, they are able to discern and know them all.
Those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra, though they have not yet attained the divine ear, [are thus enabled].
It merely uses the ear that has been produced; such are its merits.
"Furthermore, Constantly Diligent!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, or recites this sutra..."
Whether explaining it or writing it down, one accomplishes eight hundred merits of the nose;
with this purified faculty of the nose, one perceives the various fragrances— superior, inferior, internal, and external—
within the trichiliocosm, such as the fragrance of *sumanā* flowers, *jāti* flowers, and *mallikā* flowers.
